Lesson 1 – Life as an Astronaut 
An astronaut is a person who goes up into space on a shuttle. 
Some astronauts work on the International Space Station.  
Write a few sentences about what you imagine an astronaut’s 
life is like – how is life in space different from life on earth? 
What do you think astronauts do with their time? 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Activity 1 – Pre-Learn Vocabulary 
claustrophobia (n.) = fear of small, limited spaces. “Claustrophobia” describes the 
condition, and “claustrophobic” (adj.) describes a person who feels scared and 
uncomfortable in small spaces 
 
Ex) My sister doesn’t like to ride elevators because she’s claustrophobic. 
bulky (adj.) = large and inconvenient, something that takes up too much space 
Ex) In the past, cell phones were so bulky that they couldn’t fit in your pocket 
easily. 
disembark (v.) = get off of a ship, plane, or train 
 
Ex) After three days at sea, the passengers disembarked from the cruise ship. 
dehydrated (adj.) = without water (for example, food after being dried out and 
the water removed) 
Ex) Dehydrated foods can last for many months without needing to be 
refrigerated. 
sip (v.) = to drink something slowly, in small portions. 


Ex) He sipped a glass of wine as he relaxed after work. 
germs (n.) = bacteria, tiny organisms that make you sick 
 
Ex) You should cover your mouth when you sneeze, to avoid spreading germs. 
conundrums (n.) = complex problems or difficulties 
Ex) The issue of illegal immigration is a real conundrum; politicians have 
tried to solve it for years without success. 
filter (v.) = make something (like air or water) pure and clean by removing dirt 
and contaminants 
 
Ex) The water here is of poor quality; you must filter it before drinking. 
onboard (adj.) = on a ship, plane, or train 
 
Ex) All airplanes must have an onboard first aid kit. 
susceptible (adj.) = vulnerable, unprotected (especially against disease – if you 
are “susceptible” to a disease, you are likely to become sick) 
 
Ex) If not properly cleaned and covered, cuts are susceptible to infection. 
treadmill (n.) = a type of exercise machine where you walk/run on a moving belt 
 
Ex) It was raining, so I stayed inside and ran ten miles on the treadmill. 
 
Activity 2 – Listen for General Ideas 
Speaker: Amanda – British  
This audio discusses various aspects of life as an 
astronaut. Put the topics in the correct order from 1 to 7: 
• Fitness

• Waste 
• Food 


Activity 3 – Listen for Specific Details

2. The improvement in space food comes from…

b. Increasing the nutritional value of astronauts’ food 
c. Giving the astronauts training from famous chefs 
 
3. Which of these things is NOT used when astronauts shower? 
a. A plastic sleeve 
b. A vacuum 
c. Disinfectant 
 
4. What is done with liquid waste on the space station? 
a. It is cleaned and purified 
b. It is kept until landing 
c. It is released into space 
 
5. Astronauts exercise a lot because… 
a. Their work requires a lot of strength 
b. If they don’t, they could lose bone density 
c. They have lots of free time 
 
6. One of the recent projects on the space station is… 
a. Observing and documenting changes on Earth over time 
b. Developing vehicles for transporting humans through space 
c. Testing the effect of solar radiation on newly-developed materials 
 
7. Do astronauts have internet? 
a. Yes, all the time 
b. Yes, 3 times a day 
c. No, only radio

Activity 5 – Listen with Complete Transcript 
As an astronaut in a NASA space shuttle, it would be particularly unfortunate if 
you suffered from claustrophobia. A typical shuttle is occupied by a crew of seven, 
and inside the space shuttle the space is equivalent to a smallish tent on a camping 
expedition, only filled with seven astronauts wearing bulky suits! Obviously, a 
claustrophobic astronaut would relish the opportunity to disembark onto the 
slightly less cramped International Space Station.  
Food-wise, an astronaut’s lot has improved considerably from times gone by, 
although dehydrated food is still used on space flights. The military innovation of 
MREs (Meals Ready To Eat), which are not dehydrated, from the late 1960s to the 
1980s led to many improvements in the diet of the astronaut, and today’s space 
food still owes much to this innovation.  
The International Space Station has even boasted chefs from top Parisian 
restaurants providing food for the astronauts. Each space suit is fitted with an In-
suit Drink Bag providing 32 fluid ounces of water, which can be sipped from a 
straw, built into the suit for long periods of suit-wear. 
It is incredibly important to maintain good personal hygiene in the space station 
or on a space flight as germs can multiply faster in space. Low gravity poses 
obvious conundrums where water-based activities are concerned!  To maintain 
cleanliness, shuttle astronauts treasure their personal hygiene kit – a set that 
includes toothpaste, a toothbrush, dental floss, a razor and a comb.  
Showers are taken inside a large specially-designed cylinder with a plastic sleeve 
to prohibit the escape of water into the air. The astronauts must essentially 
vacuum the water off their skin before exiting the cylinder – and for those who 
savor a nice hair wash; the practice is reduced to application of a rinseless 
shampoo!  
The practice of waste disposal from space toilets must also consider the low-
gravity environment. Onboard lavatories flush with air instead of water. The air 
in the toilet is filtered to remove bacteria and odors and is then returned to the 
living quarters. The solid waste matter must be kept onboard until landing, while 
liquid wastes are sent out into space.  
In case an astronaut must go out ‘space-walking’ in their suit for long periods, 
their suit is fitted with an adult absorbent diaper known as a Maximum Absorption 
Garment to trap and collect both urine and feces. The garment can be 
disconnected and disposed of once the spacewalk is over. 


A fitness regime is of paramount importance to astronauts in space. On top of the 
usual reasons for keeping in shape, being in space makes them susceptible to a 
condition similar to osteoporosis. Researchers found that after months in a 
weightless environment, astronauts suffer a significant loss of bone mineral 
density – so a large amount of an astronaut’s routine (at least 2 ½ hours a day) is 
dedicated to keeping fit. On the International Space Station, there is a specially 
designed treadmill and exercise bike to help astronauts fight against bone 
degeneration and maintain normal health. 
Obviously, the main reason for astronauts being up there on the ISS is for the 
advancement of science and to carry out a variety of experiments. Some examples 
of projects that have been undertaken by Expedition 10 (which arrived at the 
station in October of 2004) are: 
• 
Observing and photographing natural and manmade changes on Earth over 
time as well as short timescale events like storms so we can better 
understand our planet 
• 
Studying how humans behave in isolation and confinement 
• 
Leaving potential future spacecraft equipment outside to see how well it 
withstands being in space  
• 
Studying fluids that react to magnetic fields, in order to aid in the 
construction of better brake systems, seat suspensions, and airplane 
landing gear  
Of course, as in most jobs, astronauts are allowed some free time! Like most of us 
these days this revolves around the internet, which they use to call their families 
and check their e-mail. Unlike us, and probably a great source of frustration, their 
email and internet connection is only updated 3 times a day.

"Leaving potential future spacecraft equipment outside to see how well it 
withstands being in space" 
withstand (v.) = to resist or endure

4. Waste

6. Work 
7. Free time

Lesson 2 –  
Playing Musical Instruments 
Warm-up:  
A) How many musical instruments can you think of 
in English? Write their names here: 
 
 
 
B) Have you ever learned to play a musical 
instrument? How was the experience?  
Or, if not: which instrument would you like to learn and why? 
 
 
 
Activity 1 – Pre-Learn Vocabulary 
reed (n.) = a small strip located in the mouthpiece of certain musical instruments, 
which vibrates with the flow of air and helps make the sound. 
 


marching band (n.) = a group of people playing musical instruments (“band”) that 
plays music together while walking in unison (“marching”). Marching bands often 
perform in parades and sometimes sports games. 
 
pit band (n.) = Also called a “pit orchestra” – a band that plays music to accompany 
dance or theater performances. The musicians sit in a low area (“pit”) in front of the 
stage. 
 
neat (adj.) = The word “neat” can mean something is well-organized (the opposite 
of “messy”). However, in this audio it is used to mean “good” or “interesting.”  
 
Ex) My son has a really neat idea for a new website. 
run into = This phrasal verb is used in two different ways in the audio. One is to 
“meet someone by chance” and the other is to “encounter” problems/difficulties. 
 
Ex) At the mall, I ran into a friend from college who I hadn’t seen in years! 
Ex) I tried to translate this document from French to English, but I ran into 
trouble with a couple of the more technical terms; I’m not sure what they mean. 


on the spot (idiom) = to do something spontaneously at that moment, without 
previous planning 
Ex) At the last minute, my co-worker said he couldn’t go to the meeting and 
asked if I could fill in for him – so I had to give his presentation on the spot. 
chord (n.) = in music, a combination of 2 or 
more notes played together at the same time: 
 
 
Activity 2 – Listen for the General Idea 
Speaker: Peter – American 
Peter mentions several different instruments in the 
beginning, but then he focuses on two in particular. What 
are the TWO instruments that he mainly talks about? 
    
  
 
           
  
  
 
clarinet 
 
 
recorder 
 
 
guitar 
   
 
 
 
bass guitar  
 
 
piano  
 
 
 
trumpet 


Activity 3 – Listen for Specific Details 
1. Peter started playing trumpet in the... 
a. 6th grade 
b. 8th grade 
c. 12th grade 
2. One of the hardest things about playing the trumpet is... 
a. controlling the volume of the sound 
b. playing clear, distinct notes 
c. the correct position of your lips 
3. Peter favorite part of playing trumpet was... 
a. performing a solo on national TV 
b. playing in groups 
c. teaching a friend how to play 
4. Which of these hard things about playing guitar is NOT mentioned? 
a. developing the muscle memory of your hands 
b. getting tired after playing for some time 
c. memorizing all the different chords 
5. What's one thing he really loves about guitar? 
a. Being able to sing and play songs he hears on the radio 
b. Composing new music with friends 
c. Taking his guitar along while traveling 
 
 
 
 


Activity 4 – Listen for Specific Words 
Hi, my name is Peter, and I wanted to _____________________ you about some of the 
musical instruments that I have played. I have played the clarinet, the recorder, the 
guitar, the bass guitar, the piano, and the instrument I’ve played the 
_____________________ is the trumpet. I started playing trumpet in sixth grade, and 
played all the way through twelfth grade on a regular _____________________. 
One of the hardest things about learning to play trumpet is how to position your 
lips. With a clarinet you have a reed, and with a guitar you have a 
_____________________, to make the sounds that you need. But with trumpet, you 
have to hold your lips in just the right way in order to make the proper sound. One 
of the _____________________ my teacher taught me was to say the letter “M” – once 
I say the letter “M,” then I have my lips in the proper position to play. 
The cool thing about playing trumpet is that it can play a wide 
_____________________ of music. I was able to be in the jazz band, the marching 
band, concert band, and pit band, because I knew how to play – and we had a lot of 
wonderful experiences.  
The really neat thing about playing an instrument like this is it’s 
_____________________ when you play in a group – and music has a way of bonding 
people. I made new friends, I made old friendships stronger, and it was a really neat 
experience to be able to perform for an _____________________. We performed for a 
wide variety of groups, and it’s – there’s something about music that really 
entertains people. 
Now I haven’t been playing my trumpet since high school, but I do play guitar. And 
one of the great things about guitar is that you will run into a lot more guitar players 
– and so there’s greater opportunity for _____________________, and just sitting 
down and having a good time on the spot. 
The hardest thing about playing guitar is teaching your hands to do what you want 
them to do. It’s all about muscle memory. You may know in your head what you 
wanna do, but you have to help your _____________________ learn where to go, 
playing chords, getting your fingers to move to the proper spots every time.  
The other difficult thing that you might run into is fatigue. After a while, your hands 
just get tired in the _____________________. But as you keep playing and building up 
your muscles, that won’t be a problem anymore.  


One of the things that I like most about guitar is that I can listen to a song on the

trumpet, I could either sing or play – but with my guitar I can do both. I enjoy 
playing for friends and family, with friends and family, and sometimes just 
_____________________ down and playing for myself.  
But if you get the chance to play a musical instrument, I _____________________ you 
take that opportunity. It really is a fun time. I’ve had so much fun throughout my life 
because of music – and it’s something that you just can’t _____________________ to 
anything else. So I hope you take the opportunity, and thanks for taking the time to 
listen. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Complete Transcript 
Hi, my name is Peter, and I wanted to tell you about some of the musical 
instruments that I have played. I have played the clarinet, the recorder, the guitar, 
the bass guitar, the piano, and the instrument I’ve played the most is the trumpet. I 
started playing trumpet in sixth grade, and played all the way through twelfth grade 
on a regular basis. 
One of the hardest things about learning to play trumpet is how to position your 
lips. With a clarinet you have a reed, and with a guitar you have a string, to make 
the sounds that you need. But with trumpet, you have to hold your lips in just the 
right way in order to make the proper sound. One of the tricks my teacher taught 
me was to say the letter “M” – once I say the letter “M,” then I have my lips in the 
proper position to play. 
The cool thing about playing trumpet is that it can play a wide variety of music. I 
was able to be in the jazz band, the marching band, concert band, and pit band, 
because I knew how to play – and we had a lot of wonderful experiences.  
The really neat thing about playing an instrument like this is it’s best when you play 
in a group – and music has a way of bonding people. I made new friends, I made old 
friendships stronger, and it was a really neat experience to be able to perform for an 
audience. We performed for a wide variety of groups, and it’s – there’s something 
about music that really entertains people. 
Now I haven’t been playing my trumpet since high school, but I do play guitar. And 
one of the great things about guitar is that you will run into a lot more guitar players 
– and so there’s greater opportunity for collaboration, and just sitting down and 
having a good time on the spot. 
The hardest thing about playing guitar is teaching your hands to do what you want 
them to do. It’s all about muscle memory. You may know in your head what you 
wanna do, but you have to help your fingers learn where to go, playing chords, 
getting your fingers to move to the proper spots every time.  
The other difficult thing that you might run into is fatigue. After a while, your hands 
just get tired in the beginning. But as you keep playing and building up your 
muscles, that won’t be a problem anymore.  
One of the things that I like most about guitar is that I can listen to a song on the 
radio, and learn how to play it – AND sing along with it. With my trumpet, I could 


either sing or play – but with my guitar I can do both. I enjoy playing for friends and 
family, with friends and family, and sometimes just sitting down and playing for 
myself.  
But if you get the chance to play a musical instrument, I hope you take that 
opportunity. It really is a fun time. I’ve had so much fun throughout my life because 
of music – and it’s something that you just can’t compare to anything else. So I hope 
you take the opportunity, and thanks for taking the time to listen. 
 
Activity 2 Answers: 
trumpet 
guitar

1. a 
2. c 
3. b 
4. a 
5. a

Lesson 3 – Internet Addiction 
Write a little bit about how much time you 
spend online, and how you typically use the 
internet. Do you think you use the internet 
too much? 
 
 
 
 
 
Activity 1 – Pre-Learn Vocabulary 
debut (n./v.) = the first public presentation/appearance of something – 
especially a performance or work of art. 
 
Ex) My cousin’s band is releasing their debut album in July. 
bona fide (adj.) = real, true, genuine (this expression comes from a Latin phrase) 
 
Ex) Is that a bona fide painting by Picasso, or a reproduction? 
urge (n.) = an involuntary impulse to do something 
Ex) I haven’t had a cigarette in six months, but I still get the urge to smoke – 
especially when I’m stressed. 
wilderness (n.) = a natural area, without human civilization nearby 
 
Ex) The airplane crashed in a very remote area of the Alaskan wilderness. 
lure (n.) = something that attracts or appeals to you, with the promise of reward.  
Ex) Even happily married men may have trouble resisting the lure of an 
attractive woman who is interested in them. 
hotbed (n.) = an environment that encourages the growth or development of 
something (usually something bad) 
 
Ex) That neighborhood is very dangerous; it’s a hotbed of gang activity. 


abstain (v.) = choose NOT to do something, or NOT to participate in something 
Ex) Many religions encourage people to abstain from sex until marriage. 
 
Activity 2 – Listen for General Ideas 
Speaker: Janet – British 
What does this text, as a whole, mainly focus on? 
a. How internet addiction will damage our relationships and society 
b. Real-life personal stories about experiences with internet addiction 
c. How certain websites and online games are designed to be addictive 
d. The signs of internet addiction and treatment options 
e. The various causes of internet addiction 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Activity 3a – Listen for Specific Ideas 
Mark the following statements TRUE or FALSE: 
1. There has been little research on internet addiction 
2. There are some specific differences between regular internet use and 
internet addiction 
3. Addicts are honest about how much time they spend on the internet 
4. Young adults ages 20-30 suffer the most from internet addiction 
5. In Korea, horses are used to help people overcome internet addiction 
6. You can avoid internet addiction by setting limits for your online use. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Activity 3b – Listen for More Specific Details! 
1. Internet addiction was first recognized in… 
a. 1986 
b. 1996 
c. 2006 
2. Check the characteristics of internet addiction mentioned:  
(more than one answer) 
• checking email on your phone every 5 minutes 
• trying and failing to reduce the amount of time you spend online 
• feeling bad when you're not online 
• having more online friends than offline friends 
• ignoring real real-life responsibilities because of the internet 
3. It's time to seek help when... 
a. Your time online is making you increasingly depressed 
b. You spend more than 10 hours a day online 
c. Your internet use is having a negative effect on your life 
4. The treatment used in Korea is especially effective because... 
a. Kids learn to be more conscious of their decisions in life 
b. There’s both a physical activity and an emotional connection 
c. It requires a lot of patience and time to master 
5. Which suggestion is NOT mentioned at the end of the text? 
a. installing software to block certain programs and websites 
b. interacting with friends in person 
c. turning off instant notifications 
 
 
 


Activity 4 – Listen for Specific Words 
Internet addiction was first recognized in 1996 by Dr. Kimberley Young. Her 
debut paper on the _____________________ was entitled “Internet Addiction: The 
Emergence of a New Disorder” and was presented at the American Psychological 
Association’s annual _____________________ in Toronto. Since those early days, there 
has been a mountain of further research, as internet addiction has taken more of 
a grip than even Dr. Young might have _____________________. 
So, what are the signs or symptoms of internet addiction? You might think that it 
would be difficult to _____________________ reliance on the internet (which most of us 
would probably admit to) from internet addiction. This is true to some degree, 
but there are actually several clear _____________________ that indicate a bona fide 
addiction.  
These _____________________ an urge to increase the percentage of your day spent 
online over time, and an inability to curtail the amount of time you spend online, 
despite concerted _____________________. You could be addicted to the internet if you 
feel restless, agitated and anxious if you are offline – or if you lie to people close 
to you about the _____________________ of time you spend online.  
Perhaps the most worrying sign of addiction is using the internet to mask 
_____________________ of depression, guilt, anxiety or hopelessness. Some internet 
addicts even reach the _____________________ of neglecting real-life relationships and 
responsibilities due to their online involvement. When compulsive internet use 
begins to _____________________ with daily life, it’s time to seek help. 
There are a range of treatment options, especially for teens, who represent the 
_____________________ age group suffering from internet addiction. Some programs 
involve disconnecting completely and spending a long period of time in the 
wilderness away from _____________________. Other treatment options include 
individual, group and family therapy, offline recreation and _____________________ 
expression and even, interestingly, equine therapy! In Korea, young internet 
addicts have been encouraged to take up horseback riding to help guide them 
away from the lures of the online _____________________.  
Studies have shown that Korea is a hotbed of internet addiction in children, with 
680,000 young addicts between the ages of 10 and 19 – and equine therapy has 
proven _____________________ in creating a new, healthier passion. According to a 
doctor of child psychiatry at Samsung Medical Centre, the fact that riding and 
caring for horses involves both a physical activity and an _____________________ 


connection with a living being makes it especially effective in overcoming 
internet addiction. 
Professionals generally agree that _____________________ internet use and setting 
healthy boundaries is better than abstaining from it entirely. The internet should 
enhance real life, not _____________________ it. A few ways to limit your screen time 
include turning off instant notifications from email and social media, calling or 
_____________________ friends rather than interacting online, and setting (and 
sticking to!) time limits for your internet usage. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Activity 5 – Listen with Transcript 
Internet addiction was first recognized in 1996 by Dr. Kimberley Young. Her 
debut paper on the subject was entitled “Internet Addiction: The Emergence of a 
New Disorder” and was presented at the American Psychological Association’s 
annual conference in Toronto. Since those early days, there has been a mountain 
of further research, as internet addiction has taken more of a grip than even Dr. 
Young might have imagined. 
So, what are the signs or symptoms of internet addiction? You might think that it 
would be difficult to separate reliance on the internet (which most of us would 
probably admit to) from internet addiction. This is true to some degree, but there 
are actually several clear markers that indicate a bona fide addiction.  
These include an urge to increase the percentage of your day spent online over 
time, and an inability to curtail the amount of time you spend online, despite 
concerted efforts. You could be addicted to the internet if you feel restless, 
agitated and anxious if you are offline – or if you lie to people close to you about 
the amount of time you spend online.  
Perhaps the most worrying sign of addiction is using the internet to mask 
feelings of depression, guilt, anxiety or hopelessness. Some internet addicts even 
reach the point of neglecting real-life relationships and responsibilities due to 
their online involvement. When compulsive internet use begins to interfere with 
daily life, it’s time to seek help. 
There are a range of treatment options, especially for teens, who represent the 
largest age group suffering from internet addiction. Some programs involve 
disconnecting completely and spending a long period of time in the wilderness 
away from technology. Other treatment options include individual, group and 
family therapy, offline recreation and artistic expression and even, interestingly, 
equine therapy! In Korea, young internet addicts have been encouraged to take 
up horseback riding to help guide them away from the lures of the online world.  
Studies have shown that Korea is a hotbed of internet addiction in children, with 
680,000 young addicts between the ages of 10 and 19 – and equine therapy has 
proven successful in creating a new, healthier passion. According to a doctor of 
child psychiatry at Samsung Medical Centre, the fact that riding and caring for 
horses involves both a physical activity and an emotional connection with a 
living being makes it especially effective in overcoming internet addiction. 


Professionals generally agree that controlling internet use and setting healthy 
boundaries is better than abstaining from it entirely. The internet should 
enhance real life, not replace it. A few ways to limit your screen time include 
turning off instant notifications from email and social media, calling or visiting 
friends rather than interacting online, and setting (and sticking to!) time limits 
for your internet usage. 
 
Extra Vocabulary 
"internet addiction has taken more of a grip than even Dr. Young might have 
imagined." 
 
This means that internet addiction has become stronger and more prevalent. 
"an inability to curtail the amount of time you spend online, despite concerted 
efforts." 
 
Concerted efforts are planned or especially intentional efforts 
"using the internet to mask feelings of depression, guilt, anxiety or hopelessness" 
 
In this context, mask means “hide” 
"The internet should enhance real life, not replace it." 
Enhance means to improve; to provide something additional that makes the 
original thing better. 
"setting (and sticking to!) time limits" 
 
To stick to the time limits means to actually follow/obey them

Lesson 4 – Exercise Habits & Mistakes 
Warm-Up: 
How often do you exercise, and what types of exercise do 
you like to do? Do you enjoy exercising, or see it as an 
annoying necessity? 
 
 
PART 1: JULIE TALKS ABOUT EXERCISE MISTAKES 
Activity 1: Pre-Learn Vocabulary 
cardio (n.) – Short for “cardiovascular” exercise, meaning exercise that makes your 
heart beat much faster. For example, running. 
metabolism (n.) – the processes of how your body stays alive – processing 
nutrients, giving energy, growing, etc. 
carbohydrates (n.) – a type of nutrient found especially in bread, rice, pasta, grains, 
and sugars. 
protein (n.) – a type of nutrient found especially in meat, fish, eggs, milk, and beans. 
sore (adj.) – when your muscles hurt after exercising (or after an injury) 
fuel (n./v.) – a substance that provides power/energy

Weight training is so _____________________ because it builds your foundation of

To me, the best schedule is alternating between weight training and cardio. Monday,

Speaking of rest, after 30 minutes of an _____________________ workout, you 
should have a recovery drink. The recovery drink is a 4:1 ratio of carbohydrates to 
protein. For example, if your drink has 40 grams of carbohydrates, it 
_____________________ have 10 grams of protein - like chocolate milk.  
Without really getting into the _____________________ of the science behind the 
recovery drink, basically you won't be as sore and you'll have more energy the next

_____________________, the biggest mistake is in the kitchen. Yes, that's right - it's

Complete Transcript 
There are a couple of common exercise and fitness mistakes I see regularly. One of 
those mistakes is too much cardio. If you really wanna see great results, you have to 
diversify. For instance, three days a week do weight training; three days a week, do 
cardio.  
Weight training is so important because it builds your foundation of muscle, and 
that muscle dictates your metabolism. As we get older, we start to lose muscle mass 
naturally, so by keeping up your weight training, you prevent that from happening.  
To me, the best schedule is alternating between weight training and cardio. Monday, 
Wednesday, Friday - are great days to do weight training. Tuesday, Thursday, and 
Saturday, do your cardio. Always make sure you take a rest day. 
Speaking of rest, after 30 minutes of an intense workout, you should have a 
recovery drink. The recovery drink is a 4:1 ratio of carbohydrates to protein. For 
example, if your drink has 40 grams of carbohydrates, it should have 10 grams of 
protein - like chocolate milk.  
Without really getting into the details of the science behind the recovery drink, 
basically you won't be as sore and you'll have more energy the next day.  
Lastly, the biggest mistake is in the kitchen. Yes, that's right - it's in the kitchen. You 
can't out-work a bad diet. If you're not seeing the results that you want in your 
fitness, then make sure you're fueling your body like the hard-working machine it 
is.

Complete Transcript 
I'm answering the question, "Do you like to exercise?" Well, I like to exercise, but I 
don't do it as often as I should. I only ride my bike from time to time, every once in a 
while. Last week, for example, I had my first surf class, and the teacher was amazed 
when I told him I didn't exercise regularly. He told me what everybody knows - we 
need to exercise to live longer.  
Later on, when I was at the sea, I realized I was in bad shape. I got tired very, very 
quickly. After four or five attempts, I could no longer get up on the board.  
But back to the question - I always feel good after exercise. It seems that it opens

handball and basketball.  
I feel that team sports have a different competitive side. They are a collective game 
with many people working together to win something. In this case, sweat has a 
purpose - to win.  
Well, but either way - please exercise. You end up always winning. You win years of 
life.

Lesson 5: Animal Intelligence 
Which animals do you think are the most intelligent? 
In your opinion, what are some signs of intelligence 
in animals? 
 
 
 
 
Activity 1 – Pre-Learn Vocabulary 
ponder (v.) = think a lot about something, in a deep and reflective way 
 
Ex) As she gazed out at the ocean, she pondered the meaning of life. 
elaborate (adj.) = complex, with many different details 
Ex) The stone is covered with elaborate carvings. 
 
bubbles (n.) = little balls of air surrounded by water 
 


hoard (v.) = keep/collect a lot of something for yourself, without sharing with 
anyone else, in order to use it later 
 
Ex) Hey, stop hoarding all the snacks! I’m hungry, too! 
shackles (n.) = the locked metal cuffs used to secure the hands or feet of a 
prisoner or slave 
 
altruistic (adj.) = caring about other people, not just yourself 
Ex) Bill Gates is a billionaire who is known for his altruistic work; he 
contributes to many organizations that help the poor. 
log (n.) = a thick, round piece of wood used in construction 
 
mourn (v.) = crying and being sad over a death or loss 
 
Ex) The entire country mourned the death of one of its most famous singers. 
termite (n.) = a type of insect that eats wood 


puzzle (n.) = a problem – usually done for fun – that requires thought and 
creativity in order to solve it. One of the most common types is a jigsaw puzzle, 
where you have to put the pieces together. However, there are many other types 
of puzzles. 
 
Activity 2 – Listen for General Ideas 
Speaker: Robert – Australian 
Put the different types of intelligence in the category of 
each animal: 
communication (x2) 
counting & arithmetic 
planning for the future 
compassion 
death ritual 
problem-solving (x2) 
complex play 
excellent memory 
use of tools 
 
DOLPHINS  
(3 THINGS)  
ELEPHANTS  
(4 THINGS) 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
CHIMPANZEES  
(4 THINGS) 
          
 


Activity 3 – Listen for Specific Ideas 
1. A good indicator of animal intelligence is... 
a. its ability to imitate humans 
b. the complexity of its brain 
c. the size of its brain 
2. Dolphins communicate through... 
a. clicks and whistles 
b. making rings of bubbles 
c. gestures and movements 
3. At the Institute for Marine Mammal Studies, dolphins receive fish as a 
reward for... 
a. delivering trash in their tanks to a keeper 
b. learning to use objects in creative ways 
c. performing flips and tricks for an audience 
4. One elephant in an Asian zoo was able to... 
a. build a basic structure 
b. free herself and other elephants 
c. recognize herself in a mirror 
5. In India, the trained elephant refused to put the log in the hole 
because... 
a. a child was standing in its path 
b. the supervisor had punished the elephant 
c. there was a dog at the bottom of the hole 
6. Chimps can be trained to use sign language, but... 
a. it takes them a long time to learn 
b. they can only use simple words/phrases 
c. young chimps are better communicators than older chimps 
7. In the memory text, chimps performed... 
a. slightly worse than humans 
b. equally as well as humans 
c. better than humans 
8. In the London experiment, chimps worked on puzzles even though... 
a. the puzzles were too difficult for them 
b. they did not receive rewards 
c. there were other toys and tools available 


Activity 4 – Listen for Specific Words 
Throughout history, humans have pondered animal intelligence and especially the 
possibility of consciousness in _____________________ species. Previously an animal’s 
brain size was often used to determine its _____________________ for intelligence, but 
a better indicator of intelligence is brain complexity. Experiments are also used to 
_____________________ animals' ability to learn, memorize, solve problems, and 
communicate. 
Dolphins are one of the _____________________ sea creatures. In the wild, dolphins 
exhibit complex play behavior involving making and playing with elaborate rings 
of bubbles in _____________________. They also communicate through a “language” of 
clicks and whistles, using distinctive signals to _____________________ and call each 
other. 
One incredible example of dolphin cleverness was demonstrated in a captive 
environment. In the Institute for Marine Mammal Studies in Mississippi, the 
dolphins are rewarded for _____________________ their own tank clean. They do this by 
retrieving rubbish and bringing it to a keeper, receiving a fish as a reward. One 
dolphin _____________________ the ability to plan for the future – instead of delivering 
the trash right away, she started hoarding it under a _____________________ at the 
bottom of the pool. Then, she would bring it up one small piece at a time whenever 
she wanted a fish. 
The elephant is another highly intelligent animal – in fact, some parts of an 
elephant’s brain are more complex than our own. Research in _____________________ 
has shown that elephants have the ability to count and even handle rudimentary 
arithmetic. There have been numerous _____________________ of elephants’ problem-
solving abilities, such as an elephant in a zoo in Asia that worked out how to unlock 
the shackles on her _____________________ – and even helped other elephants escape! 
Elephants are incredibly altruistic and often give aid to other species in need. In 
India, an elephant was _____________________ to help in a construction project by 
lifting logs and placing them into holes in the ground. At one point, it refused to 
insert a log into a hole – and when the supervisor went to _____________________, he 
found a dog sleeping at the bottom of the hole. The elephant would only insert the 
log after the dog had been removed. 
Finally, elephants are the only species besides humans to have a recognizable 
ritual around death. They have been observed mourning and _____________________ 


the body of a dead elephant with dirt and leaves. Elephants show strong interest 
in the _____________________ of their own kind, and even visit “elephant graveyards.” 
Chimpanzees, our close genetic relatives, also demonstrate remarkable 
intelligence. They can make and use _____________________ tools – for example, using 
rocks as hammers to crack open nuts, and using sticks to extract termites from 
their nests. Chimps can also _____________________ to use sign language to 
communicate with their human trainers, although their vocabulary is limited and 
they can only express simple _____________________. 
In some memory tasks, chimpanzees actually outperform humans. In one 
experiment, the numbers one through nine appeared on a computer 
_____________________ in random positions. The numbers were only visible for about 
a second, and then disappeared. Chimps were able to place all the numbers back 
in the correct positions with a _____________________ degree of accuracy, whereas 
humans who took the test could remember no more than a few. 
Perhaps the most interesting finding is that chimps appear to enjoy an 
intellectual _____________________. During an experiment in London, chimps 
voluntarily worked on puzzles of increasing difficulty, even when they did not 
receive a reward for _____________________ it. This suggests that they enjoy solving 
brain teasers for _____________________, just as humans do. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Complete Transcript 
Throughout history, humans have pondered animal intelligence and especially the 
possibility of consciousness in other species. Previously an animal’s brain size was 
often used to determine its capacity for intelligence, but a better indicator of 
intelligence is brain complexity. Experiments are also used to test animals' ability 
to learn, memorize, solve problems, and communicate. 
Dolphins are one of the smartest sea creatures. In the wild, dolphins exhibit 
complex play behavior involving making and playing with elaborate rings of 
bubbles in groups. They also communicate through a “language” of clicks and 
whistles, using distinctive signals to identify and call each other. 
One incredible example of dolphin cleverness was demonstrated in a captive 
environment. In the Institute for Marine Mammal Studies in Mississippi, the 
dolphins are rewarded for keeping their own tank clean. They do this by 
retrieving rubbish and bringing it to a keeper, receiving a fish as a reward. One 
dolphin showed the ability to plan for the future – instead of delivering the trash 
right away, she started hoarding it under a rock at the bottom of the pool. Then, 
she would bring it up one small piece at a time whenever she wanted a fish. 
The elephant is another highly intelligent animal – in fact, some parts of an 
elephant’s brain are more complex than our own. Research in Japan has shown 
that elephants have the ability to count and even handle rudimentary arithmetic. 
There have been numerous demonstrations of elephants’ problem-solving 
abilities, such as an elephant in a zoo in Asia that worked out how to unlock the 
shackles on her feet – and even helped other elephants escape! 
Elephants are incredibly altruistic and often give aid to other species in need. In 
India, an elephant was trained to help in a construction project by lifting logs and 
placing them into holes in the ground. At one point, it refused to insert a log into a 
hole – and when the supervisor went to investigate, he found a dog sleeping at the 
bottom of the hole. The elephant would only insert the log after the dog had been 
removed. 
Finally, elephants are the only species besides humans to have a recognizable 
ritual around death. They have been observed mourning and covering the body 
of a dead elephant with dirt and leaves. Elephants show strong interest in the 
bones of their own kind, and even visit “elephant graveyards.” 
Chimpanzees, our close genetic relatives, also demonstrate remarkable 
intelligence. They can make and use simple tools – for example, using rocks as 


hammers to crack open nuts, and using sticks to extract termites from their nests. 
Chimps can also learn to use sign language to communicate with their human 
trainers, although their vocabulary is limited and they can only express simple 
concepts. 
In some memory tasks, chimpanzees actually outperform humans. In one 
experiment, the numbers one through nine appeared on a computer screen in 
random positions. The numbers were only visible for about a second, and then 
disappeared. Chimps were able to place all the numbers back in the correct 
positions with a high degree of accuracy, whereas humans who took the test 
could remember no more than a few. 
Perhaps the most interesting finding is that chimps appear to enjoy an 
intellectual challenge. During an experiment in London, chimps voluntarily 
worked on puzzles of increasing difficulty, even when they did not receive a 
reward for completing them. This suggests that they enjoy solving brain teasers 
for fun, just as humans do. 
 
Extra Vocabulary 
"In the wild, dolphins exhibit complex play behavior..." 
“In the wild” means the dolphins are in their natural habitat, not in zoos or 
in human captivity. 
"One incredible example of dolphin cleverness..." 
“Cleverness” is a little bit different from “intelligence” – it means intelligence 
that is especially creative and brings an advantage to the person/animal 
using it. 
"elephants have the ability to count and even handle rudimentary arithmetic." 
 
“Rudimentary” means very basic. 
"In some memory tasks, chimpanzees actually outperform humans." 
 
“Outperform” means to perform better. 
"This suggests that they enjoy solving brain teasers for fun" 
 
“Brain teasers” is another expression for puzzles or riddles that

lessons.fullText:
Lesson 6: Worst Job 
Warm-Up: 
Describe the worst job you’ve ever had. Why was it so bad? 
 
 
 
 
Activity 1: Pre-Learn Vocabulary 
bed and breakfast (n.) = a type of small hotel which is a family’s home, and the 
family rents out a few rooms for travelers/visitors to stay overnight 
Amish (n./adj.) = the Amish people are a religious/cultural group that live in the 
rural areas of the northeastern United States. They have a simple lifestyle and do not 
use modern technology. 
 
tight-knit (adj.) = this adjective describes a group whose members are very closely 
and firmly integrated with each other 
Ex) There is a small but tight-knit community of Chinese immigrants in this 
town – since there aren’t very many of them, they tend to stick together. 
quaint (adj.) = old-fashioned in a charming and pleasant way 


Ex) We stayed in a quaint little village in the mountains. 
 
achy (adj.) = painful. This is the adjective form of ache (which means “pain”) 
Ex) I’ve been sitting at the computer for the past eight hours and my back is all 
achy. 
handle (n.) = an attachment to an object that can be used with the hand 
 
knock (v.) = hit a surface (usually a door or window) to make a sound and get the 
attention of someone inside 
 
 
 
 


Activity 2: Listen for General Ideas

Which TWO aspects of the bad job does Katie  
primarily talk about? 
• Getting locked inside the walk-in freezer

Activity 4: Listen for Specific Words 
The worst job that I ever had was actually the _____________________ job that I 
ever had. I was fifteen years old and I was a plate-washer at a bed and breakfast in 
Amish country. And where I grew up in the mid-west, there were these tight-knit 
Amish communities that were far-off from everything; far from electricity, and from 
buzzing cars and _____________________, and it was the perfect setting for a little 
quaint bed and breakfast. People would come in from the city and they would spend 
a weekend or spend some time there and enjoy _____________________.  
But part of the quaintness was this cozy little restaurant that didn't have a 
_____________________; that served one thing every meal. There were no options, 
they just cooked it and brought it to you. And I was the dish washer. And I would go 
there with my brother, who was _____________________ enough to drive, we would 
go there and would always just have the most exotic things come back on plates. I 
felt like you couldn't get plates any _____________________ with this food.  
I had to not only rinse everything off in scalding hot water, but dry it in this 
industrial dishwasher and dryer that would just burn your hands every time you 
_____________________ a plate - but they kept coming, so you had to wash them and 
get them in and then get them out. And I remember my hands being burnt and just 
achy all the time. I knew I was gonna get burnt touching these plates. 
And then there was also the other _____________________, there was a freezer, a 
walk-in freezer that you had to go into to get certain things, certain supplies, it was 
the grunt work to get things. And actually my first day there, I got locked in the 
walk-in freezer. There was no handle on the inside, but instead there was a 
_____________________ that no one had ever really showed me, and when I was in 
there I actually got stuck in there. 
Thankfully there was a small _____________________ in the middle that I was able 
to knock on and you try to get somebody's  attention - but I was in there before 5 or 
10 minutes before anyone came and got me. 


And long story short, I didn't last very long in the plate-washing industry. It was not

made enough money to buy a new bike, and I was outta there. 
Complete Transcript 
The worst job that I ever had was actually the first job that I ever had. I was fifteen 
years old and I was a plate-washer at a bed and breakfast in Amish country. And 
where I grew up in the mid-west, there were these tight-knit Amish communities 
that were far-off from everything; far from electricity, and from buzzing cars and 
noise, and it was the perfect setting for a little quaint bed and breakfast. People 
would come in from the city and they would spend a weekend or spend some time 
there and enjoy nature.  
But part of the quaintness was this cozy little restaurant that didn't have a menu; 
that served one thing every meal. There were no options, they just cooked it and 
brought it to you. And I was the dish washer. And I would go there with my brother, 
who was old enough to drive, we would go there and would always just have the 
most exotic things come back on plates. I felt like you couldn't get plates any dirtier 
with this food.  
I had to not only rinse everything off in scalding hot water, but dry it in this 
industrial dishwasher and dryer that would just burn your hands every time you 
touched a plate - but they kept coming, so you had to wash them and get them in 
and then get them out. And I remember my hands being burnt and just achy all the 
time. I knew I was gonna get burnt touching these plates. 
And then there was also the other extreme, there was a freezer, a walk-in freezer 
that you had to go into to get certain things, certain supplies, it was the grunt work 
to get things. And actually my first day there, I got locked in the walk-in freezer. 
There was no handle on the inside, but instead there was a button that no one had 
ever really showed me, and when I was in there I actually got stuck in there. 
Thankfully there was a small window in the middle that I was able to knock on and 
you try to get somebody's attention - but I was in there before 5 or 10 minutes 
before anyone came and got me. 
And long story short, I didn't last very long in the plate-washing industry. It was not 
my career of choice. I only worked there for about six months; made enough money 
to buy a new bike, and I was outta there. 


Extra Vocabulary 
"far from electricity, and from buzzing cars and noise" 
 
The word buzz (n./v.) refers to the ZZZZZ noise made by insects and machines. 
"cozy little restaurant" 
 
The word cozy (adj.) means small, warm, and comfortable. 
"I had to not only rinse everything off in scalding hot water" 
To rinse (v.) is to pass water over something to clean it. If water is scalding 
hot, it is extremely hot – hot enough to burn you. 
"it was the grunt work to get things" 
“Grunt work” refers to tasks that are not very interesting, and not appreciated. 
They are the things that nobody wants to do, so it’s usually the employee with 
the lowest status who has to do them. 
"And long story short…" 
This is a shortened version of the expression “to make a long story short” – 
meaning “I will give a short summary/conclusion, because all the details would 
take a long time to tell you.” 
"I only worked there for about six months; made enough money to buy a new bike, 
and I was outta there." 
This expression means “I left” – usually, leaving very fast because it’s not good 
for you to stay. A similar expression is “Let’s get outta here!” meaning “Let’s 
leave.” 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Activity 2 Answers 
• Getting locked inside the walk-in freezer 
• The very hot dish washer/dryer 
 
Activity 3 Answers 
1. False - she worked there when she was 15 years old 
2. True 
3. False - her brother drove her to work, and also worked with her there 
4. True 
5. True 
6. False - she was inside for 5-10 minutes 
7. False - she worked there for six months 
8. False - she bought a new bike

Lesson 7: The History of Jeans 
Warm-Up: 
Describe some of your favorite outfits (sets of clothing). What 
types of clothing do you like/don’t you like to wear? Do you 
have a favorite pair of jeans? 
 
 
 
Activity 1 – Learn Vocabulary 
staple (n.) = in the context of this audio, it means a “basic, essential item.” 
 
Ex) Rice is a staple in the diets of many people in Asia. 
tailor (n.) = a person who works making, repairing, or adjusting clothing 
 
durable (adj.) = describes something strong that lasts a long time 
Ex) This water bottle is really durable. I’ve dropped it many times and it has 
never broken. 
copper rivets (n.) = “rivets” are metal pins (like the ones commonly used in jeans) 
and “copper” is a type of metal, which the rivets are made of. 


seams (n.) = the seams are the lines where two pieces of fabric are sewn together 
 
canvas (n.) = a type of strong fabric that is used for backpacks and tents. Artists 
also use canvas to paint on. 
 
dye (n./v.) = change the color of hair or fabric. The word “dye” is used for both the 
action and for the colored liquid itself. The difference between dye and paint is that 
paint covers a surface, but dye actually changes the color of the thing itself. 
 
Ex) Her natural hair color is brown, but she dyed her hair blonde recently. 
fade (v.) = become less intense over time. Can be used for colors, sounds, feelings, 
etc. 
 
Ex) The sound of the music faded as we drove away from the concert. 
portray (v.) = describe, show, or represent (not necessarily a true representation) 


Ex) I hate that TV show. It portrays all women as being stupid, and 
encourages sexism. 
eager (adj.) = excited to do something 
Ex) I just bought a new pair of skis and I’m eager to try them out on the 
mountain! 
iron (n./v.) = an appliance used to remove wrinkles/lines from fabric, using hot 
water vapor. The word “iron” means both the object itself, and the action of passing 
it over clothes 
 
 
Activity 2 – Listen for General Ideas 
Speaker: Sam – British 
Mark each sentence as TRUE or FALSE 
1. Jeans were invented in the U.S. 
2. Jeans were created as strong pants for workers 
3. Levi Strauss stole Jacob Davis's design 
4. The original jeans were black, not blue 
5. Jeans were used by soldiers in World War II 
6. Characters in movies made jeans more popular 
7. Women liked jeans because they fit well and were easy to care for 
 
 


Activity 3 – Listen for Specific Ideas 
1. According to one anthropologist's observations, what percentage of 
people wear jeans in daily life, on average? 
a. one-fifth 
b. almost half 
c. two-thirds 
2. Jeans were created in... 
a. The 1850s 
b. The 1870s 
c. The 1890s 
3. Jacob Davis asked Levi Strauss for help because... 
a. He didn't have enough money to pay for the patent 
b. He didn't know how to operate a large factory 
c. He wanted assistance with marketing the brand 
4. Denim jeans were the most popular type because... 
a. The color changed over time 
b. The fabric was lighter 
c. They were stronger and more durable 
5. Before World War II, jeans were seen as ________ clothing. 
a. miner 
b. farmer 
c. cowboy 
6. Films helped associate jeans with the image of... 
a. a young person 
b. a cool rebel 
c. wealth and elegance 
7. Author Paul Trynka says we love jeans because... 
a. there are many different fashions 
b. they are casual and comfortable 
c. they reflect our lives and identities 


Activity 4 – Listen for Specific Words 
Nearly everybody has a _____________________ pair of jeans. Invented in a simple 
tailor’s shop in the U.S., jeans are now a staple in wardrobes across the globe. One 
anthropologist _____________________ hundreds of people on the street in dozens of 
countries and found that nearly half of passers-by wear jeans on any given day. 
How did this American _____________________ win over the world? 
Sometime in the 1870s, a woman asked a tailor named Jacob Davis to make a 
durable pair of pants for her husband, who was a woodcutter. To make the pants, 
Davis used a strong fabric, which he _____________________ from a supplier owned by 
Mr. Levi Strauss. He then reinforced the pants with copper rivets to prevent 
tearing along the seams and around the _____________________. Word about this robust 
new style of pants spread like wildfire among manual laborers, and soon Davis was 
receiving so many _____________________ for the pants that he could barely keep up 
with the demand.  
Davis wanted to patent his _____________________, but he couldn’t afford the patent 
application fee. This spurred him to call Levi Strauss to ask for financial assistance. 
As a result of this _____________________, the famous brand of Levi’s jeans was born, 
and Strauss and Davis opened a large manufacturing plant in San Francisco. Jacob 
Davis continued to manage the _____________________ for the rest of his life. 
Levi’s jeans were initially made in two fabrics – one was cotton duck (which is 
similar to canvas) and the other was denim. _____________________ both pairs were 
dyed blue, the denim jeans turned out to be far more popular. The blue dye didn’t 
penetrate the denim as deeply, and the result was that the color faded and changed 
over time – giving the denim jeans a _____________________ “character.” In addition, 
denim was a _____________________ and more comfortable fabric, and became even 
more so with age.  
Jeans are certainly practical for workers - but their _____________________ in 
popularity can be credited to Hollywood. Before World War II, jeans were 
primarily worn in the _____________________ part of the United States. They were 
considered cowboy clothing - a symbol of rugged American individualism - but 
hardly appropriate for more casual or _____________________ wear. 
In the 1950s, two legendary American _____________________ - Marlon Brando and 
James Dean - wore jeans in films where their characters were portrayed as rebels 


who were "cool." Jeans became associated with the "bad-boy" image, and were 
even banned in _____________________ - which of course made teenagers all the more 
eager to wear them.  
Within a decade, jeans had spread to the _____________________ class and many 
variations of color and cut were being produced. Women loved the fact that they 
didn’t require frequent _____________________, and didn’t need to be ironed at all. Not 
only that, but they fit close to the body in a way that rivaled even tailored clothing. 
Today jeans are an everyday item and a _____________________ of youth, casualness, 
and comfort. According to Paul Trynka, the author of a book about jeans, we love 
our jeans because they come to represent our identity. He says, "The eternal appeal 
of jeans is just that they reflect us and they reflect the lives that we've had in them." 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Complete Transcript 
Nearly everybody has a favorite pair of jeans. Invented in a simple tailor’s shop in 
the U.S., jeans are now a staple in wardrobes across the globe. One anthropologist 
observed hundreds of people on the street in dozens of countries and found that 
nearly half of passers-by wear jeans on any given day. How did this American 
invention win over the world? 
Sometime in the 1870s, a woman asked a tailor named Jacob Davis to make a 
durable pair of pants for her husband, who was a woodcutter. To make the pants, 
Davis used a strong fabric, which he bought from a supplier owned by Mr. Levi 
Strauss. He then reinforced the pants with copper rivets to prevent tearing along 
the seams and around the pockets. Word about this robust new style of pants 
spread like wildfire among manual laborers, and soon Davis was receiving so many 
orders for the pants that he could barely keep up with the demand.  
Davis wanted to patent his invention, but he couldn’t afford the patent application 
fee. This spurred him to call Levi Strauss to ask for financial assistance. As a result 
of this conversation, the famous brand of Levi’s jeans was born, and Strauss and 
Davis opened a large manufacturing plant in San Francisco. Jacob Davis continued 
to manage the factory for the rest of his life. 
Levi’s jeans were initially made in two fabrics – one was cotton duck (which is 
similar to canvas) and the other was denim. Although both pairs were dyed blue, 
the denim jeans turned out to be far more popular. The blue dye didn’t penetrate 
the denim as deeply, and the result was that the color faded and changed over time 
– giving the denim jeans a unique “character.” In addition, denim was a softer and 
more comfortable fabric, and became even more so with age.  
Jeans are certainly practical for workers - but their explosion in popularity can be 
credited to Hollywood. Before World War II, jeans were primarily worn in the 
western part of the United States. They were considered cowboy clothing - a 
symbol of rugged American individualism - but hardly appropriate for more casual 
or elegant wear. 
In the 1950s, two legendary American actors - Marlon Brando and James Dean - 
wore jeans in films where their characters were portrayed as rebels who were 
"cool." Jeans became associated with the "bad-boy" image, and were even banned 
in schools - which of course made teenagers all the more eager to wear them.  


Within a decade, jeans had spread to the middle class and many variations of color 
and cut were being produced. Women loved the fact that they didn’t require 
frequent washing, and didn’t need to be ironed at all. Not only that, but they fit 
close to the body in a way that rivaled even tailored clothing. 
Today jeans are an everyday item and a symbol of youth, casualness, and comfort. 
According to Paul Trynka, the author of a book about jeans, we love our jeans 
because they come to represent our identity. He says, "The eternal appeal of jeans 
is just that they reflect us and they reflect the lives that we've had in them." 
 
Extra Vocabulary 
"nearly half of passers-by wear jeans on any given day." 
The word “passers-by” refers to people walking in the street. The singular is 
“passer-by” 
"Word about this robust new style of pants spread like wildfire among manual 
laborers" 
The expression “word spread” means that people told other people about it, 
resulting in a large number of people knowing about jeans. To “spread like 
wildfire” means this process happened very fast. 
"This spurred him to call Levi Strauss to ask for financial assistance." 
The verb “spur” means to motivate/encourage another action/result. Davis’ 
financial problems motivated him to call Levi Strauss. 
"a symbol of rugged American individualism" 
The expression “rugged individualism” means a belief in freedom, 
independence, and self-reliance – that people should be strong enough to take 
care of themselves and control their own lives. 
"they fit close to the body in a way that rivaled even tailored clothing." 
“Tailored clothing” refers to clothes that are custom-made or adjusted to a 
person’s individual measurements. The word “rivaled” in this context means 
“be equal to” – so the sentence is saying that jeans fit so well that they were 
like custom-made clothing. 


Activity 2 Answers 
1. True 
2. True 
3. False 
4. False 
5. False 
6. True 
7. True 
 
Activity 3 Answers 
1. b 
2. b 
3. a 
4. a 
5. c 
6. b 
7. c

lessons.fullText:
Lesson 8: College and Career 
Warm-Up: 
What was your favorite subject in 
school/college, and why? Is your area of study 
related to your job now, or not? Why did you 
choose to enter your current profession? 
 
 
 
 
 
Activity 1: Pre-Learn Vocabulary 
major (n./v.) = a university student’s area of concentrated study. It is the subject 
that the student studies most, and the student will receive a degree in this topic. 
This word can be used as either a noun (describing the subject OR the person who is 
studying it) or as a verb: 
 
As a noun: My brother is an economics major. 
 
As a noun: This program is an interdisciplinary major in biology and chemistry. 
As a verb: I was planning to major in journalism, but I changed my mind and 
ended up majoring in philosophy. 
 
fossil (n.) = remains of animals or plants from a 
very long time ago, which have been preserved in 
rock 
 
lab (n.) = short for “laboratory” – a place where 
science experiments are done 
 
Ex) The doctor sent the blood samples to the lab for testing. 


hands-on (adj.) = describes something that involves active participation, practical 
things, not just learning theory 
Ex) My teenage daughter loves working with animals. She just joined a program 
that will give her some hands-on experience at a veterinary clinic. 
undergrads (n.) = short for “undergraduates” – people who are studying in the 
regular college program to get a bachelor’s degree (typically four years). 
This is in contrast to “grad students,” who are studying in a more advanced program 
like a master’s or doctorate degree. 
 
Ex) Peter is an undergrad at Columbia University. He’s in his third year. 
algae (n.) = plants in the ocean. “Seaweed” is one common type of algae. 
 
second-guess (v.) = wonder/doubt if your ideas or decisions are really correct 
Ex) My parents raised me with very conservative beliefs, but when I left home I 
began to second-guess many of the things I’d been taught. 
sure-fire (adj.) = describes something that will definitely have a particular result 
(can be positive or negative) 
Ex) Elena has so many fans of her blog, that any book she publishes will be a 
sure-fire success. = will definitely have the positive result of succeeding 
 
Ex) Being late for a job interview is a sure-fire way to make a bad impression. 
 
= will definitely have the negative result of making a bad impression 
 
 
 


Activity 2 – Listen for General Ideas 
Speaker: Shayna – American 
True or false? 
1. Shayna was interested in science as a child. 
2. In high school, Shayna found chemistry boring because of the teacher. 
3. Shayna had to finish college before having the opportunity to do research. 
4. Shayna decided not to continue in chemistry because the salary wasn't good. 
5. Shayna's chemistry experience has helped her in English teaching. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Activity 3 - Listen for Specific Details 
1. Shayna's parents... 
a. are high school teachers 
b. are knowledgeable about science 
c. wanted her to be a doctor 
2. Shayna liked her high school chemistry teacher because... 
a. she gave Shayna some advanced books to read  
b. she made chemistry interesting 
c. she was a role model for women in science 
3. The advantage of attending a small college was the opportunity to...  
a. work closely with the professors 
b. find job opportunities more easily 
c. use advanced equipment 
4. Shayna studied sea creatures in order to... 
a. develop new medical treatments 
b. discover ways to purify the ocean water 
c. understand the biological processes of life 
5. Which of these is NOT a reason Shayna didn't like chemistry work? 
a. she felt limited doing such specialized work 
b. the progress was very slow 
c. you need a graduate degree to get a good job 
6. Which of these is NOT a way that chemistry has helped Shayna in 
teaching English? 
a. ability to experiment with teaching methods 
b. learning how to communicate clearly 
c. working with international colleagues in the laboratory 
 


Activity 4 – Listen for Specific Words 
I was a chemistry major in college, and I picked that because I had always been 
interested in science as a kid. I was really into volcanos and _____________________, 
dinosaurs and fossils, and stuff like that, and I used to read some pretty advanced 
books for my age on those _____________________.  
Both of my parents have a science background - my dad was an 
_____________________, and my mom has a psychology degree - so they always 
encouraged me, and my dad would do these science experiments for me and my 
brother to see and learn some of the _____________________ of chemistry and 
physics and whatnot. 
Also in high school I had a wonderful chemistry teacher, she really made the subject 
fascinating, and not just like a boring list of chemical reactions and 
_____________________ to memorize. We would have class with her, but we would 
also do lab work, you know, experiments and it was very hands-on. So when it came 
time to pick a major in college, it was a toss-up between chemistry and 
_____________________, but I eventually settled on chemistry. 
I went to a pretty small college, and what was great about that is that I had the 
opportunity to use lab equipment that _____________________ undergrads wouldn't 
get a chance to use. We were trained to use some really sophisticated machinery 
and we were able to do research that is really quite _____________________ to what 
we'd be doing if we continued into a career in chemistry.  
And I absolutely loved the process of _____________________, of using what was 
already known to investigate things that were unknown. My area of specialization 
was marine natural products chemistry – so basically, studying sea creatures like 
sponges and algae, and trying to extract and _____________________ some of the 
chemical compounds in them that had anti-bacterial and cancer-fighting properties, 
so that these could eventually be _____________________ into new drugs and 
medicines. 
Both during and after my college years I did a couple of internships in a 
pharmaceutical company, which was doing the same kind of work, and it was there 


that I started to second-guess myself and _____________________ whether or not I 
really wanted to do this type of work for the rest of my life. Although the work was 
interesting, it was also very slow – it can take _____________________ to make 
progress in this area – and it was also extremely, extremely specialized, which felt 
limiting because I have a really broad _____________________ of interests.  
So I decided not to continue – I turned down a scholarship to go to grad school – and 
it was a tough decision because I was basically turning my _____________________ 
on a sure-fire career with a great starting salary, and instead choosing a path of 
uncertainty. But I know it was ultimately the _____________________ decision. 
Nowadays, now that people know me as an English teacher, they’re often pretty 
_____________________ to hear that I have a degree in chemistry – but I actually 
think my science background has helped me in some _____________________ ways. 
That ability to research and investigate means I’m always experimenting and testing 
to discover the best ways to help my students learn, and I’m always learning new 
things myself in the process.  
Also, in college I did a lot of _____________________ of my chemistry research, and 
so I learned how to communicate some very complicated concepts in layman’s 
terms, so that they would be clear and understandable to someone even if they 
didn’t have any knowledge of chemistry at all. And now it’s a fundamental 
_____________________ of my teaching style, this ability to simplify what seems 
confusing and complex, and I can thank my experience in the 
_____________________ of chemistry for that, too. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Complete Transcript 


I was a chemistry major in college, and I picked that because I had always been 
interested in science as a kid. I was really into volcanos and geology, dinosaurs and 
fossils, and stuff like that, and I used to read some pretty advanced books for my age 
on those topics.  
Both of my parents have a science background - my dad was an engineer, and my 
mom has a psychology degree - so they always encouraged me, and my dad would 
do these science experiments for me and my brother to see and learn some of the 
principles of chemistry and physics and whatnot. 
Also in high school I had a wonderful chemistry teacher, she really made the subject 
fascinating, and not just like a boring list of chemical reactions and rules to 
memorize. We would have class with her, but we would also do lab work, you know, 
experiments and it was very hands-on. So when it came time to pick a major in 
college, it was a toss-up between chemistry and physics, but I eventually settled on 
chemistry. 
I went to a pretty small college, and what was great about that is that I had the 
opportunity to use lab equipment that normally undergrads wouldn't get a chance 
to use. We were trained to use some really sophisticated machinery and we were 
able to do research that is really quite similar to what we'd be doing if we 
continued into a career in chemistry.  
And I absolutely loved the process of discovery, of using what was already known 
to investigate things that were unknown. My area of specialization was marine 
natural products chemistry – so basically, studying sea creatures like sponges and 
algae, and trying to extract and identify some of the chemical compounds in them 
that had anti-bacterial and cancer-fighting properties, so that these could eventually 
be developed into new drugs and medicines. 
Both during and after my college years I did a couple of internships in a 
pharmaceutical company, which was doing the same kind of work, and it was there 
that I started to second-guess myself and question whether or not I really wanted 
to do this type of work for the rest of my life. Although the work was interesting, it 
was also very slow – it can take years to make progress in this area – and it was also 
extremely, extremely specialized, which felt limiting because I have a really broad 
range of interests.  


So I decided not to continue – I turned down a scholarship to go to grad school – and 
it was a tough decision because I was basically turning my back on a sure-fire 
career with a great starting salary, and instead choosing a path of uncertainty. But I 
know it was ultimately the right decision. 
Nowadays, now that people know me as an English teacher, they’re often pretty 
surprised to hear that I have a degree in chemistry – but I actually think my science 
background has helped me in some indirect ways. That ability to research and 
investigate means I’m always experimenting and testing to discover the best ways to 
help my students learn, and I’m always learning new things myself in the process.  
Also, in college I did a lot of presentations of my chemistry research, and so I 
learned how to communicate some very complicated concepts in layman’s terms, so 
that they would be clear and understandable to someone even if they didn’t have 
any knowledge of chemistry at all. And now it’s a fundamental characteristic of my 
teaching style, this ability to simplify what seems confusing and complex, and I can 
thank my experience in the field of chemistry for that, too. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Extra Vocabulary 
"Both of my parents have a science background" 


If a person has a “background” in a particular area, it means they have studied 
it or have experience in that subject. 
"chemistry and physics and whatnot." 
“…and whatnot” is an informal way to say “and other related things.” It is 
similar to “et cetera” or “etc.” 
 "it was a toss-up between chemistry and physics" 
A “toss-up” means an undecided choice, often one that is 
decided by chance. This expression comes from the 
tradition of “flipping a coin” (called a “coin flip” or “coin 
toss”) to decide things. 
"new drugs and medicines." 
The word “drug” in English can be used to describe either medical substances 
that are used to treat diseases OR illegal drugs (cocaine, heroin, etc.) You’ll 
know which meaning it has based on the context. 
"I turned down a scholarship to go to grad school" 
The phrasal verb “turn down” means to reject, or not to accept an 
opportunity. “Grad school” refers to more advanced university studies 
(master’s and doctorate degrees) 
"communicate some very complicated concepts in layman’s terms" 
A “layman” is someone who is not an expert in a particular area. The 
expression “in layman’s terms” means to say something in a way that an 
everyday person can understand, not using rare and complicated words that 
only a professional in the area would know. 
 
 
Activity 2 Answers 
1. True 
2. False 


3. False 
4. False 
5. True 
 
Activity 3 Answers 
1. b 
2. b 
3. c 
4. a 
5. c 
6. c 
 
 
 
 
Image sources: Abac college, Toby Hudson, Thomas Ihle

lessons.title: Urban-Agriculture
lessons.fullText:
Lesson 9: Urban Agriculture 
Warm-Up: 
Would you prefer to live in an urban or rural environment? 
Why? 
 
 
 
Activity 1 – Learn Vocabulary 
crops (n.) = a general word for plants that are cultivated for food such as rice, corn, 
fruit, vegetables, etc. 
 
sever (v.) = cut off 
Ex) There was a terrible accident at the factory; a worker’s arm was severed 
by a machine. 
fossil fuels (n.) = petroleum, coal, and natural gas – hydrocarbon substances that 
are used for providing power 
 
Ex) Wind energy and solar energy are natural alternatives to fossil fuels. 
dwindle (v.) = to become less and less until nothing remains 
Ex) After being unemployed for ten months, his savings have dwindled and 
now he’s even more desperate to find a job. 
revitalize (v.) = to give new energy or excitement 


Ex) The country is doing a big international advertising campaign in order to 
revitalize its tourism industry.  
pesticides (n.) = chemicals used to kill insects so that 
they don’t damage plants 
gravitate (v.) = to be strongly attracted to something as 
if by an invisible force that you can’t resist 
Ex) Taylor is a natural leader; people just seem to gravitate towards him. 
aesthetic (adj.) = related to appearance and beauty 
Ex) The surgery wasn’t medically necessary; she had the operation for 
aesthetic reasons. 
hub (n.) = a center of activity 
Ex) Silicon Valley in California is considered the technology hub of the United 
States; many of the world’s largest tech companies are located there.  
greenhouse (n.) = a special building, usually made of glass, for growing plants, 
flowers, and vegetables inside 
 
Activity 2 – Listen for General Ideas 
Speaker: Paul – British  
Choose the correct option between the two choices in each sentence: 
1. The beginning of the listening covers the benefits / history of urban 
agriculture. 
2. The middle of the listening focuses on the reasons for interest in / 
obstacles in implementing urban agriculture. 
3. The end of the listening describes some current / future urban agriculture 
projects in New York City. 


Activity 3 – Listen for Specific Details 
1. Society lost interest in urban agriculture because...  
(check the two correct answers) 
a. A clear separation was made between rural and urban areas 
b. Modern industrialized farming requires large areas of open space 
c. Urban pollution can harm food grown in cities 
d. Fewer people work as farmers
