Urban agriculture is, quite simply, the practice of cultivating food in a town or city 
environment. It is not a new concept; for many centuries, humans have tended to 
crops and raised animals in and around cities.  
However, urban farming fell out of favor in the second half of the twentieth 
century. City planners in many countries – especially in the US – have sought to 
sever the links between the city and the country, creating the idea of the modern 
metropolis as being distinct from the rural and agricultural areas. In addition, 
economic development has led to a shift in the workforce; nowadays, not as many 
people pursue farming as their main livelihood. But now the ancient practice of 
urban agriculture is coming back into vogue. 
One reason for the renewed interest in urban farming is the rising prices of fossil 
fuels, which makes it expensive to transport food from faraway farms into the 
cities. This is prompting people to look for more local food sources – such as fruits 
and vegetables grown in backyards and on balconies. As environmental resources 
dwindle, urban agriculture offers a potential solution for providing food to the 
global population. It is projected that sixty percent of the world’s people will live 
in cities by the year 2030. 
Another factor that has revitalized the urban agriculture movement is the growing 
demand for organic food. Urban gardens often use sustainable farming practices 
and avoid pesticides. Nowadays, more and more consumers are gravitating to 
fresh, locally-grown food as opposed to the mass-produced and industrialized 
items found in big supermarkets. Food grown in urban gardens is also more 
nourishing because of the decrease in time between production and consumption 
– in the 5-10 days it takes to transport food from the farm to the dinner table, 30-
50% of the nutrients can be lost. 
Besides the practical benefits, urban agriculture also has an element of aesthetic 
appeal – city gardens add a cheerful touch of greenery to the stark urban 
landscape. Urban farming projects can also improve the overall health of a 
neighborhood. People who participate in caring for community gardens report 
less stress, better social relationships, and increased community pride. In some 
cases, the crime and suicide rates even go down in areas that practice urban 
agriculture. 
Even New York City, one of the largest cities in the world, is becoming a hub for 
urban agriculture, with more than 600 projects throughout the city’s 


neighborhoods. Fruit and vegetables are grown in rooftop greenhouses and 
agricultural spaces within city parks.  
Most of the programs are run by volunteers, and a number have free educational 
programs in which participants can learn about nutrition and farming. There is 
even a restaurant which serves food from its own rooftop garden; the menu 
changes based on which foods are in season.

"humans have tended to crops and raised animals in and around cities" 
 
In this context, “tend to crops” means to care for them. 
"urban farming fell out of favor" 
 
If something falls out of favor, it means it becomes generally unpopular 
"not as many people pursue farming as their main livelihood." 
Your “livelihood” is your occupation or employment; the way you earn 
money to live. 
"the ancient practice of urban agriculture is coming back into vogue." 
 
If something is “in vogue,” it means it is popular and fashionable. 
"Urban gardens often use sustainable farming practices" 
“Sustainable” practices are ones that help preserve the environment and 
resources. 
"city gardens add a cheerful touch of greenery to the stark urban landscape." 
Describing something as “stark” means it has little or no beauty or 
decoration. 
"the menu changes based on which foods are in season." 
If a fruit or vegetable is “in season,” it means it is currently the right time of 
year to get that fruit or vegetable naturally.

Lesson 10: Life in New York City 
Warm-Up: 
What are some of the things you love/hate about where you currently live? Do you 
now live in the same city where you grew up, or have you moved? 
 
 
 
 
Activity 1 – Pre-Learn Vocabulary 
obscure (adj.) = not well-known – the opposite of famous/popular 
Ex) She did her research on the work of an obscure 17th-century poet; it was 
hard for her to find any information on his life. 
vibe (n. – slang) = a feeling that you get from a person, situation, or environment 
Ex) Even though I didn’t know anybody at the party, it had a great vibe because 
everyone was very welcoming. 
on the flip side (n. – slang) = considering the opposite side of the issue (like the 
expression “on the other hand”) 
Ex) Working from home is nice because there are very few distractions – but on 
the flip side, it can get lonely at times. 
overwhelming (adj.) = so intense that it makes you feel weak and powerless, like it 
is too much for you to accept or handle. 
Ex) My history professor wants us to read two 300-page books before the exam 
next week – AND prepare a presentation! This class is so overwhelming. 
 
 
 
 


PART 1 – Emily from the U.S. 
 
Activity 2 – Listen for General Ideas 
Speaker: Emily – American 
1. The TWO good points mentioned about life in NYC 
are the city’s… 
a. career opportunities 
b. convenience 
c. diversity 
d. energy 
e. nightlife 
2. The TWO bad points mentioned about life in NYC are that the city is… 
a. dangerous 
b. dirty/polluted 
c. expensive 
d. noisy 
e. stressful 
3. If you move to NYC, Emily recommends (ONE correct answer): 
a. joining a group/club to meet people 
b. moving to NYC with a friend 
c. saving up a lot of money before you go 
d. visiting as many of the city’s attractions as possible 
e. working only part-time so you’re not so busy 
 
 
 


Activity 3 – Listen for Specific Details 
1. What's one element of New York City's diversity that Emily does NOT 
mention? 
a. activities 
b. food

2. According to Emily, New York City's energy comes from its...

5. Emily recommends getting involved in something that… 
a. Is very different from your day job 
b. You already have some experience in

Activity 4 – Listen for Specific Words 
The best part about living in New York City is that anything you could possibly 
_____________________, you can find there. There are so many different cultures 
and subcultures. You can try food from pretty much any country or 
_____________________ on the planet, and it's just a train ride away. Any type of 
activity or interest – no matter how unusual or how obscure – I’m sure you can find 
it in New York. The city has something for everyone. It's impossible to be 
_____________________. And even though it's one city, every neighborhood is 
different, they all have their own unique kind of vibe. 
Another thing I loved about New York City is that it has a special kind of energy 
about it, it's very _____________________. And I think part of this comes from the 
fact that a lot of people in the city aren't originally from there. So not only do you 
have a lot of immigrants from other countries, but also people from other 
_____________________ in the U.S. who have moved to New York City - and they 
usually have some sort of goal or mission that they’re trying to accomplish, whether 
for their career or for _____________________ reasons... so New York is just full of 
go-getters and people who are doing exciting things. You won't really find a lot of 
people who are _____________________ and just let life pass them by. 
Now, the flip side is that living in New York can stress you out if you're not 
_____________________. They call it “the city that never sleeps” because there is 
something going on 24/7, and it's just pretty fast-paced in general. So that could be a 
_____________________ if you're not used to it – people walk fast, they expect fast 
customer service, and everything to be really snappy and _____________________. 
So if you’re living at this speed and you also have a demanding job, then you really 
need to consciously make room in your _____________________ to relax and plan to 
have some downtime. 
And then there’s financial stress, too, because New York is definitely pricey. Mainly 
rent – like, compared to other places in the country, you'll pay 
_____________________ times as much for a ridiculously small apartment. But it’s 
not out of reach, you just have to budget and be adaptable… and you probably won’t 


be _____________________ much time in your apartment, anyway, so in my opinion, 
it’s worth it. 
If you're thinking of living in New York, my main suggestion is to get plugged in to 
some sort of group, club, or community, or take up a new activity to meet people, 
‘cause _____________________ the city can be overwhelming and you can end up 
feeling kind of isolated. On the streets people usually keep to themselves. Everyone 
minds their own business, so at first glance it seems like New Yorkers are pretty 
_____________________ off – but it’s way easier to make friends if you join a group 
or take a class, you know? You should definitely take advantage of the chance to do 
something you've never done before, maybe that you’ve always wanted to try, and 
get _____________________ your comfort zone a little bit. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Complete Transcript 
The best part about living in New York City is that anything you could possibly 
want, you can find there. There are so many different cultures and subcultures. You 
can try food from pretty much any country or ethnicity on the planet, and it's just a 
train ride away. Any type of activity or interest – no matter how unusual or how 
obscure – I’m sure you can find it in New York. The city has something for everyone. 
It's impossible to be bored. And even though it's one city, every neighborhood is 
different, they all have their own unique kind of vibe. 
Another thing I loved about New York City is that it has a special kind of energy 
about it, it's very dynamic. And I think part of this comes from the fact that a lot of 
people in the city aren't originally from there. So not only do you have a lot of 
immigrants from other countries, but also people from other places in the U.S. who 
have moved to New York City - and they usually have some sort of goal or mission 
that they’re trying to accomplish, whether for their career or for personal reasons... 
so New York is just full of go-getters and people who are doing exciting things. You 
won't really find a lot of people who are passive and just let life pass them by. 
Now, the flip side is that living in New York can stress you out if you're not careful. 
They call it “the city that never sleeps” because there is something going on 24/7, 
and it's just pretty fast-paced in general. So that could be a shock if you're not used 
to it – people walk fast, they expect fast customer service, and everything to be 
really snappy and efficient. So if you’re living at this speed and you also have a 
demanding job, then you really need to consciously make room in your schedule to 
relax and plan to have some downtime. 
And then there’s financial stress, too, because New York is definitely pricey. Mainly 
rent – like, compared to other places in the country, you'll pay three times as much 
for a ridiculously small apartment. But it’s not out of reach, you just have to budget 
and be adaptable… and you probably won’t be spending much time in your 
apartment, anyway, so in my opinion, it’s worth it. 
If you're thinking of living in New York, my main suggestion is to get plugged in to 
some sort of group, club, or community, or take up a new activity to meet people, 
‘cause otherwise the city can be overwhelming and you can end up feeling kind of 
isolated. On the streets people usually keep to themselves. Everyone minds their 
own business, so at first glance it seems like New Yorkers are pretty closed off – but 
it’s way easier to make friends if you join a group or take a class, you know? You 


should definitely take advantage of the chance to do something you've never done 
before, maybe that you’ve always wanted to try, and get outside your comfort zone 
a little bit. 
 
Extra Vocabulary 
“There are so many different cultures and subcultures” 
A “subculture” is a distinct smaller cultural group within a larger cultural 
group. Subcultures usually form around particular activities, interests, or 
beliefs, and have their own typical style, appearances, and slang/expressions. 
“New York is just full of go-getters” 
A “go-getter” is a person who takes action and makes things happen.  
“and everything to be really snappy and efficient.” 
 
“Snappy” is an informal word meaning “quick and energetic.” 
“plan to have some downtime.” 
 
“Downtime” means a period of rest, relaxation, and little activity. 
“on the streets people usually keep to themselves. Everyone minds their own 
business” 
Both “keep to themselves” and “minds their own business” are ways of saying 
that people don’t interact very much with others; they don’t get involved in 
other people’s situations. 
“get outside your comfort zone a little bit.” 
Your “comfort zone” is the collection of activities/situations that you are 
already comfortable with, so to “get outside your comfort zone” means to do 
something that challenges you or makes you a little uncomfortable. 
 
 
 
 


PART 2 – Nicole from Australia 
Speaker: Nicole – Australian  
 
Listening Activity: True or False? 
1. She moved to New York City two months ago. 
2. She thinks New Yorkers don't take time to relax. 
3. There are many car wash cafés in Sydney. 
4. Her husband is also from Australia. 
5. Her husband thought it was a great idea. 
6. One of New York City's nicknames is the "city of dreams." 
7. She says that if you slow down, you might miss a good opportunity. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Listen for Specific Words 
I moved from Sydney to New York City about ten months ago. Even though I come 
from a city, it's _____________________ compared to NYC. The very first thing I 
noticed was how fast-paced everything was. Everyone was always in a 
_____________________, no one had time to just stop, relax, and just enjoy their day. 
One time I made a suggestion to my husband for us to open up a car wash cafe, just 
like all the cafes that are all over Sydney. And he's born and bred in Brooklyn - he 
_____________________ and he said "No one in New York is gonna have time to just 
sit and sip a coffee while their car is being washed. We need our car washed in 
_____________________ time, so we can get to where we need to be." 
There's always somewhere you need to be; there's always something to do. That's 
why it's called the city of dreams. There's opportunities around every 
_____________________ and if you slow down, the next person's gonna get 
_____________________ of you. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Complete Transcript 
I moved from Sydney to New York City about ten months ago. Even though I come 
from a city, it's nothing compared to NYC. The very first thing I noticed was how 
fast-paced everything was. Everyone was always in a rush, no one had time to just 
stop, relax, and just enjoy their day. 
One time I made a suggestion to my husband for us to open up a car wash cafe, just 
like all the cafes that are all over Sydney. And he's born and bred in Brooklyn - he 
laughed and he said "No one in New York is gonna have time to just sit and sip a 
coffee while their car is being washed. We need our car washed in record time, so 
we can get to where we need to be." 
There's always somewhere you need to be; there's always something to do. That's 
why it's called the city of dreams. There's opportunities around every corner and if 
you slow down, the next person's gonna get ahead of you. 
 
Extra Vocabulary: 
"he's born and bred in Brooklyn" 
This is an informal expression meaning “born and raised” – her husband was 
born in Brooklyn and also grew up there. 
"There's opportunities around every corner" 
A “corner” is the place next to an intersection, where two roads come 
together. The expression “on every corner” or “around every corner” means 
that something is very common/frequent in that area.

lessons.title: Stay-at-Home-Dads
lessons.fullText:
Lesson 11 – Stay-at-Home Dads 
A “stay-at-home dad” is a father who stays home with the 
children and takes care of the house instead of working 
outside the home.  
To warm up, write about your own family – what were 
your mother’s and father’s roles in the home? How about 
you and your husband/wife? 
 
 
 
 
 
Activity 1 – Pre-Learn Vocabulary 
borderline (adj.) = almost; describes something that is on the edge between one 
category and another 
 
Ex) He made a lot of money in some borderline illegal business. 
speculate (v.) = make a guess based on the evidence currently available 
Ex) The company has lost money for the past three years; people are 
speculating that it might go bankrupt soon. 
breadwinner (n.) = the main person who earns money to support a family 
Ex) Ryan’s father died when he was 16, and his mother was disabled – so he 
had to drop out of school and become the breadwinner. 
feasible (adj.) = possible 
Ex) We only have a couple days of vacation; I don’t think it’s feasible to take 
an international trip in such a short time. 
proactive (adj.) = actively doing things (not just reacting to events) 


Ex) We can’t just punish bullying when it happens – instead, we need to take 
a more proactive approach by educating kids about respect. 
peers (n.) = people who are similar to you in age and social status 
Ex) Teenagers are often unwilling to try something new and risk looking 
stupid in front of their peers. 
 
 
 
Activity 2 – Listen for the General Idea 
Speaker: Nate – Australia 
Overall, this article presents being a stay-at-home dad in… 
a. A positive way 
b. A neutral way 
c. A negative way 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Activity 3 – Listen for Specific Ideas 
1. The number of stay at home dads in the U.S. has... 
a. doubled 
b. tripled 
c. quadrupled 
2. Economists suggest that today's stay-at-home dads... 
a. are less educated than working fathers 
b. lost their jobs during the recessions 
c. place a higher priority on relationships than on money 
3. According to the text, one reason women are earning more money 
now than in the past is... 
a. laws guaranteeing fair salaries for women 
b. jobs performed by women are currently in high demand 
c. more women are graduating from college 
4. Check the two reasons that being a stay-at-home dad is good: 
a. A father's parenting style develops a child's confidence 
b. Kids are better able to bond with both parents 
c. Wives who feel fulfilled in their professional lives are better mothers 
d. The family will not have to pay for a nanny 
e. Stay-at-home dads feel less stressed than working fathers 
5. Check the two reasons that being a stay-at-home dad is hard: 
a. Fathers have less natural intuition for a child's needs 
b. Men are not able to "multi-task" as well as women, so they may get 
overwhelmed 
c. Society often looks down on stay-at-home dads 
d. Stay-at-home dads may have low self-esteem and worry about their 
lack of career progress 
e. Stay-at-home dads argue more with their wives about the best way to 
raise the children 
6. The most satisfied stay-at-home dads are: 
a. Dads who also work from home 
b. Dads who have chosen to stay home 
c. Dads whose wives earn a very comfortable salary 


Activity 4 – Listen for Specific Words 
In the past, being a “stay-at-home dad” was borderline unthinkable – but 
_____________________ statistics show that in the past twenty years, the number of 
stay-at-home dads has doubled in the U.K. and tripled in the U.S. Although 
families in which the father stays home still represent a very small percentage, 
the rapid _____________________ may indicate the early stages of a trend.  
Economists have speculated that men who were laid off during the two recent 
recessions have been unable to _____________________ another job, thus leaving their 
wives as the sole breadwinners. Also, according to a recent study in the U.S., 28% 
of women now earn higher salaries than their husbands; this makes the prospect 
of being a stay-at-home dad more financially feasible. Women’s increased 
earning _____________________ is thanks to a higher number of female college 
graduates – and this trend is bound to increase, as women now outnumber men 
in American universities. 
Researchers have suggested that having a stay-at-home dad may actually be 
better for the child, because a father’s parenting _____________________ can be more 
beneficial for the child’s development in the early years. While mothers usually 
_____________________ and reassure kids who are sad or frustrated, fathers tend to 
encourage a more proactive approach to coping with the situation. This helps the 
child become more confident and emotionally _____________________. 
In addition, studies have shown that mothers who work outside the home 
frequently engage with their children _____________________ having a full-time job. 
This is not the case for men – when the father works full-time, he tends to have 
little influence or connection with his children. This leads to the conclusion that 
having a working mother and a stay-at-home dad is the best way for children to 
form _____________________ strong bonds with both parents.  
There are a few cons to reversing the stereotypical gender roles. Stay-at-home 
dads may face a _____________________ of social support or even be ridiculed for their 
role in the family. Stay-at-home dads might also struggle with their own self-
esteem, feeling that they are less manly because they _____________________ the 
activities traditionally done by women. Some also worry that they will fall behind 
in their professional lives, as they are folding laundry and _____________________ 
diapers while their peers are climbing the career ladder. 


In general, men who have made the conscious choice to be stay-at-home dads are 
more satisfied with their _____________________ than men who have been forced into 
the role due to a layoff. 
It is clear that being a stay-at-home dad is a complex issue. From a gender 
equality standpoint, the fact that men now feel more _____________________ taking on 
this role is certainly positive. However, stay-at-home dads continue to face 
unique challenges, as this family arrangement is still far from being the norm. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Complete Transcript 
In the past, being a “stay-at-home dad” was borderline unthinkable – but recent 
statistics show that in the past twenty years, the number of stay-at-home dads 
has doubled in the U.K. and tripled in the U.S. Although families in which the 
father stays home still represent a very small percentage, the rapid growth may 
indicate the early stages of a trend.  
Economists have speculated that men who were laid off during the two recent 
recessions have been unable to find another job, thus leaving their wives as the 
sole breadwinners. Also, according to a recent study in the U.S., 28% of women 
now earn higher salaries than their husbands; this makes the prospect of being a 
stay-at-home dad more financially feasible. Women’s increased earning power is 
thanks to a higher number of female college graduates – and this trend is bound 
to increase, as women now outnumber men in American universities. 
Researchers have suggested that having a stay-at-home dad may actually be 
better for the child, because a father’s parenting style can be more beneficial for 
the child’s development in the early years. While mothers usually comfort and 
reassure kids who are sad or frustrated, fathers tend to encourage a more 
proactive approach to coping with the situation. This helps the child become 
more confident and emotionally stable. 
In addition, studies have shown that mothers who work outside the home 
frequently engage with their children despite having a full-time job. This is not 
the case for men – when the father works full-time, he tends to have little 
influence or connection with his children. This leads to the conclusion that 
having a working mother and a stay-at-home dad is the best way for children to 
form equally strong bonds with both parents.  
There are a few cons to reversing the stereotypical gender roles. Stay-at-home 
dads may face a lack of social support or even be ridiculed for their role in the 
family. Stay-at-home dads might also struggle with their own self-esteem, feeling 
that they are less manly because they perform the activities traditionally done 
by women. Some also worry that they will fall behind in their professional lives, 
as they are folding laundry and changing diapers while their peers are climbing 
the career ladder. 
In general, men who have made the conscious choice to be stay-at-home dads are 
more satisfied with their status than men who have been forced into the role due 
to a layoff. 


It is clear that being a stay-at-home dad is a complex issue. From a gender 
equality standpoint, the fact that men now feel more comfortable taking on this 
role is certainly positive. However, stay-at-home dads continue to face unique 
challenges, as this family arrangement is still far from being the norm. 
 
Extra Vocabulary 
"this trend is bound to increase" 
 
This means the trend is very likely to increase; it will probably increase. 
"fathers tend to encourage a more proactive approach to coping with the 
situation" 
“Coping with” something means to react to / handle it – especially handling 
difficulties. 
"the best way for children to form equally strong bonds with both parents." 
The word “bonds” means links or connections – in this case, emotional 
connections. 
“There are a few cons to reversing the stereotypical gender roles.” 
The word “cons” means disadvantages. It comes from the expression “pros 
and cons” (advantages and disadvantages) 
“Stay-at-home dads may… be ridiculed for their role in the family. Stay-at-home 
dads might also struggle with their own self-esteem” 
The verb “ridicule” means to say or do things that intentionally humiliate 
someone. To “struggle with” something means to have difficulty with it. 
"their peers are climbing the career ladder." 
The expression “career ladder” refers to the process of moving up in your 
career, getting promoted to higher and better positions. 
"stay-at-home dads continue to face unique challenges" 
 
In this sentence, “face” is a verb meaning to encounter or confront. 
"this family arrangement is still far from being the norm." 
 
“The norm” means something considered standard or typical. 


Activity 2 Answer: 
This article presents being a stay-at-home dad in... (b) A neutral way 
 
Activity 3 Answers: 
1. b 
2. b 
3. c 
4. a & b 
5. c & d 
6. b

lessons.title: Embarrassing-Moments
lessons.fullText:
Lesson 12 – Embarrassing Moments 
Write about a time you felt embarrassed. When embarrassing 
things happen to you, do you feel upset, or are you able to 
laugh about them? 
 
 
 
 
 
Activity 1 – Pre-Learn Vocabulary 
ankle (n.) = the joint between your leg and your foot 
 
bare (adj.) = without the usual covering or clothing; exposed to view. In this photo, 
the woman’s arms and shoulders are bare: 
 
barn (n.) = a building that is used for keeping animals and storing crops 


change (n.) = in the context of this audio, the noun “change” refers to coins, a small 
amount of money 
 
nightstand (n.) = a small table next to a bed. Also called a night table. 
 
nickel (n.) = in the United States, a nickel is a 5-cent coin. 
pit (n.) = a hole in the ground; usually one that is deep and/or wide 
 
porch (n.) = a platform on the outside of a house. Porches are often covered: 


yucky (adj.) = an informal word for “disgusting.” 
 
Ex) My son refuses to eat broccoli, he says it’s yucky. 
 
Activity 2 – Listen for General Ideas 
Speaker: Chris – American 
Chris talks about three embarrassing incidents that happened 
when he was a child. Fill in the details of the places where they 
occurred, and the people involved: 
Places:  
• home 
• a farm 
• an amusement park 
People:  
• a friend’s family 
• some girls 
• his brother 
 
 
Place 
People 
First situation 
 
 
 
Second situation 
 
 
 
Third situation 
 
 
 


Activity 3 – Listen for Specific Details 
True or False? 
1. Story 1: Chris wanted to buy some cookies. 
2. Story 1: His brother was unhappy when he found out what Chris had done. 
3. Story 2: Chris got lost at the amusement park. 
4. Story 2: Chris urinated in a public place. 
5. Story 3: Chris had permission to explore the farm. 
6. Story 3: Chris tried to jump across the pit. 
7. Story 3: The pit was filled with garbage. 
8. Story 3: The family didn’t let Chris into the house after he got dirty. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Activity 4 – Listen for Specific Words 
Hi, my name is Chris and I wanted to tell you about some embarrassing moments 
that I had from my _____________________. 
The first one isn't that big of a deal, but I still remember being embarrassed. I 
wanted to go get some candy, and I didn't have _____________________ change. 
Well, I noticed that my brother had some sitting on his nightstand - and so I figured 
I'd _____________________ a little bit. Well later on, I found out that I accidentally 
spent his two-headed nickel, and he was really, really upset – and I was so 
embarrassed because I couldn't do _____________________ about it.  
The next embarrassing moment happened when I was about three or four years old. 
My _____________________ took us to a roller coaster park called King’s Island. 
Now, during the day I had to go to the bathroom. Well, I did what a lot of three or 
four-year-old boys do: I _____________________ my pants and underwear down to 
my ankles, and I was ready to go right where I was standing. Fortunately, my 
parents were able to _____________________ me before I did anything. 
Unfortunately, during this time a couple of girls walked by, and they started 
laughing at my bare bottom. Looking back, they were probably just laughing 
because it was _____________________, but I remember being so embarrassed as a 
child. 
This one is probably the most embarrassing moment that I can recall. My uncle 
Ronnie took me to a friend's farm. They invited us over for _____________________ 
and said that I could explore their farm before we ate. So I went out and I checked 
things out. I ended up going inside of one of the barns. I got to see some cats, some 
_____________________ and some cows. Well after a while my uncle called for me, 
saying it was time for dinner. So I headed out of the barn, but before I made it to the 


door, I noticed this pit - it was about two feet wide, one foot 
_____________________, and spanned the length of the barn - so I jumped across it.  
The problem is, I didn't make it - I fell down inside of the pit. And I noticed it was 
pretty sticky and gooey and yucky, and it _____________________ really bad. I cried 
out for some help; my uncle rushed in and discovered that I was covered from 
_____________________ to toe in cow poop. He took me back to the house, and I 
remember standing there on their porch with the entire family 
_____________________ at me, and I was just covered. It was so embarrassing! 
But luckily they were so gracious and _____________________; they let me use their 
bathroom, and I got a shower and got cleaned up. And they even still 
_____________________ me the best dinner that I ever had. 
So my advice to you is if you ever find yourself in that same situation, make sure you 
can jump the _____________________ pit, or don't bother trying at all. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Complete Transcript 
Hi, my name is Chris and I wanted to tell you about some embarrassing moments 
that I had from my childhood. 
The first one isn't that big of a deal, but I still remember being embarrassed. I 
wanted to go get some candy, and I didn't have enough change. Well, I noticed that 
my brother had some sitting on his nightstand - and so I figured I'd borrow a little 
bit. Well later on, I found out that I accidentally spent his two-headed nickel, and he 
was really, really upset – and I was so embarrassed because I couldn't do anything 
about it.  
The next embarrassing moment happened when I was about three or four years old. 
My family took us to a roller coaster park called King’s Island. Now, during the day I 
had to go to the bathroom. Well, I did what a lot of three or four-year-old boys do: I 
pulled my pants and underwear down to my ankles, and I was ready to go right 
where I was standing. Fortunately, my parents were able to stop me before I did 
anything. Unfortunately, during this time a couple of girls walked by, and they 
started laughing at my bare bottom. Looking back, they were probably just laughing 
because it was cute, but I remember being so embarrassed as a child. 
This one is probably the most embarrassing moment that I can recall. My uncle 
Ronnie took me to a friend's farm. They invited us over for dinner and said that I 
could explore their farm before we ate. So I went out and I checked things out. I 
ended up going inside of one of the barns. I got to see some cats, some pigs and 
some cows. Well after a while my uncle called for me, saying it was time for dinner. 
So I headed out of the barn, but before I made it to the door, I noticed this pit - it was 
about two feet wide, one foot deep, and spanned the length of the barn - so I jumped 
across it.  
The problem is, I didn't make it - I fell down inside of the pit. And I noticed it was 
pretty sticky and gooey and yucky, and it smelled really bad. I cried out for some 
help; my uncle rushed in and discovered that I was covered from head to toe in cow 
poop. He took me back to the house, and I remember standing there on their porch 
with the entire family looking at me, and I was just covered. It was so embarrassing! 
But luckily they were so gracious and kind; they let me use their bathroom, and I 
got a shower and got cleaned up. And they even still served me the best dinner that 
I ever had. 


So my advice to you is if you ever find yourself in that same situation, make sure you 
can jump the entire pit, or don't bother trying at all. 
 
Extra Vocabulary 
"The first one isn't that big of a deal" 
If something is “a big deal” it means it’s very important, very significant – so 
something that isn’t a big deal means it’s not very important/significant. 
"I accidentally spent his two-headed nickel" 
The two sides of a coin are called heads and tails. 
A “two-headed nickel” means a 5-cent coin on 
which both sides have the “heads” image. It would 
be an unusual item, a collector’s item. 
"the pit… spanned the length of the barn" 
 
This means that the pit extended throughout the length of the barn. 
"it was pretty sticky and gooey and yucky" 
“Sticky” describes a substance that is adhesive. Tape and glue are sticky. The 
adjective “gooey” refers to a thick liquid that is also sticky. Honey and 
chocolate sauce can be described as gooey. 
"But luckily they were so gracious and kind" 
If a person is “gracious,” it means he/she is nice, polite, friendly, and 
compassionate. This is different from “graceful,” which describes a person 
who is elegant in his/her movements (a dancer is graceful).

Lesson 13 –  
The Stanford Prison Experiment 
Why do prison guards mistreat and abuse 
prisoners? Today, you’ll learn about a famous 
psychology experiment that tried to find an 
answer to this question. 
To warm up, write your opinion about prisons. 
How comfortable (or not) should they be? Are 
they effective in punishing criminals? What 
kinds of crimes should or should not result in 
time in prison? 
 
 
 
 
Activity 1 – Pre-Learn Vocabulary 
basement (n.) – the level of a house/building that is underground 
 
Ex) I keep all the tools and extra cleaning supplies in the basement. 
premise (n.) – a basic idea, especially one that is used as proof of a theory 
Ex) The premises of his argument are true, but I think he comes to the 
wrong conclusion. 
brutality (n.) – the quality of being brutal, cruel, treating other people very 
badly, usually with violence 
Ex) A child was killed and his body cut into pieces. The brutality of the crime 
shocked the community. 
innate (adj.) – if a quality is “innate,” it means you are born with it 


Ex) If you don’t have innate talent, you can still succeed if you work hard.  
blindfolded (v./adj.) – having a cloth covering your eyes 
so that you can’t see 
Ex) The circus performer can walk across a tightrope 
while blindfolded. 
harass (v.) – irritate someone with verbal attacks or 
actions 
Ex) In that country, beautiful women wearing revealing clothing often get 
harassed by men on the street. 
petty (adj.) – small and unimportant 
Ex) My sister and her husband often have huge fights over petty issues that 
aren’t worth arguing over. 
demeaning (adj.) – humiliating in an insulting way, which makes the person feel 
or seem less than human 
Ex) That commercial attempts to use racial stereotypes in a humorous way, 
but many people view it as demeaning. 
veer (v.) – to turn suddenly from the main direction, to a very different direction 
Ex) The driver, trying to avoid hitting a dog, veered off the road and crashed 
into a tree. 
curtail (v.) – to stop something or cut it short 
 
Ex) New laws are being passed to curtail corruption in the government. 
trauma (n.) – serious injury; can be physical or emotional 
Ex) After the accident, the biker was taken to the hospital with severe head 
trauma. 
 
 
 
 


Activity 2 – Listen for General Ideas 
Speaker: Janet – British 
The first time you listen, focus only on the numbers.  
Which is the correct number for each phrase? 
1. The experiment took place in 1973 / 1983. 
2. The volunteers were offered $15 / $50 a day to participate. 
3. The number of participants was 21 / 31. 
4. The experiment was scheduled to run for 10 / 14 days. 
5. The first prisoner had to be removed after just 24 / 36 hours. 
6. The experiment was ended after 4 / 6 days. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Activity 3 – Listen for Specific Details 
Mark each sentence as true or false – and correct the false ones if you can. 
1. The experiment was done at a university. 
2. The volunteers were not tested for potential psychological problems 
beforehand. 
3. The police were involved in the simulation. 
4. The basement was made to look like a real prison. 
5. The guards received some items like whistles and handcuffs. 
6. There were no rules in the prison. 
7. The prisoners tried to gain special favor with the guards. 
8. Some of the prisoners' mental states began to deteriorate. 
9. The researchers stopped the experiment because it was getting physically 
violent. 
10. The study concludes that people with certain types of personalities are 
more likely to abuse others. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Activity 4 – Listen for Specific Words 
The treatment of prisoners by prison guards has been a hot topic in psychology 
and _____________________ over the years. In 1973, Philip Zimbardo decided to set up 
an experiment in a basement at Stanford University to _____________________ the 
extent to which groups of volunteers would conform to their respective roles as 
guards and prisoners.  
The main premise of this _____________________ was to test the assertion that the 
perceived brutality of prison guards owed more to their innate personalities than 
the _____________________ of the prison environment. 
After the mock prison was constructed, seventy-five volunteers were screened for 
psychological abnormalities and offered $15 dollars a day to play their roles as 
guards or prisoners. Twenty-one participants were selected and randomly 
_____________________ their roles as prisoners or guards.  
To keep the situation as _____________________ as possible, the ‘prisoners’ were 
arrested at their homes on an unannounced day and taken to the local police 
station, before being processed and _____________________ to the ‘prison.’ During 
processing the prisoners were fingerprinted, photographed and ‘booked’ as 
though they were real criminals. Afterwards they were blindfolded and driven to 
the psychology department basement, which had been converted into a prison, 
complete with tiny cells, _____________________ on the doors and windows, and bare, 
whitewashed walls. 
The ‘guards’ were given _____________________, whistles, handcuffs and shaded glasses 
to restrict eye contact with ‘prisoners.’ The only real rule set in place was the 
prohibition of physical violence – and Zimbardo settled back to _____________________ 
the situation as it unfolded. The experiment was scheduled to run for 14 days. 
Within just a few _____________________, the prison ‘guards’ had begun harassing the 
‘prisoners’ with insults and assigning them petty and demeaning tasks and duties. 
The prisoners also began to assume their roles, gossiping about prison 
_____________________ and sneakily telling the guards snippets of information about 
their co-prisoners in the hope of gaining favor. They took the rules of the prison 
increasingly _____________________, even siding with guards over potential 
troublemaking inmates.  


As the prisoners became more submissive, the guards became more aggressive 
and strict. One of the prisoners began to _____________________ and cry uncontrollably, 
and had to be removed from the role-play after just 36 hours of incarceration. His 
thoughts had spiraled into the realm of irrationality and he had begun to veer 
towards deep _____________________. Three others had to be removed over the 
following days due to fears about the deterioration of their mental state. All of 
these ‘prisoners’ were able to resume their normal mental functions 
_____________________ after removal from the experiment. 
After just six days the researchers decided to curtail the experiment, concerned 
about possibly _____________________ serious psychological or emotional trauma to 
the participants.  
The study _____________________ some interesting conclusions about personality, 
human nature, and the power of socially- and institutionally-supported authority. 
When prison guards are accused of being vicious and despicable towards 
prisoners, it may not necessarily be due to _____________________ in their individual 
character – perhaps it is the result of an inherently flawed system and 
circumstances that _____________________ abuse. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Complete Transcript 
The treatment of prisoners by prison guards has been a hot topic in psychology 
and sociology over the years. In 1973, Philip Zimbardo decided to set up an 
experiment in a basement at Stanford University to investigate the extent to 
which groups of volunteers would conform to their respective roles as guards and 
prisoners.  
The main premise of this study was to test the assertion that the perceived 
brutality of prison guards owed more to their innate personalities than the 
dynamics of the prison environment. 
After the mock prison was constructed, seventy-five volunteers were screened for 
psychological abnormalities and offered fifteen dollars a day to play their roles as 
guards or prisoners. Twenty-one participants were selected and randomly 
assigned their roles as prisoners or guards.  
To keep the situation as realistic as possible, the ‘prisoners’ were arrested at their 
homes on an unannounced day and taken to the local police station, before being 
processed and transferred to the ‘prison.’ During processing the prisoners were 
fingerprinted, photographed and ‘booked’ as though they were real 
criminals. Afterwards they were blindfolded and driven to the psychology 
department basement, which had been converted into a prison, complete with tiny 
cells, bars on the doors and windows, and bare, whitewashed walls. 
The ‘guards’ were given uniforms, whistles, handcuffs and shaded glasses to 
restrict eye contact with ‘prisoners.’ The only real rule set in place was the 
prohibition of physical violence – and Zimbardo settled back to observe the 
situation as it unfolded. The experiment was scheduled to run for 14 days. 
Within just a few hours, the prison ‘guards’ had begun harassing the ‘prisoners’ 
with insults and assigning them petty and demeaning tasks and duties. The 
prisoners also began to assume their roles, gossiping about prison issues and 
sneakily telling the guards snippets of information about their co-prisoners in the 
hope of gaining favor. They took the rules of the prison increasingly seriously, 
even siding with guards over potential troublemaking inmates.  
As the prisoners became more submissive, the guards became more aggressive 
and strict. One of the prisoners began to scream and cry uncontrollably, and had 
to be removed from the role-play after just 36 hours of incarceration. His thoughts 
had spiraled into the realm of irrationality and he had begun to veer towards deep 
depression. Three others had to be removed over the following days due to fears 


about the deterioration of their mental state. All of these ‘prisoners’ were able to 
resume their normal mental functions quickly after removal from the experiment. 
After just six days the researchers decided to curtail the experiment, concerned 
about possibly causing serious psychological or emotional trauma to the 
participants.  
The study suggests some interesting conclusions about personality, human 
nature, and the power of socially- and institutionally-supported authority. When 
prison guards are accused of being vicious and despicable towards prisoners, it 
may not necessarily be due to defects in their individual character – perhaps it is 
the result of an inherently flawed system and circumstances that encourage 
abuse. 
 
Extra Vocabulary 
“the extent to which groups of volunteers would conform to their respective roles 
as guards and prisoners.” 
 
To “conform” means to correspond in form or behavior. 
“seventy-five volunteers were screened for psychological abnormalities” 
To “screen” people/things means to examine them systematically, to 
determine if they are appropriate or meet certain standards 
“After the mock prison was constructed” 
 
The word “mock” as an adjective means simulated, pretend, not real. 
“a prison, complete with tiny cells, bars on the doors and windows, and bare, 
whitewashed walls.” 
“Cells” are the rooms in a prison. If something is “bare,” it means it is plain, 
without any decoration – and “whitewashed” simply means painted white. 
This word is typically used for walls and buildings. 
“observe the situation as it unfolded.” 
 
In this context, the word “unfolded” means “developed.” 
“sneakily telling the guards snippets of information” 


A “snippet” is a tiny piece of something 
“even siding with guards over potential troublemaking inmates.” 
To “side with” someone means to take their “side” in a conflict, to agree with 
and support them. “Inmates” are prisoners; people confined to a prison. 
“36 hours of incarceration.” 
 
The word “incarceration” means being in prison. 
“His thoughts had spiraled into the realm of irrationality” 
This means that his thoughts quickly went down (spiraled) into the area 
(realm) of non-logical thinking (irrationality). 
 “perhaps it is the result of an inherently flawed system” 
If something is “inherently flawed,” it means that a mistake, error, or 
problem (flaw) is included and can’t be avoided/removed (inherent). The 
only way to correct an “inherent flaw” is to completely change or replace the 
system. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Activity 2 Answers: 
1. The experiment took place in 1973. 
2. The volunteers were offered $15 a day to participate. 
3. The number of participants was 21. 
4. The experiment was scheduled to run for 14 days. 
5. The first prisoner had to be removed after just 36 hours. 
6. The experiment was ended after 6 days. 
 
 
 
Activity 3 Answers: 
1. True 
2. False - the volunteers were checked for possible problems, and many were 
eliminated 
3. True 
4. True 
5. True 
6. False - there was a rule prohibiting physical violence 
7. True 
8. True 
9. False - they stopped it because there was a risk of emotional/psychological 
damage to the participants 
10. False - it suggests that the problem is the system, not necessarily the 
individuals

Lesson 14 – About My Pets 
Have you ever had a pet? If so, write about it.  
If not, what type of pet would you like to have? 
 
 
 
Activity 1 – Pre-Learn Vocabulary 
auction (n.) = a public sale in which each item is sold to the person who offers the 
highest price for it. The various offers of prices at an auction are called “bids.” 
Ex) I bid $200 for an antique table at an auction, but I didn’t get it because 
someone else bid $350. 
autistic (adj.) = a person who is autistic has the medical condition called autism, 
which seriously limits the person’s ability to communicate and interact socially 
Ex) iPads can sometimes help autistic kids communicate through pictures and 
symbols. 
fixed (adj.) = in the context of this audio, a pet being “fixed” means it has been 
neutered; it has had an operation on its sexual organs so that it can’t reproduce 
Ex) Our dog had eight puppies and we had to give them all up for adoption. The 
following month, we had her fixed so that this won’t happen again. 
litter (n.) = in the context of this audio, “litter” refers to an absorbent material that 
is used inside an animal’s cage or box (called a “litter box”), which can absorb the 
animal’s urine/feces: 
 


flea / tick (n.) = both of these are tiny insects that drink blood and are often found 
on cats and dogs 
 
flea   
 
 tick 
mischief (n.) = this word refers to trouble or behavior that causes annoyance or a 
disturbance – but usually of a fun and innocent type 
Ex) My son got into some mischief at school – he put a rubber snake on the 
teacher’s chair. 
fond (adj.) = if you are “fond of” someone or something, it means you have a strong 
liking for it, you feel affection for it 
Ex) I’m very fond of that author’s writing; I’ve read all her books and loved 
every single one.

"Shadow," so I said hey, let's call it Nightshadow. He agreed and he loved that. 
I have two little boys and we wanted a pet in the house and so we went ahead and 
we got this cat. Now the way we got the cat was really nice. There's an auction site 
that I go to and I buy things from. The lady who worked there put a cat up on sale 
and it was for free. It needed a good home because it was a rescue cat and the other 
cats in the house weren't treating it so nice, so she needed to find a good home for 
it.  
So I said "Hey, we're looking for a pet," she gave me information, and we talked for 
a little bit and she said, "Wow, I think that would be a great place for the cat to live," 
because I told her about me being a single dad, and my two boys, my youngest 
being autistic and them really wanting an animal in the house. 
So she came over, brought all the items - it was really cool too because the cat was 
not only fixed, it had a chip inside of it and it’s got our address, she made sure it 
went to our address in case the cat ever gets lost. She brought food, she brought 
over cat litter, a cat box, a cat drink bowl and food bowl - I mean, she gave me 
everything, even flea and tick repellent 
So it's a really great pet, she’s so much fun, she climbs, she even jumps up on my 
shoulder, she's really fearless, jumps everywhere. Loves to play, loves to eat, and so 
- really great cat.  
CHRISTINA 
Hi, my name is Christina and I want to tell you about some of the animals that I have 
at my house. The only animal that we have living indoors with us is a white 


Labrador puppy, and her name is Izzy. We've had her for about a month now, and 
she is about four months old. 
I usually get up about six AM and I feed her and take her outside to go to the 
bathroom, and then we spend about five minutes running around outside, chasing 
each other and tossing a ball. She's always ready to go early in the morning, and I 
usually am not - so it's a good way to get my body moving and wake up. 
Izzy is really, really good with kids, she really likes them a lot, and she loves to kiss 
them and she is very protective of them, especially my four-month-old son. 
Whenever he is crying, she is always going over to him to try to take care of him - 
but she doesn't realize how big she is, and so usually we have to pull her back so 
she doesn't hurt him.  
Since I've only had her a month, I can't really say that she's been in a whole lot of 
trouble - but she did get into a little bit of mischief about a week ago. It had rained 
pretty hard here and there is a part of the road that runs into a hill. And between the 
road and the hill is a small drainage area for water to go into the creek. It was filled 
with water and my boys made their way over there and started splashing in the 
water. 
Well, they had their raincoats on and their rain boots on, so that wasn't so big of a 
deal, but my little dog Izzy had no raincoat and no boots, and she went splashing 
through all of the water - so as I told you before, she is a white Labrador, and after 
she did this, she was more of the color of a brown Labrador. I immediately had to 
wash her up right away and make sure she didn't have any ticks on her. But she's 
been a real blessing in our house and we really love her very very much. 
I also have some chickens, and the chickens are pretty easy to take care of. We go 
outside in the morning, usually when I'm taking my dog out, and I'll let them out of 
their chicken coop so that they can walk around. I usually feed them once a day. 
I also have a rabbit that my oldest got when he was two years old, and so of course 
he named the rabbit Two after his age. And this rabbit is so much fun because every 
other rabbit I walk up to runs away from me as fast as possible. But this rabbit, Two, 
will actually run towards me, and I've grown really fond of him. 
 
 


Extra Vocabulary 
"It needed a good home because it was a rescue cat" 
 
This means the cat was rescued from living on the streets. 
Labrador puppy (n.) = a “puppy” is a baby dog; and “Labrador” is the name of the 
dog’s breed (type): 
 
“we spend about five minutes running around outside, chasing each other and 
tossing a ball” 
 
The verb “toss” means to throw something lightly and casually. 
"between the road and the hill is a small drainage area for water to go into the 
creek." 
A creek is a very, very small river. The word “drainage” refers to excess water 
leaving an area and going out into another place. 
 "my boys started splashing in the water" 
The word “splash” means to make movements in the 
water so that water flies everywhere. 
"I'll let them out of their chicken coop" 
 
A “chicken coop” is a place to keep chickens. 
 
 
 
 


Activity 2 Answers 
Adam's pet is a cat. 
Christina's pets are a puppy (dog), chickens, and a rabbit.

2. c 
3. b

12. a

Lesson 15 – The LEGO Story 
What were some of your favorite toys and games 
when you were a child? 
 
 
 
Activity 1 – Learn Vocabulary  
saga (n.) – a long detailed story or report 
 
Ex) This book tells the saga of the royal family in 17th-century England. 
iconic (adj.) – very famous for a long time in culture and society 
 
Ex) Russell Crowe starred in the iconic film Gladiator. 
motto (n.) – a short phrase that expresses a main guiding principle or ideal, 
which a person or organization always tries to follow 
 
Ex) The motto of the city police department is “to protect and serve.” 
patent (n./v.) – official legal protection for an idea or product, so that only one 
person/company has permission to use, produce, and sell it for a period of time 
Ex) George patented his invention to prevent it from being copied by 
competitors. 
ingenious (adj.) – intelligent, skillful, and creative (can describe a physical 
product, or an idea or plan) 
Ex) Sarah created an ingenious program in order to get the students more 
interested in reading. 
medieval (adj.) – related to the Middle Ages (with castles, knights, etc.) 
 
Ex) My kids loved attending the medieval fair. 
overtly (adv.) – obviously, visibly 
Ex) Bob overtly dislikes Alan; he doesn’t even try to hide his feelings. 


license (v.) – get official authorization or permission 
Ex) In order to open a restaurant, you need to get licensed by the city after 
an inspection by the health department.  
plethora (n.) – many, an excess 
Ex) I received a plethora of e-mail inquiries after posting pictures online of 
six adorable puppies available for adoption. 
landmarks (n.) – famous points in a city or country 
 
Ex) The Statue of Liberty is one of the landmarks of New York City. 
milestone (n.) – an important event or achievement in a process 
Ex) The opening of a new community center was a milestone for our 
organization. 
acclaim (v.) – publicly approve and praise 
Ex) Rebecca is an internationally-acclaimed artist; her work has been 
featured in twenty-five countries. 
 
Activity 2 – Listen for General Ideas 
Speaker: Robert – Australian 
Listen and put the events in order from 1 to 9: 
1. LEGO is founded in 1932 
      The first official LEGO World Cup building championships are held 
      LEGO creates sets with different themes 
      LEGO develops robotic sets that connect to computers 
      The LEGO Movie is produced 
      The LEGOLAND theme park opens 
      LEGO begins making plastic toys 
      The workshop and factory are destroyed 
      Two Guinness World Records involving LEGOs are set 


Activity 3 – Listen for Specific Details 
1. Lego is the world’s _________ toy manufacturer. 
a. largest 
b. second-largest 
c. third-largest 
2. Lego's company motto is: 
a. Creative play 
b. Building fun 
c. Play well 
3. Lego originally made: 
a. children’s clothes 
b. household items 
c. wooden toys 
4. Lego's factory was destroyed three times by: 
a. fire 
b. war 
c. financial problems 
5. Lego's main innovation was: 
a. the interlocking brick 
b. the marketing of themed sets 
c. toys that encourage creativity 
6. Lego does NOT have toys with a theme that is: 
a. feminine 
b. military 
c. for kids under age 5 
7. The LEGOLAND theme park includes both rides and: 
a. LEGO-building competitions 
b. educational activities 
c. special, limited-edition LEGO sets 
 


8. The Guinness World Records set in 1992 involve: 
a. a castle and a railway line 
b. realistic replicas of famous landmarks 
c. a boat and the tallest LEGO tower  
9. Legos are also used by: 
a. architects 
b. scientists 
c. writers 
10. 
The LEGO movie earned $400m in the first: 
a. day 
b. week 
c. month 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Activity 4 – Listen for Specific Words 
From its humble beginnings in a poor carpenter’s shop to its current 
_____________________ as the world’s third-largest manufacturer of toys, the LEGO saga 
spans more than 80 years.  
This iconic global _____________________ was founded in Denmark in 1932 by a 
carpenter named Ole Kirk Christiansen. The name LEGO derives from two Danish 
words “leg” and “godt” meaning “play” and “good” – with the _____________________ of 
transmitting the company’s motto ‘play well.’ The original LEGO toys were made 
of wood. 
LEGO was not very _____________________ in its early days due to the Great Depression, 
and Christiansen’s workshop and toy factory burned down not once, not twice, but 
three times. After World War II, _____________________ became available in Denmark 
and LEGO began selling plastic toys. However, these were initially not well-
received by the public. Not only were sales poor, but many purchased products 
were _____________________. 
The company’s key innovation, patented in the late 1950s, remains the 
_____________________ yet ingenious LEGO brick, which has been named ‘Toy of the 
Century’ on two occasions. The brick’s unique interlocking facility offers 
_____________________ possibilities for creative play.  
LEGO has released thousands of sets with dozens of themes such as 
_____________________ exploration, pirates, the medieval world, undersea exploration, 
the wild west, and town and city. Notably absent are LEGO sets with an overtly 
military theme – this is _____________________, based on Christiansen’s belief that 
children’s toys should not encourage war.  
LEGO has also introduced a number of special product _____________________, such as 
their DUPLO range for players under the age of five, and has also licensed rights to 
use _____________________ and themes from films and cartoons such as Star Wars, 
Harry Potter, and Toy Story. 
In 1968, the LEGOLAND theme park _____________________ its gates in Billund, 
Denmark with a plethora of rides and hands-on educational activities. It now 
receives 1.6 million visitors annually and is the largest tourist attraction in 
Denmark outside of the _____________________.  


In 1988 the first official LEGO World Cup building championships were held with 
the participation of 38 children from 17 different countries. In 1992, two Guinness 
World Records _____________________ LEGO products were set: a castle built from 
nearly half a million LEGO bricks, and a LEGO railway line 545 meters in 
_____________________. 
LEGO is not only the domain of children. Many architects use it to 
_____________________ their ideas, and artist Warren Elsmore demonstrated the vast 
potential of our much-loved plastic bricks by building more than 70 models of 
international landmarks, eventually _____________________ a book about his labor of 
love entitled Brick City: Lego For Grown-ups. 
In the 2000s, LEGO began developing robotic LEGO sets that connect to computers 
via USB cables to allow for education in _____________________. Another milestone was 
the 2014 production of the LEGO Movie. A massive global success, the movie 
surpassed the $400m mark in its first month in theaters and has been universally 
acclaimed by both _____________________ and viewers. A sequel is already being 
planned. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Complete Transcript 
From its humble beginnings in a poor carpenter’s shop to its current status as the 
world’s third-largest manufacturer of toys, the LEGO saga spans more than 80 
years.  
This iconic global brand was founded in Denmark in 1932 by a carpenter named 
Ole Kirk Christiansen. The name LEGO derives from two Danish words “leg” and 
“godt” meaning “play” and “good” – with the intention of transmitting the 
company’s motto ‘play well.’ The original LEGO toys were made of wood. 
LEGO was not very profitable in its early days due to the Great Depression, and 
Christiansen’s workshop and toy factory burned down not once, not twice, but 
three times. After World War II, plastic became available in Denmark and LEGO 
began selling plastic toys. However, these were initially not well-received by the 
public. Not only were sales poor, but many purchased products were returned. 
The company’s key innovation, patented in the late 1950s, remains the simple yet 
ingenious LEGO brick, which has been named ‘Toy of the Century’ on two 
occasions. The brick’s unique interlocking facility offers endless possibilities for 
creative play.  
LEGO has released thousands of sets with dozens of themes such as space 
exploration, pirates, the medieval world, undersea exploration, the wild west, and 
town and city. Notably absent are LEGO sets with an overtly military theme – this 
is intentional, based on Christiansen’s belief that children’s toys should not 
encourage war.  
LEGO has also introduced a number of special product lines, such as their DUPLO 
range for players under the age of five, and has also licensed rights to use 
characters and themes from films and cartoons such as Star Wars, Harry Potter, 
and Toy Story. 
In 1968, the LEGOLAND theme park opened its gates in Billund, Denmark with a 
plethora of rides and hands-on educational activities. It now receives 1.6 million 
visitors annually and is the largest tourist attraction in Denmark outside of the 
capital.  
In 1988 the first official LEGO World Cup building championships were held with 
the participation of 38 children from 17 different countries. In 1992, two Guinness 
World Records involving LEGO products were set: a castle built from nearly half 
a million LEGO bricks, and a LEGO railway line 545 meters in length. 


LEGO is not only the domain of children. Many architects use it to model their 
ideas, and artist Warren Elsmore demonstrated the vast potential of our much 
loved plastic bricks by building more than 70 models of international landmarks, 
eventually publishing a book about his labor of love entitled Brick City: Lego For 
Grown-ups. 
In the 2000s, LEGO began developing robotic LEGO sets that connect to computers 
via USB cables to allow for education in programming. Another milestone was the 
2014 production of the LEGO Movie. A massive global success, the movie 
surpassed the $400m mark in its first month in theaters and has been universally 
acclaimed by both critics and viewers. A sequel is already being planned. 
 
Extra Vocabulary 
“From its humble beginnings in a poor carpenter’s shop” 
When a project or person begins in a very poor or simple form, we say it has 
“humble beginnings” 
“The company’s key innovation” 
 
In this context, “key” is an adjective that means “important; essential” 
“Notably absent are LEGO sets with an overtly military theme” 
“Notably” means that something is worth noticing; it is interesting to pay 
attention to. 
“eventually publishing a book about his labor of love”  
A “labor of love” is work done because you love it or you are very interested 
in it, not for financial gain 
“A sequel is already being planned.” 
A “sequel” is a movie that comes after the first movie, and continues the 
story. 
 
You can also watch a short film about the LEGO story here! 
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NdDU_BBJW9Y  
 


Activity 2 Answers 
1. LEGO is founded in 1932 
2. The workshop and factory are destroyed 
3. LEGO begins making plastic toys 
4. LEGO creates sets with different themes 
5. The LEGOLAND theme park opens 
6. The first official LEGO World Cup building championships are held 
7. Two Guinness World Records involving LEGOs are set 
8. LEGO develops robotic sets that connect to computers 
9. The LEGO Movie is produced 
 
 
 
Activity 3 Answers 
1. c 
2. c 
3. c 
4. a 
5. a 
6. b 
7. b 
8. a 
9. a 
10. c

Lesson 17: 
Tattoos in Different Cultures 
Tattoos have been used in many different ways among the 
various cultures of the world. Some have celebrated tattoos; 
others have despised them. What do you think about tattoos? 
How are they viewed in your culture? 
 
 
 
 
  
Activity 1 – Pre-Learn Vocabulary 
mummy (n.) – a dead body that has been preserved from ancient times 
Ex) While digging a foundation for a new building, workers discovered two 
mummies that may be around 4,000 years old. 
hypothesis (n.) – an idea or explanation that can be tested to determine if it is 
true or not 
Ex) The scientist’s hypothesis, which was first published in a journal ten 
years ago, was then disproved by later experiments. 
deity (n.) – a god or goddess 
 
Ex) Some religions perform animal sacrifices to please their deities. 
labor (n.) – the process of giving birth to a baby, beginning with contractions of 
the mother’s uterus and ending with the baby being born 
 
Ex) Ryan rushed to the hospital when his wife went into labor. 
nobility (n.) – the royal social class in a society; the people who are born with or 
granted high rank and high status 
 
Ex) This palace was built as a summer residence for the country’s nobility. 


technique (n.) – the systematic procedure for performing a task 
Ex) The surgeon developed a new technique for performing what was once 
a rather dangerous operation. 
lineage (n.) – historical family line; ancestors 
Ex) I can trace my lineage back to the 1800s, but before that there are no 
reliable records. 
turbulent (adj.) – describes something that is very agitated and chaotic 
Ex) My brother and his wife have a very turbulent relationship – one week 
they’re fighting, and the next week they’re totally in love. 
outlaw (v.) – prohibit by law; make illegal 
Ex) Some people believe that outlawing guns will not, in fact, reduce 
violence because criminals will still find a way to get them. 
stigma (n.) – a perception of social disgrace 
Ex) Despite many campaigns against racism, there is still an unfortunate 
stigma in society against people with darker skin tones. 
deviant (adj.) – different from the norms of society, outside of what is 
considered acceptable (this word has a negative connotation) 
Ex) The dictator imprisoned people who were spreading ideas that he viewed 
as deviant. 
mainstream (adj.) – related to the main current of thought or belief in society; 
common and accepted by the majority of people 
Ex) I don’t watch the news because I believe the mainstream media doesn’t 
give an accurate representation of the facts. 
 
 
 
 


Activity 2 – Listen for General Ideas 
Speaker: Gary – American  
Circle the countries/cultures mentioned in the recording: 
Americas 
Arabs 
British 
Caribbean 
Egypt 
Greeks 
India 
Japan 
New Zealand 
Peru 
Romans 
Vikings 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Activity 3 – Listen for Specific Ideas 
Mark each sentence TRUE or FALSE. Also, try to correct the false sentences 
according to the listening. 
1. The Iceman's tattoos may have served medical purposes. 
2. In ancient Egypt, tattoos were used to enhance the beauty of members of 
royalty. 
3. The Greeks and Romans prohibited tattoos. 
4. The ancient method of tattooing with a sharp wooden point is still 
practiced by some people today. 
5. In the traditional Maori culture, married men and women received 
identical tattoos. 
6. Tattoos have always been fashionable in Japan. 
7. Tattoos have been associated with sailors and circus freaks in the United 
States. 
8. In the Western world today, a wide variety of people have tattoos. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Activity 4 – Listen for Specific Words 
Tattooing is an age-old way of creating _____________________ art on the body. The 
_____________________ known tattoo was discovered on the ‘The Iceman,’ a 5,200-
year-old mummy found on the Italian-Austrian border.  
When inspecting the seemingly random pattern of dots and small crosses on the 
Iceman’s lower back and right knee and ankle, Professor Brothwell at the 
University of York, England, found that the tattooed body parts corresponded 
with the _____________________ areas of stress-induced damage. This leads to the 
hypothesis that the tattoos had an essentially therapeutic role in that ancient 
_____________________; the markings may have been believed to alleviate joint pain. 
Among Egyptian mummies, tattoos were almost exclusively on females – this 
fact, combined with evidence of _____________________ status, led to the belief that 
tattoos were used to mark prostitutes in ancient Egypt. However, the theory that 
tattoos also had a supernatural protective role at the time of pregnancy and 
childbirth has recently _____________________ popularity. The distribution of tattoos 
around the abdomen, thighs, and breasts – especially the figure of a deity 
considered to be the protector of women in labor – lends _____________________ to 
this theory.  
Other ancient cultures, such as the tribes living in the Altai Mountain region 
tattooed themselves with mythical _____________________ and marks of nobility. The 
absence of tattoos was considered a mark of low birth. On the other end of the 
spectrum, the Greeks and Romans often used tattoos to mark _____________________.  
Of course, in ancient times no machines were used and tattoos were 
_____________________ by hand, using a sharp point with a wooden handle. This 
technique is still used among the indigenous Maori people of New Zealand today. 
These tattoos served a crucial role in traditional Maori culture, where facial 
tattoos represented one’s lineage and marked an important rite of passage into 
adulthood. Men were usually tattooed on their _____________________, buttocks, and 


thighs, while the women were historically tattooed around their lips and noses, 
as this prevented the skin from _____________________ wrinkled with age. 
The history of tattoos in Japan has been an especially turbulent one. Initially 
tattoos were fashionable and _____________________ high social status, then they 
became markers for prisoners, and were later outlawed. For many years they 
were associated with criminals and gangs. Although tattoos have experienced a 
resurgence in popularity among Japanese youth, there is still a stigma on them 
among the general population, and people with tattoos may be banned from 
certain _____________________, such as fitness centers and public baths. 
In the Americas, the pre-Columbian Native American cultures also used tattoos 
on women to help _____________________ them during pregnancy. For a number of 
years, tattoos were mainly found on sailors, and heavily tattooed people were 
part of “freak shows” in American circuses. In recent decades, tattoos have gone 
from a somewhat deviant practice to a mainstream part of Western 
_____________________, transcending genders, economic classes, and age groups. 
Humans have used tattoos for myriad reasons for _____________________ of years. 
Perhaps this is essentially what tattoos represent today: a _____________________ to 
our ancestral roots. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Complete Transcript 
Tattooing is an age-old way of creating permanent art on the body. The oldest 
known tattoo was discovered on the ‘The Iceman,’ a 5,200-year-old mummy 
found on the Italian-Austrian border.  
When inspecting the seemingly random pattern of dots and small crosses on the 
Iceman’s lower back and right knee and ankle, Professor Brothwell at the 
University of York, England, found that the tattooed body parts corresponded 
with the worst areas of stress-induced damage. This leads to the hypothesis that 
the tattoos had an essentially therapeutic role in that ancient culture; the 
markings may have been believed to alleviate joint pain. 
Among Egyptian mummies, tattoos were almost exclusively on females – this 
fact, combined with evidence of social status, led to the belief that tattoos were 
used to mark prostitutes in ancient Egypt. However, the theory that tattoos also 
had a supernatural protective role at the time of pregnancy and childbirth has 
recently gained popularity. The distribution of tattoos around the abdomen, 
thighs, and breasts – especially the figure of a deity considered to be the 
protector of women in labor – lends support to this theory.  
Other ancient cultures, such as the tribes living in the Altai Mountain region 
tattooed themselves with mythical animals and marks of nobility. The absence of 
tattoos was considered a mark of low birth. On the other end of the spectrum, the 
Greeks and Romans often used tattoos to mark criminals.  
Of course, in ancient times no machines were used and tattoos were applied by 
hand, using a sharp point with a wooden handle. This technique is still used 
among the indigenous Maori people of New Zealand today. 
These tattoos served a crucial role in traditional Maori culture, where facial 
tattoos represented one’s lineage and marked an important rite of passage into 
adulthood. Men were usually tattooed on their faces, buttocks, and thighs, while 
the women were historically tattooed around their lips and noses, as this 
prevented the skin from becoming wrinkled with age. 
The history of tattoos in Japan has been an especially turbulent one. Initially 
tattoos were fashionable and represented high social status, then they became 
markers for prisoners, and were later outlawed. For many years they were 
associated with criminals and gangs. Although tattoos have experienced a 
resurgence in popularity among Japanese youth, there is still a stigma on them 


among the general population, and people with tattoos may be banned from 
certain businesses, such as fitness centers and public baths. 
In the Americas, the pre-Columbian Native American cultures also used tattoos 
on women to help protect them during pregnancy. For a number of years, tattoos 
were mainly found on sailors, and heavily tattooed people were part of “freak 
shows” in American circuses. In recent decades, tattoos have gone from a 
somewhat deviant practice to a mainstream part of Western fashion, 
transcending genders, economic classes, and age groups. 
Humans have used tattoos for myriad reasons for thousands of years. Perhaps 
this is essentially what tattoos represent today: a link to our ancestral roots. 
 
Extra Vocabulary 
“the Italian-Austrian border.” 
The border is the dividing line between two countries, or two areas of 
land. 
“This leads to the hypothesis that the tattoos had an essentially therapeutic role 
in that ancient culture.” 
Something described as therapeutic is related to treating disease/injury 
or maintaining good health. 
 “the indigenous Maori people of New Zealand” 
The word indigenous refers to the people who originally lived in an area, 
before the arrival of outsiders, colonizers, etc. 
“an important rite of passage into adulthood” 
A rite of passage is any event or ritual that signifies a transition from one 
life stage to another – often, from being a child/adolescent to being an 
adult 
“tattoos have experienced a resurgence in popularity among Japanese youth” 
A resurgence is a renewal; in the context of this sentence it means that 
tattoos are now becoming popular again (after a long time when they were 
not popular) 


“people with tattoos may be banned from certain businesses” 
Banned, in this sentence, means “prevented from entering.” It can also 
mean “prohibited” as in the case of an object or action (“The new law bans 
using your cell phone while driving.”) 
“heavily tattooed people were part of “freak shows” in circuses.” 
The word freak refers to someone/something that is completely abnormal 
(not normal). It usually has a negative connotation, implying that 
something is different from the norm in a bad way. 
 
 
 
 
Activity 2 Answers: 
Americas, Egypt, Greeks, Japan, New Zealand, Romans 
 
Activity 3 Answers: 
1. True 
2. False - they were used on prostitutes and also on women to protect them 
during childbirth 
3. False - tattoos were used on criminals 
4. True 
5. False - men and women were tattooed on different parts of their bodies 
6. False - tattoos have been both loved and hated throughout Japanese 
history 
7. True 
8. True
