Lesson 18: Parents 
Warm-Up: 
Write a bit about your parents. What kind of 
work/activities do they like to do? What are their 
personalities like? Are you more similar to your 
mother or your father? 
 
 
 
 
Activity 1 – Pre-Learn Vocabulary 
outgoing (adj.) = extroverted; a person who loves social situations 
Ex) People who are outgoing can walk into a party where they don’t know 
anybody and make a dozen friends by the end of the night. 
gifted (adj.) = describing a person as “gifted” means they have special natural 
intelligence or talent 
Ex) She’s a very gifted writer – her first book was published when she was just 
14 years old. 
Navy (n.) = the branch of the military forces that involves ships, submarines, and 
other operations in the ocean 
 
combat (n.) = fighting, battle 
 
Ex) My grandfather fought in World War II and was injured in combat. 


MBA (n.) = Master of Business Administration – an advanced university degree in 
business 
repertoire (n.) = the range of skills or accomplishments of a particular person or 
group. Often used for the set of songs that a musician or musical group can play. 
Ex) I play mostly rock music, but I’d like to add some jazz songs to my 
repertoire.

Today I’m going to tell you a little bit about my parents. I’ll start with my mom. She 
is one of the most energetic people you’ll probably ever meet. She is extremely 
outgoing, the type of person who can strike up a conversation with absolutely 
anyone, and if you get her talking on one of the topics she loves – like fitness or 
music – she might just talk your ear off! 
My mom is really into exercise and healthy living – but that wasn’t always the case. 
She was overweight for many years, but over the past seven years or so, she’s lost a 
ton of weight and completely changed her lifestyle. Now she’s passionate about 
nutrition and she works out six days a week. One of her favorite workouts is called 
Zumba, which is a mixture of different Latin dance forms that’s used for exercise; 
it’s all the rage in the U.S. nowadays.

piano teacher and students would come to our house for their lessons. She also 
taught me and my brother to play. Of course we couldn’t get away with not 
practicing because we lived with our piano teacher! Nowadays she sings in two 
choirs that perform both locally and internationally – they’ve had concerts in 
Europe, Australia and New Zealand, and they’re planning one in South America. 
My mom worked for many years as a math teacher – not in a regular classroom, but 
with groups of gifted kids who needed more of a challenge than the math they were 
getting in their grade. So she would come up with games and creative ways to teach

struggling in math as well, and used these same creative teaching techniques to help

Lesson 19: The Origin of Santa Claus 
Do you know where the famous Christmas character 
of Santa Claus comes from? His origins come from a 
combination of cultural traditions and folkloric 
figures, and he has changed a lot over the years!  
To warm up, describe the Christmas traditions in 
your country/family: 
 
 
 
Activity 1 – Learn Vocabulary 
mythology (n.) – a collection of myths (stories and legends) about a 
people’s/culture’s origins, gods, heroes, etc. 
 
Ex) In Greek mythology, Zeus was the most powerful god. 
assertion (n.) – statement 
Ex) This article is not accurate; it makes a number of assertions that have 
no evidence to support them. 
chimney (n.) – the tube in your house that takes the 
smoke from the fireplace up and out. On Christmas 
Eve, Santa Claus is said to enter the house through 
the chimney, in order to deliver the presents. 
tale (n.) – story 
 
Ex) She entertained us at dinner with tales about her travels. 
depict (v.) – to represent in words or pictures 
Ex) Many European paintings depict Jesus as white, but in reality he 
probably had an olive-skinned complexion. 
far-fetched (adj.) – not easy to believe because of elements that are not likely 


Ex) Thanks to advancements in technology, many ideas that seemed far-
fetched in the past are now becoming reality. 
compelling (adj.) – very interesting and intriguing 
Ex) I’m watching a compelling documentary about history’s greatest 
unsolved mysteries. 
dowry (n.) – in some cultures, when a woman gets married, she or her family 
must give a gift of money or property to her husband. This gift is called a dowry. 
folkloric (adj.) – The word “folklore” refers to the traditional stories, beliefs, and 
myths of a people group – so something “folkloric” is related to these traditional 
stories, which may be true, imaginary, or exaggerated.  
Ex) In Mexico, we saw a folkloric dance group perform some of the country’s 
traditional dances. 
mischievous (adj.) – A person who is “mischievous” is playful and likes to have 
fun and get into trouble, often bothering other people or playing jokes/tricks on 
other people for their own amusement. 
 
Ex) My kids are very mischievous and often get in trouble at school. 
ascertain (v.) – come to a conclusion after observation or examination 
Ex) Scientists monitored the animals to ascertain the effect of the chemicals 
on their health. 
typify (v.) – be typical of something, be the perfect representation of something 
Ex) This painting typifies the artist’s work – it is very characteristic of her 
style. 
treat (n.) – something that is a special source of delight or pleasure – can be a 
special food, or a special experience 
Ex) I grew up in a big city, and it was a real treat to go camping in the 
countryside every once in a while. 
wish list (n.) – a list of things you want or hope for. These are usually objects 
that you want to buy (or hope to receive as gifts) but can also be 
events/experiences 
 
Ex) Wow, I love those shoes – they’re definitely going on my wish list. 


Activity 2 – Listen for General Ideas

Match each folkloric figure to their main characteristic: 
1. Odin 
2. Saint Nicholas 
3. Sinterklaas

7. Sinterklaas wore white and red clothing. 
8. The punishment for being bad was being sent in a bag to the North Pole. 
9. Father Christmas was an American invention.

along. Saint Nicholas was a Christian bishop who lived in the region of modern-day

to help the poor. One tale says that he miraculously supplied gifts of

Over time and after the Reformation, Saint Nicholas was largely _____________________, 
except for in Holland – where he had become the folkloric figure of Sinterklaas; a 
wise and kindly old man with a white beard, dressed in white and red clothing and 
_____________________ the skies and roofs of the houses on his horse, accompanied by 
his mischievous helpers.  
These helpers, which would 
later 
become elves, had the 
uncanny 
_____________________ to ascertain your behavior and know whether you deserved 
presents or harsh punishment – this is thought to be a Christian disciplinarian 


_____________________. If you were bad, you were said to be sent in a bag to Spain, 
where Sinterklaas was said to reside.  
In the 17th century, the Dutch took to the seas and _____________________ in North 
America, bringing their Sinterklaas stories with them. This name was anglicized to

_____________________ with a fleet of reindeer and Santa Claus’ residence was moved

come up with a _____________________ advertisement for the company using Coca-
Cola’s traditional red and white colors, thus popularizing the modern image of 
Santa Claus.

as milk and cookies, as well as to write him letters with their Christmas wish lists.

Complete Transcript 
The story of the origin of our dear old Santa Claus is fascinating – there are several 
major characters that have contributed to the creation of this cultural legend.  
Most people in the West have been told that Santa Claus is simply a caricature of 
Saint Nicholas, who lived in Asia Minor around 270-343 AD. However there are a 
huge number of elements and symbols surrounding Santa Claus that are derived 
from Norse mythology.  
For example, in Scandinavian households the god by the name of Odin was usually 
said to have left presents for the children, and the assertion that Santa climbs 
down into your house through the chimney developed from a tale in Old Norse 
legend wherein the goddess Hertha manifested in the fireplace and brought good 
luck to the home. 
Odin was depicted as a tall, old man with a white beard, wearing a cloak, who rode 
the skies and the seas on his lightning-fast eight-legged horse – you can see that 
the relation to our modern concept of Santa Claus soaring through the sky with 
his reindeer is not too far-fetched.   
Later, as Christianity evolved, the compelling figure of Saint Nicholas comes 
along. Saint Nicholas was a Christian bishop who lived in the region of modern-day 
Turkey. He was known for his benevolence and for performing miracles to help 
the poor. One tale says that he miraculously supplied gifts of gold to three girls as 
marriage dowries so that they could avoid the fate of becoming prostitutes. Saint 
Nicholas’ feast day (and perhaps his birthday) was in early December. 
Over time and after the Reformation, Saint Nicholas was largely forgotten, except 
for in Holland – where he had become the folkloric figure of Sinterklaas; a wise and 
kindly old man with a white beard, dressed in white and red clothing and riding 
the skies and roofs of the houses on his horse, accompanied by his mischievous 
helpers.  
These helpers, which would later become elves, had the uncanny ability to 
ascertain your behavior and know whether you deserved presents or harsh 
punishment – this is thought to be a Christian disciplinarian element. If you were 
bad, you were said to be sent in a bag to Spain, where Sinterklaas was said to 
reside.  
In the 17th century, the Dutch took to the seas and arrived in North America, 
bringing their Sinterklaas stories with them. This name was anglicized to Santa 
Claus, and merged with the English figure known as “Father Christmas,” a large 
man in fur-lined robes who typified the spirit of good cheer at Christmastime, 
bringing peace, joy, and good food and wine. 


Sometime in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the eight-legged horse was 
replaced with a fleet of reindeer and Santa Claus’ residence was moved from Spain 
to the North Pole. In 1930, the designer for Coca Cola was asked to come up with a 
winter advertisement for the company using Coca-Cola’s traditional red and white 
colors, thus popularizing the modern image of Santa Claus. 
Today, it is traditional for children to leave out treats for Santa such as milk and 
cookies, as well as to write him letters with their Christmas wish lists. When 
mailed, these letters are actually answered by postal workers and volunteers; in 
2009 Canadian workers replied to more than 1 million letters to Santa Claus 
written in 30 different languages. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Extra Vocabulary 
“Santa Claus is simply a caricature of Saint Nicholas” 
caricature (n.) – an exaggerated representation of a person 
“Odin was depicted as a tall, old man with a white beard, wearing a cloak” 
cloak (n.) – a long item of outer clothing that covers most of the body 
“so that they could avoid the fate of becoming prostitutes.” 
fate (n.) – destiny, end result, something that happens to you which you 
cannot control 
“These helpers, which would later become elves, had the uncanny ability to 
ascertain your behavior” 
uncanny (adj.) – so unusual that it seems a little bit supernatural, and may 
be disturbing 
“This name was anglicized to Santa Claus, and merged with the English figure 
known as Father Christmas.” 
anglicize (v.) – make more similar to English in form or style. For example, 
many immigrants who have names that are difficult for English speakers to 
pronounce “anglicize” their names when they come to the U.S. 
merge (v.) – combine, when two things mix and come together into one 
“a fleet of reindeer” 
 fleet (n.) – a group of things operated as a unit. 
We usually refer to a “fleet” of ships on the ocean. 
reindeer (n.) – the animals that are said to pull 
Santa’s sleigh 
“popularizing the modern image of Santa Claus.” 
popularize (v.) – to make popular and common, make something known 
by many people 
 
 


Activity 2 Answers 
1. b 
2. e 
3. a 
4. c 
5. d 
 
 
Activity 3 Answers 
1. False - he lived in Asia minor, in present-day Turkey 
2. True 
3. True 
4. False - he was described as an old man with a white beard. 
5. True 
6. False - it was in early December 
7. True 
8. True 
9. False - Father Christmas was an English character 
10. True

Lesson 20: Just in Time! 
Warm-Up: 
Describe a situation in which you resolved a situation in the nick 
of time – exactly at the right moment, just before it was too late. 
 
 
 
Activity 1 – Pre-Learn Vocabulary 
bumpy (adj.) = full of bumps (raised, rounded spots that make a surface uneven). In 
this picture, the ground is “bumpy”: 
 
stall (n.) = many public bathrooms have several small compartments, with a toilet 
in each one. These individual compartments are called “stalls.” 
 


elation (n.) = very great happiness/joy. The adjective form is “elated.” 
 
Ex) I was elated when I found out I’d won a free trip to Hawaii. 
peek (v.) = to look quickly; usually either looking at something secret or looking 
from a hidden/secret place  
Ex) Bob cheated on his test – he peeked at his friend’s paper and copied the 
answers. 
startled (adj.) = lightly frightened by a sudden noise or disturbance 
Ex) I was concentrating so hard on my book that it startled me when my 
husband tapped me on the shoulder. 
predicament (n.) = a complicated, difficult, and unpleasant situation 
Ex) Ellen’s in quite a predicament – she slept with three different men last 
month and now she’s pregnant with no idea who the father is. 
 
Activity 2 – Listen for General Ideas 
Speaker: Chris – American  
1. Chris needed to go to the bathroom... 
a. at his new girlfriend's house 
b. during a long road trip 
c. in the middle of a performance

Activity 4 – Listen for Specific Words

Now, this was a single bathroom; there was only one stall. And once I caught my

or that I could ever recall - but that elation would not last very long. Eventually, I 
realized that it was time to go - and I reached for the toilet paper. But much to my 
_____________________, I realized there was no toilet paper. There was not even a

_____________________, this bathroom had not been stocked in quite some time. 
I began going through my options - what can I possibly do here? And then it dawned 
on me that the only thing that I could do was to use my shirt. I 
_____________________ to myself, "I have no other options, but... if I use my shirt, 
what is it going to look like when I walk out of the restaurant without my shirt? 


They'll _____________________ at me; I will never, ever live down the fact that I 
used my shirt." 
But I couldn't sit in there forever - so after a time I took a deep breath and I 
_____________________ began to take my shirt off. Well, before I even had it off, 
there was a knock at the door and I was startled. The _____________________ in my

A _____________________ voice answered, "Hey Chris, it's Frank. Are you okay, 
buddy? You've been in there a while." I replied "Yes, yes, I'm fine - just a few more

_____________________ in a bathroom in Haiti. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Complete Transcript 
I was on a mission trip in the country of Haiti. We had just finished our business in 
the city of Port-au-Prince, and we were about to head out to the city of Port-de-Paix. 
It was a long trip - I believe it took us about 12 hours to go from Port-au-Prince to 
Port-de-Paix. It was a very, very bumpy trip, and we were probably about 15 
minutes into this trip - and of course, that's when it dawned on me that I needed to 
use the restroom. 
Well, after about another fifteen minutes, we were getting further and further away 
from the city, and my need to use the restroom was only growing greater. 
Eventually I got to a point where I knew that I would NOT be able to wait until we 
arrived in Port-de-Paix 12 hours later - so I kept saying that I needed to stop and 
use the restroom. 
My youth coach, Tangi, said "Well, I'm sorry, but there's nothing along the way, and 
we can't afford to stop, we have to keep our schedule.” Well, this just made it all the 
worse - there was no way that I was going to be able to hold this for twelve hours.  
The stars aligned - we came across a restaurant out in the middle of nowhere, and I 
moved out of that van faster than anything I had ever seen. And before I knew it, I 
was in the restaurant, in the bathroom, and on the toilet. 
Now, this was a single bathroom; there was only one stall. And once I caught my 
breath, I was thanking God so hard and so much for providing this miracle. There 
was nothing more precious in my life at that moment, or that I could ever recall - 
but that elation would not last very long. Eventually, I realized that it was time to go 
- and I reached for the toilet paper. But much to my distress, I realized there was no 
toilet paper. There was not even a cardboard tube hinting that there was once toilet 
paper.  
As I said, there was no other stalls in the bathroom, and my mind began to race - 
what was I going to do? What am I going to do? I peeked out of the stall to see if 
there was any hand towels by the sink, and from what I observed, this bathroom 
had not been stocked in quite some time. 
I began going through my options - what can I possibly do here? And then it dawned 
on me that the only thing that I could do was to use my shirt. I thought to myself, "I 
have no other options, but... if I use my shirt, what is it going to look like when I walk 
out of the restaurant without my shirt? They'll laugh at me; I will never, ever live 
down the fact that I used my shirt." 


But I couldn't sit in there forever - so after a time I took a deep breath and I slowly 
began to take my shirt off. Well, before I even had it off, there was a knock at the 
door and I was startled. The panic in my voice probably showed through my 
question: "Who is it?" 
A familiar voice answered, "Hey Chris, it's Frank. Are you okay, buddy? You've been 
in there a while." I replied "Yes, yes, I'm fine - just a few more minutes." I wasn't sure 
if I was ready to tell him about my predicament. Well, he came in and he said, "We 
thought you might need this." I cracked the stall to the bathroom, and from around 
the corner I saw a nice, new, fresh roll of toilet paper! It was even more beautiful 
than the toilet I had found only a short time before.

The phrasal verb “live down” means “to overcome shame from something 
embarrassing over a period of time.” It’s usually used in the expression “I’ll

As the famous playwright George Bernard Shaw once said, "England and America 
are two countries divided by a common language." Although the U.S. and the U.K. 
share a common history and language, the differences in business culture can be 
jarring for a businessperson going from the U.S. to the U.K. or vice versa. What is 
common, accepted, and even celebrated in one place may be seen as awkward or 
even unprofessional in the other. 
For one thing, work attire in the U.K. tends to be more formal than in the U.S. - so 
Americans would be well-advised to dress impeccably when meeting with British 
clients or colleagues. In both countries, it's common to have a few minutes of chit-
chat before getting down to business – though the topics of conversation are likely 
to differ. For Americans, small talk often centers on sports, celebrity gossip, and 
events in the U.S.; whereas the British usually chat about the weather and world 
news. 
Americans tend to be more overtly friendly and welcoming right away, even when 
interacting with perfect strangers - and the British may appear rather standoffish by 
comparison. However, relationships are extremely important in business in the U.K. 
- perhaps even more so than in the U.S. Americans often see "networking" as a 
means to an end - a way to get a promotion or find the best business deal. For Brits, 
on the other hand, the relationships themselves are an important indicator of 
success. Also, Americans tend not to socialize with their coworkers, preferring to 
spend time with their families or other circles of friends - but for Brits, having a 
drink with colleagues after work is a near-universal pastime. 
People who have worked in both countries describe the American business 
environment as far more intense and cutthroat. It is highly competitive and 
Americans tend to want everything done "yesterday." This urgency ends up blurring 
the lines of work-life balance; it is common for American employees to stay at the 
office late and check work e-mail even while at home or on vacation. In the U.K., 
business moves at a slower pace and there is no expectation of 24/7 availability. 
British companies tend to reward employees by offering more time off or more 
flexible hours, whereas American companies pay employees extra for working 
overtime. 
Although the American model puts more pressure on its employees, it is 
advantageous in terms of progress - American companies can innovate, adapt, and 
implement new ideas faster. A strong entrepreneurial spirit pervades the business 
culture of the U.S., whereas the British tend to be more risk-averse. British 


businesses typically seek to preserve the status quo, whereas American businesses 
often aim to disrupt it. One American in the U.K. commented that British businesses 
miss out on opportunities to make more money because they are wary of changing 
their traditional way of doing business. 
One of the deepest-running differences between American and British business 
cultures has to do with hierarchy. The U.K. is one of the oldest monarchies in the 
world, and the focus on social class and seniority is apparent in the business 
environment as well. By contrast, the U.S. has developed a culture with a strong 
emphasis on individual competency and achievement.  
This difference may be striking during meetings. American meetings often appear to 
be free-for-all brainstorming sessions, where employees of various levels of 
seniority freely contribute suggestions, and may even challenge their superiors’ 
ideas. This type of initiative and assertiveness would be out of place at British 
meetings, where there is a clear order and a socially-accepted time and place for 
each person to speak. 
Another result of the American exaltation of the individual is that in the U.S., self-
promotion is an art and skill for getting ahead in one's career. Americans aren't shy 
about highlighting their accomplishments or "selling themselves" in order to land a 
job, close a deal, or get a promotion. In the U.K., however, "tooting your own horn" is 
essentially taboo. Brits prefer to deflect compliments and downplay their own 
accomplishments rather than basking in the spotlight like Americans do. 
Finally, Americans and British have markedly different communication styles - and 
the differences go beyond spelling and pronunciation. Americans tend to be 
forthright with their thoughts and do not hesitate to offer criticism. They are also 
more likely to demonstrate strong emotion, such as enthusiasm, at work. The British 
are more reserved and indirect, often speaking in understatements such as 
describing a complete disaster by saying something like "things didn't quite go 
according to plan." Americans doing business in the U.K. must learn to "read 
between the lines" in order to understand what's really being said.  
When giving directions to their subordinates, British supervisors tend to phrase 
their directives in terms of polite requests or suggestions rather than direct 
commands – and this can certainly cause confusion in day-to-day interaction at 
work. In the U.K., a manager might say, “If you have time, you might want to look 
into that problem” – and an American employee would interpret this as being an 
optional and low-priority task. On the other hand, an American manager saying 
“Please find a solution for that problem right away” might rub a British employee 
the wrong way, as it would sound too blunt and even a little rude. 


Extra Vocabulary 
“a businessperson going from the U.S. to the U.K. or vice versa” 
“Vice versa” means “reversed” or “the other way around” – so in this sentence, 
it’s a short way of saying “going from the U.S. to the U.K. or the U.K. to the U.S.” 
“it's common to have a few minutes of chit-chat before getting down to business” 
“Chit-chat” is informal social conversation, without talking about anything 
serious 
“Americans often see ‘networking’ as a means to an end” 
“A means to an end” is an expression meaning “a way to achieve a different 
objective” – in other words, Americans often use networking in order to reach a 
certain goal, not because they value the activity of networking itself 
“This urgency ends up blurring the lines of work-life balance” 
 
“Blurring the lines” means making the boundaries and limits unclear. 
“American meetings often appear to be free-for-all brainstorming sessions” 
 
“Free-for-all” refers to a disorganized event without rules or order 
“In the U.K., however, ‘tooting your own horn’ is essentially taboo.” 
“Tooting your own horn” is an expression that refers to talking about yourself 
and saying great things about yourself. 
“Brits prefer to deflect compliments and downplay their own accomplishments 
rather than basking in the spotlight like Americans do.” 
To “bask in the spotlight” means to enjoy having everyone’s attention focused on 
you. 
“might rub a British employee the wrong way” 
To “rub someone the wrong way” means to irritate or annoy someone, often 
unintentionally.

Warm-Up: 
Have you ever broken a bone? Describe what happened. (If you

Activity 1 – Pre-Learn Vocabulary

curfews for their kids.

Ex) The lecture was so boring that half the class dozed off.

Ex) I felt excruciating pain when I accidentally slammed my finger in the car 
door. 
writhing in pain = this refers to a movement, when someone is twisting and 
moving around (often while lying down) because of the pain 
Ex) After the explosion in the factory, several victims were lying on the ground, 
writhing in pain. 
subside (v.) = become less intense 
Ex) It’s hard to keep working on a project after the initial excitement has 
subsided.

Complete Transcript 
I want to tell you about a time when I broke a bone. I was probably about 14 or 15 
years old, and my younger brother would've been about 12 or 13. In those days, we 
had a curfew. 
Well, on this particular evening my parents decided to go to bed before my brother 
was home, trusting that he would honor the agreement. Well, after they had gone to 
sleep, I got a call from him saying that he wanted to stay out just a little bit later with 
his friends, and wondered if I would stay up to let him in because he did not have a 
key.  
So being a good big sister, I said that I would. I grabbed my snacks and a blanket 
and I sat on the couch and stayed up watching TV. After a while, it got to be pretty 
late, and I started to doze off.  
Well, it was about the time that I was about ready to fall asleep when I heard a loud 
sound - and I was startled. I thought to myself that it must be my brother getting 
home. So I shot up as fast as I could, kicked my feet off the couch, and instantly felt 
the most excruciating pain I had ever felt in my life.  
I would have screamed so incredibly loud, but I knew I couldn't because I would 
wake my parents and they would discover that my brother was not home. So I lay 
there on the floor writhing in pain with my mouth wide open, just wanting to 
scream but staying silent.  
After a time, the pain subsided, and I hobbled my way over to the front door. And 
when I opened it, wouldn't you know it, he was not there. In fact, he was never there 
- and wouldn't be home for a couple more hours.  
It turns out that I had broken my toe when I'd kicked my feet off the couch and hit 
an exposed part of the wooden frame of the couch. So I eventually did let my 
brother in the house that night, and my parents never discovered that he was home 
late - but I sure did pay the price for that rule being broken as I hobbled around on a 
broken toe for the next couple of weeks.

To "honor" the agreement means to obey it - so, Chris's parents were trusting 
that his brother would obey the rule of being home by a certain time. 
"I grabbed my snacks and a blanket" 
The verb "grab" means to take something with your hand quickly 
"I sure did pay the price for that rule being broken" 
To "pay the price" is an idiomatic expression meaning to experience the 
unpleasant results of doing something.

Lesson 23:  
The Amazing Human Body 
How well do you know your own body? Today’s 
lesson talks about some interesting facts and recent 
discoveries about the human body. 
What do you like and dislike about your body? What 
do you do (or need to do) to stay in good health? 
 
 
 
 
Activity 1 – Pre-Learn Vocabulary 
disparity (n.) – difference, inequality 
Ex) There is a large economic disparity in this country – the richest 5% 
control 90% of the nation’s wealth. 
replenish (v.) – refill or make complete again 
 
Ex) Eating fruit can help you replenish your energy quickly after exercising. 
seep (v.) – when something (like liquid) slowly passes through small openings 
 
Ex) I put a bandage on the injury, but the blood is still seeping through it. 
concrete (n.) – a material used in construction: 
 


cube (n.) – a three-dimensional square shape 
 
Ex) Put a couple of ice cubes in the drinks. 
chronic pain – pain that is continuous and lasts for a long time 
Ex) My dad has chronic back pain after years of sitting at the computer 
with bad posture. 
trigger (v.) – activate, produce a result or reaction 
 
Ex) The door automatically opens when a person triggers the motion sensor. 
antibodies (n.) – proteins in your blood that fight disease 
Ex) Vaccines help your body create antibodies that prevent you from getting 
sick. 
alleviate (v.) – provide relief, especially from pain 
Ex) This is an all-natural medicine that will alleviate a headache within 
twenty minutes. 
cold sore (n.) – a small irritation on your lips or inside your mouth 
 
cognitive (adj.) – related to thought and mental ability 
Ex) All new students at this school must take tests to measure their 
cognitive skills. 
counteract (v.) – have contrary action, action against something 
Ex) We need to protect the environment and counteract the effects of 
human activity on the planet. 
superficial (adj.) – related to the surface; not deep, profound, or complex 
Ex) The company is making some superficial changes to its policy, but 
nothing that will really have a big impact.

Complete Transcript 
The human body is full of intriguing surprises. For example, you are actually tallest 
when you first get out of bed. The height difference between the early morning 
and late night averages around one inch. The reason for this disparity is that while 
you sleep, the spinal fluid between the discs in your vertebral column is 
replenished. As you go about the daily grind the discs compress and the spinal 
fluid seeps out, causing you to lose a bit of height. 
Did you ever stop to consider how vital your skeleton is? Your bones hold you 
together. Without them, we’d be sacks of tissue incapable of bearing our own 
weight or moving around. Human bone is about 75% water, and you may be 
surprised to learn that bone is four times stronger than concrete. A small 3 inch 
cube of bone is capable of supporting nearly 20,000 pounds of weight! The largest 
and strongest bone in your body is your femur (thigh bone). 
There may actually be a scientific basis to the saying that “Laughter is the best 
medicine.” Laughter is proven to reduce chronic pain – partially due to being a 
distraction, but also because it triggers the release of endorphins, chemicals in 
your brain that produce a sense of general well-being.  
Studies have also shown that laughter strengthens your immune system – people 
who laugh more have greater numbers of antibodies; they are thus less susceptible 
to disease and more easily able to recover from illness. Finally, laughter relaxes 
the muscles and the mind, thus alleviating stress and its many detrimental effects 
on the body. 
If you suffer from cold sores, watch out – scientists at Columbia University have 
discovered that people with cold sores were more likely to experience cognitive 
decline, such as the development of Alzheimer’s disease and dementia. The good 
news is that physical activity counteracts this effect and reduces the risk of losing 
your mental abilities. 
Finally, people in developed nations tend to worry about aging. We spend a 
fortune on anti-wrinkle cream and hair-loss treatments. This may seem 
superficial, but a recent study showed that the more wrinkled your skin, the higher 
your risk of suffering from blood pressure related conditions. The solution to both 
these problems isn’t a cosmetic quick fix – instead, maintaining a healthy lifestyle 
and diet, as well as quitting smoking, will give you both a more youthful 
appearance and a healthier heart. 
 


Extra Vocabulary 
"As you go about the daily grind" 
The expression “daily grind” refers to the tasks of daily life and routine, 
which often make you tired 
"laughter strengthens your immune system" 
The immune system is the human body’s system of fighting diseases and 
protecting you from infection 
"thus alleviating stress and its many detrimental effects on the body" 
If something is detrimental, it causes damage or harm 
"the development of Alzheimer’s disease and dementia." 
The word dementia refers to the general loss of mental abilities (memory, 
concentration, judgment) - usually when people get older. Alzheimer's 
disease is a specific form of dementia; it is the most common one. 
"We spend a fortune on anti-wrinkle cream and hair-loss treatments." 
The expression spend a fortune means spend a lot of money, an exaggerated 
amount of money. 
"The solution to both these problems isn’t a cosmetic quick fix" 
A “quick fix” is a fast and easy solution to a problem. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Activity 2 Answers: 
1. You are tallest in the morning. 
2. The text highlights your bones' strength. 
3. There are many health benefits to laughter. 
4. People who suffer from cold sores have a higher risk of cognitive decline. 
5. There is a link between wrinkles and blood pressure-related problems. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Activity 3 Answers: 
1. c 
2. c 
3. b 
4. a 
5. c 
6. b

Warm-Up: 
What are your favorite and least favorite sports to watch on 
TV, and why? Do you have a favorite team/player? 
 
 
 
Activity 1 – Pre-Learn Vocabulary

smaller than a meter. 
offense/defense (n.) = the part of a sports team that tries to score points is the 
offense, and the part of a sports team that tries to stop the other team from scoring 
is the defense. 
tackle (v.) = to grab someone and throw them to the ground, using the weight of 
your own body to do this.  
 
intercept (v.) = get something meant for someone else in the middle of its path. For 
example, if a player throws the ball to a teammate, but someone from the opposing

Complete Transcript 
I want to tell you about my favorite sport, American football. Now this game has a 
lot of rules, and I have been watching it for over ten years - and I still don't 
understand every single rule of the game. But I will try to do my best to explain it to 
you in this brief amount of time. 
I think it's easiest if I compare it to soccer. In soccer you have a field, and at the end 
of the field there are two goals, and each team is trying to protect their own goal 
while trying to put the soccer ball into the other team's goal to score a point. 
Football's the same way. The field is 100 yards long, and at either end there is an 
area known as the end zone. Now there is no goal and nets, but if a player manages 
to cross into the end zone while holding the football, they score a touchdown. In 
football, a touchdown is worth six points.  
The goal of the defense is to prevent the offense from moving down the field - and 
they can do this by tackling, and they can do this by intercepting the football - thus 
making them into the offense. The goal of the offense, aside from trying to score a 
touchdown, is to move the ball at least 10 yards from the last legal spot of the ball. 
For example, the referee will position the football at the 20-yard line. The offense 
must get the ball to at least the 30-yard line. The offense only has four chances to 
move the ball those ten yards. These chances are known as "downs" in football. If 
the offense fails to move the football at least 10 yards in those four tries, then they 
have to turn the ball over to the other team, who then goes on offense.  
One of my favorite teams in football is the Cincinnati Bengals. And the only reason 
why this is, is because I was born in Cincinnati Ohio, so I have to root for the home 
team, right? But as I learned more about football, I started to follow other teams. 
And one of my other favorite teams is the New York Giants. There were a lot of 
players on there that I really liked, and so that's what drew me to them. Most of 
them have left, but the quarterback Eli Manning still plays for the Giants. 
One of the most memorable plays that I can recall happened when the Giants faced 
the New England Patriots in Super Bowl 42. The Super Bowl is the championship 
game for the entire football season. The game was a nail-biter; it was going back and 
forth, back and forth. First the Giants were in the lead, then the Patriots.  


In the last two minutes of the game, the Patriots were ahead 14-10, and the Giants 
had to score if they wanted a chance to win. Remember the set of downs that I told 
you about? Well, the Giants failed to move those ten yards on their first three downs, 
so this was one of those situations where they were going to go for it on fourth 
down because if they did not, they were going to lose the game.  
When the quarterback gets the ball at the beginning of a play, ideally they want to 
throw the ball within three to five seconds. Eli Manning had the ball for over 
fourteen seconds, and was nearly tackled three times. The third time, he managed 
to throw the ball - and it sailed really high into the air. And one of his receivers had 
to leap really high into the air.  
And he caught the ball with one hand and brought it down to his helmet. He 
couldn't use his other hand because one of the Patriots defenders had it, and 
pushed him over while he was still in mid-air. So the Giants player sandwiched the 
football between his hand and his helmet, and hit the ground right on his back. And 
miraculously, he did not drop the ball. And this set the Giants up to win the game 
and the Super Bowl, and become champions for that year.  
It was amazing - I think most people were rooting for the Giants because the 
Patriots had already won three Super Bowls in that decade, and a lot of people 
didn't want to see them win the fourth. And sadly for the Patriots, in addition to 
losing the Super Bowl, they lost their perfect season because they had not lost a 
game up until the Super Bowl. 
 
Want to see the amazing catch that Frank is talking about?  
Watch the 1-minute video here! https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cGe65YgzV_k 
 
 
 
 
 


Extra Vocabulary 
“so I have to root for the home team, right?” 
To “root for” a team means you are a fan of that team, you are cheering for 
that team and hoping it will win. The “home team” is the local team in a 
particular city. 
“The game was a nail-biter; it was going back and forth, back and forth.” 
“A nail-biter” is a situation that makes you full of tension and anxiety, because 
you do not know what the result will be, and it could change at any moment. 
When he says it was “going back and forth” it means that first one team had 
the advantage, then the other team, then the first team again, etc. In other 
words, the two teams were very equally matched, so everyone was nervous to 
see the final result! 
“it sailed really high into the air.” 
The verb “sail” is usually used for a sailboat moving through water, but it can 
also be used to describe something moving effortlessly through the air.

Lesson 25: Wedding Traditions 
Warm-Up: 
What was the last wedding you attended? Describe the 
wedding traditions in your country. 
 
 
 
 
Activity 1 – Pre-Learn Vocabulary 
herbs (n.) = plants with an aroma, used in cooking (for adding flavor) and in 
traditional medicine 
 
Ex) The roasted potatoes are seasoned with a mixture of herbs. 
mob (n.) = a large crowd of people that is disorderly and possibly violent 
 
Ex) An angry mob attacked the man who was suspected of being a rapist. 
alliance (n.) = an association of two countries, groups, or people, formed to advance 
common interests or for strategic reasons 
 
Ex) Many countries formed an alliance to fight against Hitler in World War II. 
sinister (adj.) = suggesting or threatening evil 
Ex) Police are investigating a guy who made some sinister comments online 
about planning a terrorist attack. 
crumbs (n.) = small pieces of baked items (bread, cakes, cookies, etc.) 
 


braided (adj.) = when three ropes or sections of hair are woven 
together, this is called a “braid”: 
betrothal (n.) = an official promise to get married. This is an older 
word; the more modern word is “engagement” (n.) or to say two 
people are “engaged.” 
gemstone (n.) = a precious stone that is usually cut and polished to 
make jewelry. Rubies, sapphires, and emeralds are examples of gemstones. They are 
also called “gems.” 
 
single-handedly (adv.) = doing or achieving something alone, without help. 
 
Ex) In the movie, the hero single-handedly defeats an entire army. 
 
Activity 2 – Listen for General Ideas 
Speaker: Julie – British  
Put the wedding traditions mentioned in the listening in order 
from 1 to 8: 
• bridesmaids & groomsmen (a few of the bride’s and groom’s friends or 
relatives who accompany them during the ceremony) 
• wedding rings 
• the bouquet (a bouquet is a bunch of flowers) 
• the veil (a veil is a piece of fabric that covers a person’s face) 
• throwing the bouquet & garter to guests 
• wedding cake 
• engagement rings 
• white dress 
 


Activity 3 – Listen for Specific Details 
1. The bouquet originated as... 
a. a symbol of fertility 
b. a way to make the bride more beautiful 
c. protection from evil 
2. Wedding guests used to... 
a. fight each other for the chance to dance with the bride 
b. tear off pieces of the bride's clothing 
c. steal decorations during the ceremony 
3. The color white was a symbol of... 
a. femininity 
b. purity 
c. wealth 
4. White dresses were popularized by... 
a. a celebrity's daughter 
b. a princess 
c. a queen 
5. Groomsmen used to help a man... 
a. get enough money to purchase a wife 
b. kidnap a woman to be his wife 
c. prepare for the responsibilities of married life 
6. Wedding cakes used to be... 
a. broken over the bride's head 
b. only for decoration 
c. served before the ceremony 
7. The modern wedding cake was invented by... 
a. a British artist 
b. a French chef 
c. an Italian baker 
8. The tradition of wedding rings originated in ancient... 
a. Egypt 
b. Greece 
c. Rome 


9. Engagement rings became popular after... 
a. people began marrying for love 
b. society's elite began using them 
c. the Pope required a waiting period for marriage 
10. 
The DeBeers company's advertising campaign emphasized 
diamonds'... 
a. beauty 
b. longevity 
c. value 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Activity 4 – Listen for Specific Words 
Today it’s traditional for brides to carry a beautiful bouquet of flowers on their 
wedding day – but originally, the bouquet was _____________________ for its scent, 
not for its beauty. It consisted of fragrant herbs which were believed to ward off evil 
spirits and bad _____________________ by their strong aroma. The herbs were later 
_____________________ by roses and other flowers that are more pleasing to the 
eye. 
In modern weddings, the bride’s bouquet and garter are tossed into the waiting 
hands of guests – and it is said that whoever _____________________ them will be 
the next to marry. This tradition dates back to medieval Europe, where it was 
believed that having a piece of the bride's clothing would bring good luck – and 
sometimes a mob of overeager guests literally _____________________ the clothing 
off the bride! Brides began throwing the bouquet and garter in order to appease the 
guests and prevent them from leaving her dress and _____________________ in 
tatters. 
Wedding dresses weren't always white – in the past, women would simply get 
married in the best dress they _____________________, whatever its color. Many 
people believe that white is used because it represents purity, but it was actually a 
_____________________ of wealth – white fabrics were among the most expensive. 
Queen Victoria was the one who popularized the white wedding dress, wearing one 
for her wedding in 1840.  
What about the wedding veil? In _____________________ marriages, the veil served 
to hide the bride's face from the groom until after the ceremony - to prevent him 
from backing out if he didn’t like what he saw. At the time, marriages were seen as 
_____________________ transactions and ways to form alliances between families – 
and this is why we have the tradition of the bride’s father walking her down the 
aisle, to _____________________ “ownership” of the woman to her husband-to-be. 
In American weddings, the bride is accompanied by several female friends or 
_____________________ who are called bridesmaids. Many centuries ago, the 
bridesmaids were actually dressed nearly identically to the bride – they were 


intended to be decoys that would _____________________ evil spirits (or jealous 
suitors) who might want to ruin the wedding day! 
The tradition of the groomsmen – the male friends/relatives who accompany the 
groom – has a somewhat sinister origin. In sixteenth-century Europe, if there were 
not enough women _____________________ in the local area, men would visit a 
neighboring town and capture a woman to marry. The group of friends would assist 
the groom in kidnapping the woman and fighting off her justifiably 
_____________________ relatives.  
Did you know that originally, the wedding cake was not eaten, but instead 
_____________________ at the bride or broken over her head? It was made of wheat, 
which represented fertility and _____________________, and guests would eat only a 
few crumbs for good luck. Later, a new custom arose in the British Isles: biscuits and 
cakes were stacked on top of each other, and the couple had to 
_____________________ each other over the growing pile. A French chef later 
transformed this _____________________ mound of baked goods into a work of art – 
the iced, multi-tiered wedding cake. 
The tradition of exchanging wedding rings may have originated in ancient Egypt, 
where _____________________ would give each other rings made of braided grasses 
and reeds. We can thank the Romans for the custom of wearing wedding rings on 
the fourth finger of the left hand. They believed that this finger 
_____________________ a vein that led directly to the heart. Although later studies 
of anatomy disproved this notion, the tradition endures to this day. 
As for engagement rings, these became popular in the 13th century, after the Pope 
issued a decree establishing a _____________________ waiting period between a 
betrothal and a wedding. At the time, engagement rings were made with various 
gemstones and inscribed with poems or love messages. The _____________________ 
of the diamond engagement ring today is due to the DeBeers diamond company, 
which single-handedly established a tradition with a very _____________________ 
advertising campaign using the slogan, "A Diamond is Forever." 
 


Complete Transcript 
Today it’s traditional for brides to carry a beautiful bouquet of flowers on their 
wedding day – but originally, the bouquet was assembled for its scent, not for its 
beauty. It consisted of fragrant herbs which were believed to ward off evil spirits 
and bad luck by their strong aroma. The herbs were later replaced by roses and 
other flowers that are more pleasing to the eye. 
In modern weddings, the bride’s bouquet and garter are tossed into the waiting 
hands of guests – and it is said that whoever catches them will be the next to marry. 
This tradition dates back to medieval Europe, where it was believed that having a 
piece of the bride's clothing would bring good luck – and sometimes a mob of 
overeager guests literally tore the clothing off the bride! Brides began throwing the 
bouquet and garter in order to appease the guests and prevent them from leaving 
her dress and dignity in tatters. 
Wedding dresses weren't always white – in the past, women would simply get 
married in the best dress they owned, whatever its color. Many people believe that 
white is used because it represents purity, but it was actually a symbol of wealth – 
white fabrics were among the most expensive. Queen Victoria was the one who 
popularized the white wedding dress, wearing one for her wedding in 1840.  
What about the wedding veil? In arranged marriages, the veil served to hide the 
bride's face from the groom until after the ceremony - to prevent him from backing 
out if he didn’t like what he saw. At the time, marriages were seen as business 
transactions and ways to form alliances between families – and this is why we have 
the tradition of the bride’s father walking her down the aisle, to transfer 
“ownership” of the woman to her husband-to-be. 
In American weddings, the bride is accompanied by several female friends or 
relatives who are called bridesmaids. Many centuries ago, the bridesmaids were 
actually dressed nearly identically to the bride – they were intended to be decoys 
that would distract evil spirits (or jealous suitors) who might want to ruin the 
wedding day! 
The tradition of the groomsmen – the male friends/relatives who accompany the 
groom – has a somewhat sinister origin. In sixteenth-century Europe, if there were 


not enough women available in the local area, men would visit a neighboring town 
and capture a woman to marry. The group of friends would assist the groom in 
kidnapping the woman and fighting off her justifiably angry relatives.  
Did you know that originally, the wedding cake was not eaten, but instead thrown 
at the bride or broken over her head? It was made of wheat, which represented 
fertility and prosperity, and guests would eat only a few crumbs for good luck. 
Later, a new custom arose in the British Isles: biscuits and cakes were stacked on 
top of each other, and the couple had to kiss each other over the growing pile. A 
French chef later transformed this disorganized mound of baked goods into a work 
of art – the iced, multi-tiered wedding cake. 
The tradition of exchanging wedding rings may have originated in ancient Egypt, 
where couples would give each other rings made of braided grasses and reeds. We 
can thank the Romans for the custom of wearing wedding rings on the fourth finger 
of the left hand. They believed that this finger contained a vein that led directly to 
the heart. Although later studies of anatomy disproved this notion, the tradition 
endures to this day. 
As for engagement rings, these became popular in the 13th century, after the Pope 
issued a decree establishing a mandatory waiting period between a betrothal and a 
wedding. At the time, engagement rings were made with various gemstones and 
inscribed with poems or love messages. The predominance of the diamond 
engagement ring today is due to the DeBeers diamond company, which single-
handedly established a tradition with a very successful advertising campaign using 
the slogan, "A Diamond is Forever." 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Extra Vocabulary 
"roses and other flowers that are more pleasing to the eye." 
“Pleasing to the eye” is an expression that means attractive, something that is 
nice to look at 
"leaving her dress and dignity in tatters." 
If something is “in tatters” it means it is torn into pieces. This word is usually 
used for fabric, but it can also be used metaphorically – as in the example of her 
dignity being left “in tatters” (ruined). 
"to prevent him from backing out if he didn’t like what he saw" 
The phrasal verb “back out” means to fail to keep a commitment or promise; to 
reverse your intention. 
"they were intended to be decoys who would distract evil spirits (or jealous 
suitors)" 
A “decoy” is a person or thing used to divert attention from the real target. 
“Suitors” are men who are romantically interested in a woman, and are 
pursuing a relationship with her. 
"the iced, multi-tiered wedding cake." 
The sugary cream that covers cakes and cupcakes is called “icing,” and the 
adjective form is “iced.” A “tier” is a level – so a “multi-tiered” cake means the 
cake has many levels on top of each other. 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Activity 2 Answers 
1. the bouquet 
2. throwing the bouquet & garter to guests 
3. white dress 
4. the veil 
5. bridesmaids & groomsmen 
6. wedding cake 
7. wedding rings 
8. engagement rings 
 
 
 
 
Activity 3 Answers 
1. c 
2. b 
3. c 
4. c 
5. b 
6. a 
7. b 
8. a 
9. c 
10. b

Lesson 26: Study Abroad 
Warm-Up 
What advice would you give a foreign student who is studying 
in your country? 
 
 
 
Activity 1 – Pre-Learn Vocabulary 
taken aback = surprised and confused by something unexpected 
Ex) I was under the impression that Sally loved her job, so I was taken aback by 
her sudden decision to quit. 
take something in stride = accept something unpleasant calmly, without letting it 
have a bad effect on you 
Ex) Jim’s book was rejected by three different publishers, but he’s taking it in 
stride and working to improve the text. 
maple syrup (n.) = a thick, sweet liquid made from the sap of a tree. It is similar to 
honey: 
 


gullible (adj.) = describes someone who is easily deceived, who believes anything 
people tell them 
Ex) I have a friend who is so gullible that she believes everything she reads on 
the internet is true. 
overprotective (adj.) = too protective, excessively worried about protecting 
Ex) My overprotective father wouldn’t let me be alone with a boy at any time 
until I was 18 years old. 
adamant (adj.) = describes someone who is very firm in their opinion, and does not 
change their mind even when other people try to convince them otherwise 
Ex) I don’t think we should buy a house, but my husband is adamant that it’s a 
good investment. 
 
Activity 2 – Listen for General Ideas 
Speaker: Shayna – American 
Circle the FOUR topics Shayna talks about and number them in 
order from 1 to 4: 
• a difference of opinion

b. a nightclub 
c. a soccer game

a. get to know the city 
b. learn the language 
c. understand the cultural differences 
 
 


Activity 4 – Listen for Specific Words 
I studied abroad during my junior year in college, I _____________________ a 
semester in Brazil. And part of the program was a homestay - living with a local host 
family. My host family was a mother, a daughter who was about 12 years old at the

that my host grandmother was actually _____________________ the maple syrup 
into her milk to sweeten it, which is quite a _____________________ way to use it! So 
I got a kick out of that. 


There was another kind of funny moment when they _____________________ me 
some cookies from a jar in the kitchen. Now, I had never seen anyone from my host 
family _____________________ these cookies, but I had seen them give these cookies 
to the dog. So I wasn't sure if they were regular cookies that the dog happened to 
like, or if the family was trying to _____________________ a little prank on me, you 
know, get the gullible American girl to eat a dog biscuit. But I didn't want to be 
_____________________ and so I accepted, and luckily my fears were unfounded – it 
was just a _____________________ cookie. 
Some of the students in my program had real problematic _____________________ 
with their host families, but I didn't have any major problems. The closest we came

and see a soccer game in the local stadium, and this was something I really wanted 
to do.  
But my host mother wouldn't let me go because she said it was too dangerous - that 
there were a lot of _____________________ in the stadium and it wasn't a good place

Portuguese. I had already studied it on my own before the program, so I knew the

I’m very grateful that they _____________________ me into their home for a 
semester, and although we’ve lost _____________________, I have fond memories of 
my host family. 


Complete Transcript 
I studied abroad during my junior year in college, I spent a semester in Brazil. And 
part of the program was a homestay - living with a local host family. My host family 
was a mother, a daughter who was about 12 years old at the time, and a 
grandmother. And they also had a little white dog.  
I remember a bit of culture shock when I first met my host family, because my host 
mother complimented me on my legs and asked if my mother also had big, 
beautiful legs like mine. I was a bit taken aback, because in the States people 
probably wouldn't comment so openly on part of someone's body right upon 
meeting them - but I took it in stride - I thanked her for the compliment and said 
that yes, my mother also has a similar physique. 
One of the things that the study abroad program leaders told us to do beforehand 
was to bring a gift for our host families, something representative of the region 
where we lived. And so I brought a jug of maple syrup, which is typical of the 
northeastern United States. The only problem was that - when I gave it to them, 
they were very appreciative, but then they asked me how exactly the syrup was 
used.  
And I wasn't able to explain it to them, because in the U.S. we usually use maple 
syrup as a topping on pancakes, waffles, or French toast, none of which are common 
breakfast foods in Brazil - nor did I know the words for them in Portuguese. I think 
I ended up saying that the syrup is very sweet, and you could eat it with bread or 
cake. Later I found out that my host grandmother was actually mixing the maple 
syrup into her milk to sweeten it, which is quite a creative way to use it! I got a kick 
out of that. 
There was another kind of funny moment when they offered me some cookies from 
a jar in the kitchen. Now, I had never seen anyone from my host family eating these 


cookies, but I had seen them give these cookies to the dog. So I wasn't sure if they 
were regular cookies that the dog happened to like, or if the family was trying to 
play a little prank on me, you know, get the gullible American girl to eat a dog 
biscuit. But I didn't want to be rude and so I accepted, and luckily my fears were 
unfounded – it was just a normal cookie. 
Some of the students in my program had real problematic relationships with their 
host families, but I didn't have any major problems. The closest we came to a conflict 
was when a bunch of us students were planning to go see a soccer game in the local 
stadium, and this was something I really wanted to do.  
But my host mother wouldn't let me go because she said it was too dangerous - that 
there were a lot of fights in the stadium and it wasn't a good place for a woman to 
be. And I remember thinking this was a bit sexist and that she was being 
overprotective, and I argued a little bit, but she was pretty adamant that I shouldn’t 
go. So I missed out on the game – but in the grand scheme of things, it wasn’t a big 
deal. 
My host family definitely helped me a lot in terms of learning Portuguese. I had 
already studied it on my own before the program, so I knew the basics, but they 
were very patient in speaking in a way that I could understand, and explaining new 
words and expressions that I wasn’t familiar with. I’m very grateful that they 
welcomed me into their home for a semester, and although we’ve lost touch, I have 
fond memories of my host family. 
 
 
 
 


Extra Vocabulary 
"yes, my mother also has a similar physique." 
 
A person’s “physique” is the general size, shape, and proportion of their body 
"pancakes, waffles, or French toast" 
 
These are all breakfast foods eaten in the U.S.: 
 
"I got a kick out of that." 
 
To “get a kick out of” something means to find it amusing or enjoyable 
"my fears were unfounded" 
 
“Unfounded” means “without a basis in fact.” 
“in the grand scheme of things, it wasn’t a big deal.” 
“In the grand scheme of things” is an idiomatic expression that means 
“compared to more general, more important things.”  
"although we’ve lost touch" 
 
“Lost touch” means “lost contact” with each other. 
 
 


Activity 2 Answers 
1. meeting for the first time 
2. giving a gift 
3. a difference of opinion 
4. learning from the family 
 
 
 
Activity 3 Answers 
1. b 
2. b 
3. a 
4. c 
5. b 
6. c 
7. b

lessons.title: Tiny-Houses
lessons.fullText:
Lesson 27: Tiny Houses 
Warm-Up: 
Describe your house or apartment. Do you consider it too big 
or too small for your needs? 
 
 
 
Activity 1 – Pre-Learn Vocabulary 
insatiable (adj.) = impossible to be satisfied. This word is often used to describe 
desire, hunger, appetite, curiosity, etc. 
Ex) Pete has an insatiable appetite – he ate an entire pizza by himself and still 
had room for dessert! 
burden (n.) = a heavy weight (may be an object that is carried, but is often used 
metaphorically to describe a responsibility that is stressful or difficult to endure) 
Ex) Many middle-aged adults shoulder the burden of caring for both their 
young children and their elderly parents. 
proponent (n.) = someone who supports a cause and encourages others to be in 
favor of it, too 
Ex) Proponents of education are pressuring the government to invest more 
funds in the country’s schools. 
cluttered (adj.) = filled with many, disorganized objects 
Ex) My desk is so cluttered that I can’t even find the documents I put here 
yesterday. 
upkeep (n.) = maintenance 
 
Ex) Old cars are inexpensive to buy, but the upkeep costs a fortune! 
amateur (adj.) = a person who does an activity but not professionally; can also be 
used to describe someone with little experience 
 
Ex) My brother works as an accountant; he’s also an amateur photographer. 


crowdfunding (n.) = when there is an online campaign to get donations from many 
people in order to complete a project. Crowdfunding campaigns are often spread 
through social media. 
Ex) She couldn’t pay her medical bills, so she started a crowdfunding campaign 
to raise money for her treatment. 
loft (n.) = an upper level in a building which has one 
side open to the lower floor. It is often used for 
sleeping or storage. 
salvage (v.) = to save objects from being thrown 
away or destroyed 
Ex) The fire destroyed our entire house; I was 
only able to salvage a few family photos. 
devastating (adj.) = describes something that causes serious destruction. May be 
literal destruction (as in a war or natural disaster) or emotional destruction. 
 
Ex) The devastating force of the hurricane winds ripped the roof off the church.  
Ex) She received the devastating news that her children had died in the 
accident. 
 
Activity 2 – Listen for General Ideas 
Speaker: Aiden – British 
Put the topics in order from 1 to 4: 
• a personal story 
• benefits of a tiny house 
• factors behind the movement 
• how tiny houses are built 
 
 


Activity 3 – Listen for Specific Details 
True or False? 
1. The average American home size has increased 30% in recent years. 
2. Buying bigger and bigger houses contributed to the financial crisis. 
3. Tiny houses often have structures that can be used with two purposes. 
4. Tiny houses cost an average of $5,000 to $10,000. 
5. Residents of tiny houses sometimes complain that they don't have enough 
space for their things. 
6. The tiny house movement exists only in the U.S. 
7. You don't need a permit to build a mobile tiny house. 
8. Sicily's father was proud to see her complete the house. 
9. Sicily's tiny house is powered by solar energy. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Activity 4 – Listen for Specific Words 
Owning a home is part of the "American dream" - but the size of that dream has 
_____________________ over the years. The average American single-family home is 
now 40% larger than it was three decades ago - despite a _____________________ in 
the size of the average family.  
This insatiable desire for more space per person has led to some disastrous 
_____________________ - families take out ambitious mortgages that will take 
fifteen to thirty years to pay off, thus locking themselves into a 
_____________________ of debt that may be impossible to escape. In fact, banks' 
extension of easy credit to borrowers who could not afford the repayments was one 
of the _____________________ of the 2007 economic crisis. 
The wake-up call of the recession, coupled with the realization that a growing 
_____________________ and consumption of environmental resources are very real 
problems, are both factors that have led to the rise of the tiny house movement - a 
group of individuals and families who pare down their _____________________ and 
live in miniature homes measuring just 100-400 square feet. To optimize space, tiny 
houses make use of dual-purpose features, such as drawers built into the side of a 
_____________________.  
The financial burden of building and owning a tiny house is certainly much lighter. 
Tiny houses cost an average of twenty to fifty thousand dollars, as compared to 
nearly _____________________ hundred thousand for a traditional house. 
Proponents of the movement say they enjoy the _____________________ of mind 
that comes from living in a simpler, less cluttered environment. Less time and 
mental energy needs to be spent on upkeep, and residents of tiny houses can focus 
more on the things that matter most, such as family, _____________________, travel, 
and leisure. The tiny house movement has attracted a wide range of people in the 
U.S., and it is now gaining increased _____________________ coverage and an 
international following as well. 
Tiny houses are often self-built, offering the chance to stamp your 
_____________________ on your home's architecture, layout and design. They can 
be built from scratch or using a trailer as a shell, and can be completed in as little as 


two months. Tiny houses are often built on _____________________ so they can be 
‘transplanted’ to a new location at will - and they do not require a building permit. 
In response to safety concerns about amateur builders, _____________________ 
teaching safe construction techniques have sprung up across the nation.  
Recently in the news was 13-year-old Sicily Kolbeck, who started building her own 
tiny house together with her father. In the middle of the project, he died tragically in 
a _____________________ accident – but with the help of local ‘tiny house’ 
enthusiasts and a crowdfunding campaign, Sicily managed to finish her very own 
dark blue tiny house. It is made entirely of _____________________ and salvaged 
materials and includes a bathroom, kitchen, loft, and solar panels.  
Sicily says she wanted to not only _____________________ people to live more 
simply, but also to show that it is possible to get right back up and keep going even 
after life deals you a devastating blow. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Complete Transcript 
Owning a home is part of the "American dream" - but the size of that dream has 
expanded over the years. The average American single-family home is now 40% 
larger than it was three decades ago - despite a decrease in the size of the average 
family.  
This insatiable desire for more space per person has led to some disastrous 
consequences - families take out ambitious mortgages that will take fifteen to thirty 
years to pay off, thus locking themselves into a cycle of debt that may be impossible 
to escape. In fact, banks' extension of easy credit to borrowers who could not afford 
the repayments was one of the causes of the 2007 economic crisis. 
The wake-up call of the recession, coupled with the realization that a growing 
population and consumption of environmental resources are very real problems, 
are both factors that have led to the rise of the tiny house movement - a group of 
individuals and families who pare down their possessions and live in miniature 
homes measuring just 100-400 square feet. To optimize space, tiny houses make use 
of dual-purpose features, such as drawers built into the side of a staircase.  
The financial burden of building and owning a tiny house is certainly much lighter. 
Tiny houses cost an average of twenty to fifty thousand dollars, as compared to 
nearly three hundred thousand for a traditional house. Proponents of the 
movement say they enjoy the peace of mind that comes from living in a simpler, less 
cluttered environment. Less time and mental energy needs to be spent on upkeep, 
and residents of tiny houses can focus more on the things that matter most, such as 
family, hobbies, travel, and leisure. The tiny house movement has attracted a wide 
range of people in the U.S., and it is now gaining increased media coverage and an 
international following as well. 
Tiny houses are often self-built, offering the chance to stamp your identity on your 
home's architecture, layout and design. They can be built from scratch or using a 
trailer as a shell, and can be completed in as little as two months. Tiny houses are 
often built on wheels so they can be ‘transplanted’ to a new location at will - and 
they do not require a building permit. In response to safety concerns about amateur 


builders, workshops teaching safe construction techniques have sprung up across 
the nation.  
Recently in the news was 13-year-old Sicily Kolbeck, who started building her own 
tiny house together with her father. In the middle of the project, he died tragically in 
a car accident – but with the help of local tiny house enthusiasts and a 
crowdfunding campaign, Sicily managed to finish her very own dark blue tiny house. 
It is made entirely of donated and salvaged materials and includes a bathroom, 
kitchen, loft, and solar panels.  
Sicily says she wanted to not only inspire people to live more simply, but also to 
show that it is possible to get right back up and keep going even after life deals you a 
devastating blow. 
 
 
Extra Vocabulary 
“families take out ambitious mortgages that will take fifteen to thirty years to pay 
off” 
A mortgage is a loan from the bank specifically for the purposes of buying a 
house. 
“The wake-up call of the recession” 
 
A wake-up call is a sign or warning that alerts you to a dangerous situation. 
"The tiny house movement has attracted a wide range of people in the U.S." 
This means it has attracted a lot of people who are of many different types, 
social classes, etc. 
"They can be built from scratch" 
To make something from scratch means to make it from the beginning, from 
the very basic ingredients. We usually talk about making food from scratch. 
"even after life deals you a devastating blow." 
A “blow” is another word for a violent impact, and “deals” in this context 
means “gives.”   


Activity 2 Answers 
 
1. factors behind the movement 
2. benefits of a tiny house 
3. how tiny houses are built 
4. a personal story 
 
 
Activity 3 Answers 
1. False 
2. True 
3. True 
4. False 
5. False 
6. False 
7. True 
8. False 
9. True
