lessons.title: Vacation
lessons.fullText:
Lesson 38: Vacation 
Warm-Up: 
Describe a vacation you’ve taken in the past – or a dream 
vacation you would like to take in the future! 
 
 
 
 
Activity 1 – Pre-Learn Vocabulary 
a ton of = this is an informal way to say “a lot of”; a large number or amount 
 
Ex) A ton of people were trying to get the celebrity’s autograph. 
thrilling (adj.) = very exciting 
Ex) This book tells the thrilling story of one man’s escape from a war-torn 
country. 
wetlands (n.) = a low area where the ground is saturated with water – also called a 
“marsh” or a “swamp” 
 
packed (adj.) = very crowded or full to capacity 
Ex) The movie theater was packed on the opening night for the film. There 
wasn’t a single empty seat. 
 


overbook (v.) = when an airline, hotel, or event takes more reservations than it has 
places available 
Ex) The hotel was overbooked, so they transferred our reservation to another 
hotel in a different neighborhood. 
voucher (n.) = a certificate that allows you to claim some credit or benefit 
 
Ex) The government gives meal vouchers to low-income families. 
bankrupt (adj.) = when a person or company is in complete financial ruin, having 
no more money and not able to pay its debts 
Ex) The business went bankrupt thanks to the CEO’s terrible financial decisions.   
 
Activity 2 – Listen for General Ideas 
Speaker: Amy – American  
1. This story focuses on the trip to... 
a. California 
b. Colorado 
c. Florida 
2. Who went on the trip with Amy’s family? 
a. her best friend's family 
b. her father's colleagues 
c. her brother’s friend 
3. Amy talks mostly about... 
a. the flight 
b. the weather 
c. the sights 
 
 


Activity 3 – Listen for Specific Details 
True or False? 
1. Amy’s family went on vacation every year. 
2. They have some relatives in California. 
3. Amy has known her best friend for a very long time. 
4. They usually spend New Year's in Florida. 
5. Amy remembers seeing alligators in Florida. 
6. The flight was on December 30. 
7. Amy’s father had to argue to get seats on the plane. 
8. Nobody agreed to the offer for a free round-trip ticket. 
9. The families volunteered to get three tickets per person. 
10. The airline gave them food before the later flight. 
11. The weather was bad in Florida on that day. 
12. They used the free tickets after Amy’s father went bankrupt. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Activity 4 – Listen for Specific Words 
My family didn't take a ton of vacations when I was _____________________ up, but 
my parents would usually save up and take us all on a big trip once every two or 
three years. One time we went to the state of Colorado for a camping trip, and we 
went up one of the highest _____________________ in the U.S. And another year we 
went to California, where my parents had lived at one point – and we still have some 
_____________________ there. And then there was the time that we went to Florida 
for New Year's. 
We went together with my best friend's family. My parents and her parents have 
known each other for more than _____________________ years, and so she and I 
have been close pretty much ever since we were born. And our families always 
spend New Year's together - usually at their _____________________ house, which 
isn't terribly thrilling in the winter - but one year our fathers decided to take us all 
down _____________________. 
Now, I don't remember much about what we actually did in Florida, except for 
taking a _____________________ ride through the wetlands and seeing the 
alligators. But the _____________________ of getting there was kinda funny. 
Our flight was on December 26th, so the day after Christmas, and the airport was 
packed with holiday _____________________. When we got to the gate we found out 
that the airline had horribly overbooked the flight, and there weren’t enough 
_____________________ for everyone. So people were arguing with and even 
shouting at the _____________________ … it was a mess. 
Luckily, the eight of us – my family and my friend’s family – were able to 
_____________________ the plane and get our seats. After the plane was full, the 
_____________________ made an announcement saying that if anyone would 


voluntarily give up their seats and take a later flight, they would get a voucher for a 
free round-trip ticket anywhere in the _____________________. Nobody moved a 
muscle.  
A couple minutes later, they made another _____________________ offering TWO 
free round-trip tickets – and still, nobody budged. When they upped the offer to 
three free tickets, my dad and my friend’s dad started eyeing each other and 
_____________________ if we should take them up on it. And when they offered four 
free tickets per person, it was just too good to _____________________ up – and we 
all sprang up out of our seats. 
So they put us on another flight, which wasn’t as _____________________, a few 
hours later – and they even gave us extra snacks while we were waiting. We weren’t 
even _____________________ out on anything, because it happened to be raining in 
Florida on that day.  
But there’s one last twist to the story. We had _____________________ a grand total 
of 32 free round-trip tickets, and of course we were excited to use them. Well, sadly, 
not long after we got _____________________, that airline went bankrupt and the 
tickets became worthless. I think my dad hung onto the vouchers for a couple of 
years just on the off-chance that another airline would take them, but no such 
_____________________.  
 
 
 
 


Complete Transcript 
My family didn't take a ton of vacations when I was growing up, but my parents 
would usually save up and take us all on a big trip once every two or three years. 
One time we went to the state of Colorado for a camping trip, and we went up one of 
the highest mountains in the U.S. And another year we went to California, where 
my parents had lived at one point – and we still have some relatives there. And then 
there was the time that we went to Florida for New Year's. 
We went together with my best friend's family. My parents and her parents have 
known each other for more than thirty years, and so she and I have been close 
pretty much ever since we were born. And our families always spend New Year's 
together - usually at their beach house, which isn't terribly thrilling in the winter - 
but one year our fathers decided to take us all down south. 
Now, I don't remember much about what we actually did in Florida, except for 
taking a boat ride through the wetlands and seeing the alligators. But the process of 
getting there was kinda funny. 
Our flight was on December 26th, so the day after Christmas, and the airport was 
packed with holiday travelers. When we got to the gate we found out that the 
airline had horribly overbooked the flight, and there weren’t enough seats for 
everyone. So people were arguing with and even shouting at the attendants … it 
was a mess. 
Luckily, the eight of us – my family and my friend’s family – were able to board the 
plane and get our seats. After the plane was full, the pilot made an announcement 
saying that if anyone would voluntarily give up their seats and take a later flight, 
they would get a voucher for a free round-trip ticket anywhere in the country. 
Nobody moved a muscle.  


A couple minutes later, they made another announcement offering TWO free 
round-trip tickets – and still, nobody budged. When they upped the offer to three 
free tickets, my dad and my friend’s dad started eyeing each other and wondering if 
we should take them up on it. And when they offered four free tickets per person, it 
was just too good to pass up – and we all sprang up out of our seats. 
So they put us on another flight, which wasn’t as full, a few hours later – and they 
even gave us extra snacks while we were waiting. We weren’t even missing out on 
anything, because it happened to be raining in Florida on that day.  
But there’s one last twist to the story. We had won a grand total of 32 free round-
trip tickets, and of course we were excited to use them. Well, sadly, not long after we 
got back, that airline went bankrupt and the tickets became worthless. I think my 
dad hung onto the vouchers for a couple of years just on the off-chance that another 
airline would take them, but no such luck.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Extra Vocabulary 
"Nobody moved a muscle." 
This is an expression that means nobody moved at all, even a little bit. 
Everyone stayed perfectly still. 
"my dad and my friend’s dad started eyeing each other and wondering if we should 
take them up on it." 
The word “eye” can be used as a verb meaning to look at or watch closely, 
often with some intention – in this case the intention was to communicate 
through eye contact. To “take someone up on” an invitation or offer means to 
accept it, say “yes” to it. 
"when they offered four free tickets per person, it was just too good to pass up – 
and we all sprang up out of our seats." 
If you “pass up” an opportunity, it means you let it go by without accepting it. 
The verb “spring” (or “sprang” in the past) means to go up with energy. 
"But there’s one last twist to the story." 
 
A “twist” in a story means a change in direction, an unexpected change. 
"the tickets became worthless." 
 
“Worthless” means without value. 
"I think my dad hung onto the vouchers for a couple of years just on the off-chance 
that another airline would take them" 
To “hang onto” something means to keep it, and the word “off-chance” is an 
informal expression for a very, very small chance.

lessons.title: Junk-Food
lessons.fullText:
Lesson 39: Junk Food 
Warm-Up: 
What are some of your “guilty pleasures” – junk foods 
that you know are bad for you, but you really enjoy? 
Have you ever tried to modify your diet? What were 
the results? 
 
 
 
 
Activity 1 – Pre-Learn Vocabulary 
willpower (n.) = the strength of your desire and ability to determine your actions 
Ex) It takes a lot of willpower to practice the piano every day for five hours – 
but that’s what you need to do if you want to become a professional. 
binge (n./v.) = consume an excessive amount of something – usually food or drink 
 
Ex) My kids binged on popcorn and candy at the circus. 
starve (v.) = suffer from lack of food. The expression “I’m starving” is also used as 
an exaggerated way to say you are extremely hungry. 
 
Ex) The abandoned dog was injured and starving; it hadn’t eaten in weeks. 
tactic (n.) = a practical strategy or method for achieving a goal 
 
Ex) Making a budget is one tactic for helping you manage your money better.  
crave (v.) = have an intense desire for something 
Ex) Although I’d already eaten dinner, I was craving some pizza, so I ordered 
one for delivery. 
dampen (v.) = reduce, make less intense 
Ex) The news that some of the activities had been canceled dampened our 
enthusiasm for the event. 


overindulge (v.) = eat more than the appropriate amount 
Ex) My mother’s homemade cookies are so delicious, it’s hard not to 
overindulge!  
melt (v.) = when something solid becomes liquid 
 
Ex) She left her glass of lemonade out in the sun, and all the ice cubes melted. 
myriad (n./adj.) = many and various 
Ex) The cultural center has myriad classes in dance, photography, art, and 
theater. 
misleading (adj.) = deceptive, leading someone to the wrong conclusion 
Ex) The wording on the advertisement is misleading – it implies that the 
service is free when it’s actually not. 
serving (n.) = when talking about food, one “serving” is a single portion, the normal 
amount for eating. (Another word for this is a “helping.”) 
 
Ex) I liked the mashed potatoes so much that I ordered another serving. 
 
Activity 2 – Listen for General Ideas 
Speaker: Nate – Australia 
This audio focuses on... (one correct answer) 
a. effects of an unhealthy diet on the body 
b. how companies encourage us to eat more 
c. government regulation of the food market 
d. the ingredients inside some popular snacks 
e. tips for cutting down on junk food 
 
 
 


Activity 3 – Listen for Specific Details 
True or False? 
1. The science experiment mentioned was done with monkeys. 
2. The experiment lasted several months. 
3. The animals were willing to endure pain to eat junk food. 
4. The "bliss point" is the exact amount of food that satisfies you. 
5. One soda company tested 61 different formulas. 
6. The average American drinks 1,000 cans of soda per year. 
7. The way chips feel in your mouth influence you to keep eating. 
8. Too much salt and fat causes high blood pressure. 
9. Sugar is added to eighty percent of American food. 
10. The term "processed sugar" is required to appear on the label. 
11. "Light" foods always have fewer calories. 
12. The average serving size on the label is often inaccurate. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Activity 4 – Listen for Specific Words 
If you just can’t seem to cut down on cookies, _____________________, and soda, it 
may not be entirely due to a lack of willpower on your part. The disturbing 
_____________________ is that food companies have intentionally designed their 
products to be addictive. 
The addictive _____________________ of junk food are illustrated in an experiment 
in which rats were allowed to binge on high-fat foods for several weeks. The junk 
food was then taken away and healthier food was _____________________ - but the 
rats preferred to starve themselves rather than eat the healthier food. Researchers 
then offered the rats a choice between eating junk food, which was 
_____________________ with an electric shock, and regular food - and the rats still 
preferred the unhealthy option, regardless of the pain. 
Here are three examples of the sneaky tactics that are used to 
_____________________ our taste buds and keep us hooked on food that is harmful 
to our health. One is something called the "bliss point" - the specific 
_____________________ of flavors that maximizes your pleasure while still leaving 
you craving more. If there is too little taste, you won’t enjoy the food – but if the 
flavor is too _____________________, it will satisfy you and dampen your desire to 
overindulge. 
One brand of soda _____________________ 61 formulas with subtle differences and 
tested them with thousands of people until it gathered enough 
_____________________ to determine the perfect blend of ingredients - perfect for 
turning you into an addict, that is. The _____________________ soda drinkers can 
consume upwards of 1,000 cans a year, resulting in million-dollar profits for the 
company.  


Chips and other puffy snacks take _____________________ of a phenomenon called 
"vanishing caloric density" - because they are light and easily melt in your mouth, 
your brain _____________________ there's no calories in them - and you can keep 
eating them forever. Of course, the chips are loaded with salt and fat, which 
_____________________ to high blood pressure and myriad health problems. 
Finally, misleading advertising and labeling _____________________ can confuse 
even people who are trying to be health- _____________________. Eighty percent of 
food sold in the United States – even food that is billed as “healthy” such as whole 
wheat _____________________ – has added sugar. But you might never know it, 
because there are fifty-six different terms for _____________________ sugar. So if 
you don’t see the word “sugar” on the label, it may be masquerading under a 
different name. 
Sometimes the _____________________ advertises a positive point to convince us 
we’re making a healthy choice – conveniently omitting the fact that unhealthy 
ingredients lurk within. The label "all _____________________ " may be slapped on a 
product that is high in sodium, and the word "light" may mean the food has less fat, 
but the same number of calories. Many "fat free" foods are loaded with 
_____________________, and snacks that claim to be "made with real fruit" may only 
include a tiny percentage of it.  
Perhaps the most insidious trick has to do with the _____________________ serving 
size - to make the product look lower in calories, the nutritional information on the 
label is based on an _____________________ small serving. Most people eat two or 
three times that amount in one sitting – so the next time you’re looking at a label, 
remember to _____________________ the calories for the serving size listed.  
 
 


Complete Transcript 
If you just can’t seem to cut down on cookies, chips, and soda, it may not be entirely 
due to a lack of willpower on your part. The disturbing truth is that food companies 
have intentionally designed their products to be addictive. 
The addictive properties of junk food are illustrated in an experiment in which rats 
were allowed to binge on high-fat foods for several weeks. The junk food was then 
taken away and healthier food was given - but the rats preferred to starve 
themselves rather than eat the healthier food. Researchers then offered the rats a 
choice between eating junk food, which was punished with an electric shock, and 
regular food - and the rats still preferred the unhealthy option, regardless of the 
pain. 
Here are three examples of the sneaky tactics that are used to manipulate our taste 
buds and keep us hooked on food that is harmful to our health. One is something 
called the "bliss point" - the specific balance of flavors that maximizes your pleasure 
while still leaving you craving more. If there is too little taste, you won’t enjoy the 
food – but if the flavor is too strong, it will satisfy you and dampen your desire to 
overindulge. 
One brand of soda prepared 61 formulas with subtle differences and tested them 
with thousands of people until it gathered enough data to determine the perfect 
blend of ingredients - perfect for turning you into an addict, that is. The heaviest 
soda drinkers can consume upwards of 1,000 cans a year, resulting in million-dollar 
profits for the company.  
Chips and other puffy snacks take advantage of a phenomenon called "vanishing 
caloric density" - because they are light and easily melt in your mouth, your brain 
assumes there's no calories in them - and you can keep eating them forever. Of 


course, the chips are loaded with salt and fat, which contribute to high blood 
pressure and myriad health problems. 
Finally, misleading advertising and labeling practices can confuse even people who 
are trying to be health- conscious. Eighty percent of food sold in the United States – 
even food that is billed as “healthy” such as whole wheat bread – has added sugar. 
But you might never know it, because there are fifty-six different terms for 
processed sugar. So if you don’t see the word “sugar” on the label, it may be 
masquerading under a different name. 
Sometimes the packaging advertises a positive point to convince us we’re making a 
healthy choice – conveniently omitting the fact that unhealthy ingredients lurk 
within. The label "all natural " may be slapped on a product that is high in sodium, 
and the word "light" may mean the food has less fat, but the same number of 
calories. Many "fat free" foods are loaded with sugar, and snacks that claim to be 
"made with real fruit" may only include a tiny percentage of it.  
Perhaps the most insidious trick has to do with the standard serving size - to make 
the product look lower in calories, the nutritional information on the label is based 
on an unrealistically small serving. Most people eat two or three times that amount 
in one sitting – so the next time you’re looking at a label, remember to double the 
calories for the serving size listed.  
 
 
 
 
 
 


Extra Vocabulary 
"Here are three examples of the sneaky tactics that are used to manipulate our 
taste buds" 
The word “sneaky” means deceptive. Your “taste buds” are the sensors on 
your tongue that detect the sensation of different flavors. 
"Chips and other puffy snacks" 
 
Something that is “puffy” is light and full of air. 
"the chips are loaded with salt and fat" 
 
The word “loaded” in this context means the chips have a LOT of salt and fat. 
"even food that is billed as “healthy” such as whole wheat bread" 
The word “billed” in this context means advertised or presented in a certain 
way. 
"So if you don’t see the word “sugar” on the label, it may be masquerading under a 
different name." 
The verb “masquerade” means to be disguised, to pretend to be something 
you’re not. 
"conveniently omitting the fact that unhealthy ingredients lurk within" 
To “omit” something means NOT to include or mention it. The verb “lurk” 
means to exist in a hidden and threatening way. 
"Perhaps the most insidious trick has to do with the standard serving size" 
The adjective “insidious” means working to cause harm in a way that is not 
obvious. 
"Most people eat two or three times that amount in one sitting" 
If you do something “in one sitting,” it means you do it during one period of 
time without stopping. 
 
 
 


Activity 2 Answer: 
b. how companies encourage us to eat more

Lesson 40: Abilities 
Warm-Up: 
What’s one thing you’re good at, and one thing you’re not very 
good at? 
 
 
 
Activity 1 – Pre-Learn Vocabulary 
tryout (n.) = a test or trial period to see if an athlete or performer is good enough to 
be accepted. (For the performing arts, this can also be called an “audition”) 
Ex) Our dance group is looking for some new members; we’re holding a tryout 
on Friday. 
regular (n.) = if you describe a person as a “regular”, it means he/she frequently 
goes to that place or participates in that activity. 
 
Ex) The bartender knows all the regulars at the bar by name. 
edible (adj.) = describes something that can be eaten 
 
Ex) Do you know which of these plants are edible? 
hassle (n.) = a difficult/annoying task 
Ex) Trying to register on the website was a hassle – I had to fill out five 
different forms. 
lid (n.) = a removable cover for a box, pot, or other container 
 


hit-or-miss (adj.) = sometimes succeeding, sometimes not 
Ex) He thinks he’s funny, but his jokes are hit-or-miss. Some of them are 
hilarious and others, not so much. 
dud (n.) = something that is disappointingly ineffective or unsuccessful 
Ex) The advertising campaign was a dud. It didn’t bring in any new clients. 
batch (n.) = a group or set of similar objects, often all coming at the same time 
 
Ex) If you want more pancakes, I can make another batch.

ended up getting really good. We even organized a tournament, and my team got all 
the way to the _____________________ – which we lost by just a couple of points. 
But I really loved those volleyball games and I looked forward to them every day. 
I’ve also been into martial arts for many years, and I’ve gotten to train with some of 
the best _____________________ in the world. Two sports I’ve only tried a few times 
but would love to do more of are skiing and rock climbing. The first time I went 
climbing, I thought I was already in pretty good _____________________, but boy, 
did I feel it the next day! It must have worked muscles I don’t 
_____________________ use. 
As for what I’m not good at, the first thing that _____________________ to mind is 
cooking. I mean, I’m not terrible at it, I can make things that are edible – but I’m not a 
_____________________. I guess I’ve just never taken the time to learn. But it’s 
always felt like a hassle to me, and I get especially _____________________ when I 
have to cook for other people.  


One time I was gonna make _____________________ for a group of friends, and I 
decided to make brisket, which is beef that’s slow-cooked with lots of onions and 
garlic. My mom told me it’s virtually _____________________ to mess up, the only 
thing I had to remember was to always keep the pot _____________________ and 
never remove the lid. 
Well, I decided to test the recipe a _____________________ before the dinner, and I 
followed my mother’s instructions religiously. However, the pot I was using had a lid 
that didn’t _____________________ properly, and all the water inside evaporated, so 
the meat ended up _____________________ to the bottom and burning. I couldn’t 
bring myself to eat it, and I think I ended up giving it to the dog. 
Nowadays I can make a _____________________ brisket, but chicken and fish have 
been sorta hit-or-miss. I think some of the recipes I find on the internet are duds, 
because sometimes even when I _____________________ them perfectly, it still 
doesn’t turn out right. Luckily I married a man who knows his way around the 
_____________________; he’s a much better cook than me. But I’ve been 
experimenting with baking _____________________, and I made two successful 
batches of cookies – so maybe there’s hope for me yet! 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Complete Transcript 
One thing I’d say I’m good at is sports. I’ve been involved in some type of sport 
pretty much ever since I was six. I played soccer for about ten years, and I was 
captain of my high school team. My parents wouldn’t let me play in any of the really 
competitive soccer leagues, though, because they wanted me to focus on my 
studies. When I went to college, I played terribly during tryouts and didn’t make the 
team – so that’s when I started getting more into volleyball instead. 
There was a group of students and teachers that would play twice a day – at 
lunchtime, and again in the evenings. It started out as a casual pickup game, but we 
played so much that all the regulars ended up getting really good. We even 
organized a tournament, and my team got all the way to the finals – which we lost 
by just a couple of points. But I really loved those volleyball games and I looked 
forward to them every day. 
I’ve also been into martial arts for many years, and I’ve gotten to train with some of 
the best masters in the world. Two sports I’ve only tried a few times but would love 
to do more of are skiing and rock climbing. The first time I went climbing, I thought I 
was already in pretty good shape, but boy, did I feel it the next day! It must have 
worked muscles I don’t normally use. 
As for what I’m not good at, the first thing that comes to mind is cooking. I mean, I’m 
not terrible at it, I can make things that are edible – but I’m not a natural. I guess 
I’ve just never taken the time to learn. But it’s always felt like a hassle to me, and I 
get especially anxious when I have to cook for other people.  
One time I was gonna make dinner for a group of friends, and I decided to make 
brisket, which is beef that’s slow-cooked with lots of onions and garlic. My mom told 
me it’s virtually impossible to mess up, the only thing I had to remember was to 
always keep the pot covered and never remove the lid. 


Well, I decided to test the recipe a week before the dinner, and I followed my 
mother’s instructions religiously. However, the pot I was using had a lid that didn’t 
fit properly, and all the water inside evaporated, so the meat ended up sticking to 
the bottom and burning. I couldn’t bring myself to eat it, and I think I ended up 
giving it to the dog. 
Nowadays I can make a decent brisket, but chicken and fish have been sorta hit-or-
miss. I think some of the recipes I find on the internet are duds, because sometimes 
even when I follow them perfectly, it still doesn’t turn out right. Luckily I married a 
man who knows his way around the kitchen; he’s a much better cook than me. But 
I’ve been experimenting with baking lately, and I made two successful batches of 
cookies – so maybe there’s hope for me yet! 
 
Extra Vocabulary 
“It started out as a casual pickup game” 
A “pickup game” is one that is informal, with the participation of anyone who 
is available. 
“I followed my mother’s instructions religiously” 
If you do something “religiously,” it doesn’t necessarily have to do with 
religion – in this context, it means to do it while being very careful to follow 
the rules. 
“I couldn’t bring myself to eat it” 
The expression “I couldn’t bring myself” to do something means I tried or I 
wanted to, but I wasn’t able to force myself to do it. 
 
 
 
 


Activity 2 Answers 
She mentions these sports: 
Soccer, volleyball, martial arts, skiing, rock climbing 
 
 
 
 
She mentions these foods: 
Beef, chicken, fish, cookies

lessons.title: World-Changing-Mistakes
lessons.fullText:
Lesson 41: World-Changing Mistakes 
Warm-Up: 
In your opinion, what are some of the major historical 
events that have changed the world? What about the 
significant moments that have changed your country? 
 
 
Activity 1 – Pre-Learn Vocabulary 
sloppy (adj.) = disorganized and careless 
Ex) This report is very sloppy. Not only are the main points unclear, but there 
are a number of grammatical mistakes. 
mold (n.) = a fungus 
 
Ex) That bread was four weeks old; I threw it out because it was moldy. 
 
(Moldy is the adjective that describes something that has mold on it). 
countless (adj.) = very many, too many to count 
 
Ex) I love looking at the countless stars in the night sky. 
limbs (n.) = arms and legs 
 
Ex) You should stretch your limbs before and after exercising. 
nascent (adj.) = just beginning to come into existence, newly created 
Ex) The school’s nascent reading program has already been extremely 
successful in its first month. 
morale (n.) = the general confidence and cheerfulness of a group of people 
Ex) Employees don’t produce their best work when morale is low. 


thwart (v.) = prevent something from happening 
 
Ex) The heavy rain thwarted our plans to go on a boat trip. 
impending (adj.) = describes something that will happen very soon 
Ex) Shoppers rushed to the supermarkets to buy groceries before the 
impending snowstorm. 
engrossed (adj.) = if someone is “engrossed” in an activity, it means that activity is 
occupying all of their attention; the person is not easily distracted 
Ex) He was so engrossed in the book that I had to call his name three times 
before he looked up. 
boost (v.) = increase (usually increasing something positive) 
 
Ex) Installing this program can boost your computer’s speed by 50%. 
 
Activity 2 – Listen for the General Idea 
Speaker: Paul – British  
1. The first incident is related to... 
a. business 
b. medicine 
c. psychology 
2. The second incident is related to... 
a. a natural disaster 
b. a political revolution 
c. a tragic accident 
 
 


Activity 3 – Listen for Specific Details 
1. The average life expectancy 100 years ago was... 
a. 30 years 
b. 40 years 
c. 50 years 
2. Sir Alexander Fleming is from... 
a. England 
b. Ireland 
c. Scotland 
3. Fleming was away from the laboratory because… 
a. he was sick 
b. he was on vacation 
c. he was visiting a colleague 
4. Where did he discover the mold? 
a. in an unwashed dish 
b. on a snack he had left on the bench 
c. under the laboratory sink 
5. Penicillin played a decisive role in... 
a. curing sick children 
b. preventing the spread of disease 
c. saving people in a war 
6. Life expectancy in developed countries is now... 
a. 70 years 
b. 80 years 
c. 90 years 
7. Which place was controlled by the British at the end of 1776? 
a. New York City 
b. Pennsylvania 


c. Washington 
8. The revolutionary army crossed the river... 
a. during a snowstorm 
b. during the night 
c. in a surprising location 
9. What was the British colonel doing when he received the note? 
a. drinking alcohol 
b. playing a game 
c. reading a book 
10. 
Which was NOT a reason that the victory was significant? 
a. it encouraged the revolutionaries 
b. more people signed up for the army 
c. the Americans captured a lot of prisoners 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Activity 4 – Listen for Specific Words 
Mistake #1 
One of the most important discoveries in medical history actually resulted from 
sloppy laboratory _____________________. A century ago, the average life 
expectancy was only around 50 years. Bacterial infections in cuts or burns were 
_____________________ 80% of the time, and staggering numbers of people used to 
die from tuberculosis and pneumonia. 
In the year 1928, Sir Alexander Fleming, a Scottish researcher, was searching for a 
“wonder drug” that would be able to _____________________ all diseases. No one 
had managed to discover or _____________________ a chemical that would kill 
bacteria without harming the human body. 
One morning in September, Fleming, who was often described as 
_____________________ in the laboratory, returned from a family vacation. Before 
leaving, he had pushed a number of unwashed Petri dishes to the side of the bench 
so that a _____________________ could use the workspace while he was away.  
When Fleming got back, he was about to _____________________ the contaminated 
dishes when he noticed that a blue-green mold _____________________ in one of 
them had killed the bacteria around it. Fleming was then able to 
_____________________ the anti-bacterial substance from the mold and develop it 
for medicinal use – and that substance is known today as penicillin, the world’s most 
widely-used antibiotic. 
During World War II, penicillin saved countless lives and _____________________ 
the amputation of many limbs. By the time the war ended, U.S. companies were 
_____________________ 650 billion units of penicillin a month. In the decades 
following this lucky discovery, life expectancy in _____________________ countries 
has shot up to around 80 years.  
 
 


Mistake #2 
By the end of the year 1776, the American Revolutionary War was in full swing – but 
things were not going well for the nascent United States. The British had 
_____________________ New York City and pushed the revolutionaries southwest 
into New Jersey and Pennsylvania. Morale among the revolutionaries was low, 
_____________________ were limited, and the harsh winter weather didn’t help. 
George Washington, the commander-in-chief of the American army, planned a 
Christmas _____________________ on the British troops encamped in Trenton, New 
Jersey. Between December 25th and 26th, while the British soldiers were 
_____________________, Washington and his men crossed the Delaware River and 
marched towards Trenton. With the element of _____________________ on their 
side, Washington’s army won a decisive victory, capturing weapons, supplies, and 
about a thousand _____________________. 
However, this triumph was almost thwarted by a spy who actually observed 
Washington and his _____________________ near the river. He then sent a note to 
warn Colonel Johann Rall, _____________________ of the British troops at Trenton, 
of the impending attack. 
But the British soldiers were in a festive _____________________ due to the 
Christmas holiday, and Colonel Rall was playing poker (or, according to some 
versions of the story, _____________________) when he received the message. 
Engrossed in the game, he stuffed the note into his _____________________ pocket 
without reading it. Rall was later killed during the battle, with the unopened note 
still in his pocket.  
If the British had been _____________________ for the attack, Washington (who 
would later become the United States’ first president) as well as other key 
_____________________ could have been killed. The victory at Trenton, though 
relatively small in scale, was seen as a _____________________ point in the war 
because it boosted morale and increased enlistments in the revolutionary army.  


The United States eventually won the war and _____________________ 
independence from British control. If not for Colonel Rall’s poker (or chess) game, 
it’s possible that the United States would not exist as an independent 
_____________________ today. 
 
Complete Transcript 
Mistake #1 
One of the most important discoveries in medical history actually resulted from 
sloppy laboratory practices. A century ago, the average life expectancy was only 
around 50 years. Bacterial infections in cuts or burns were fatal 80% of the time, 
and staggering numbers of people used to die from tuberculosis and pneumonia. 
In the year 1928, Sir Alexander Fleming, a Scottish researcher, was searching for a 
“wonder drug” that would be able to cure all diseases. No one had managed to 
discover or invent a chemical that would kill bacteria without harming the human 
body. 
One morning in September, Fleming, who was often described as careless in the 
laboratory, returned from a family vacation. Before leaving, he had pushed a 
number of unwashed Petri dishes to the side of the bench so that a colleague could 
use the workspace while he was away.  
When Fleming got back, he was about to clean the contaminated dishes when he 
noticed that a blue-green mold growing in one of them had killed the bacteria 
around it. Fleming was then able to isolate the anti-bacterial substance from the 
mold and develop it for medicinal use – and that substance is known today as 
penicillin, the world’s most widely-used antibiotic. 
During World War II, penicillin saved countless lives and prevented the amputation 
of many limbs. By the time the war ended, U.S. companies were manufacturing 650 


billion units of penicillin a month. In the decades following this lucky discovery, life 
expectancy in developed countries has shot up to around 80 years.  
Mistake #2 
By the end of the year 1776, the American Revolutionary War was in full swing – but 
things were not going well for the nascent United States. The British had captured 
New York City and pushed the revolutionaries southwest into New Jersey and 
Pennsylvania. Morale among the revolutionaries was low, supplies were limited, 
and the harsh winter weather didn’t help. 
George Washington, the commander-in-chief of the American army, planned a 
Christmas attack on the British troops encamped in Trenton, New Jersey. Between 
December 25th and 26th, while the British soldiers were sleeping, Washington and 
his men crossed the Delaware River and marched towards Trenton. With the 
element of surprise on their side, Washington’s army won a decisive victory, 
capturing weapons, supplies, and about a thousand prisoners. 
However, this triumph was almost thwarted by a spy who actually observed 
Washington and his soldiers near the river. He then sent a note to warn Colonel 
Johann Rall, commander of the British troops at Trenton, of the impending attack. 
But the British soldiers were in a festive mood due to the Christmas holiday, and 
Colonel Rall was playing poker (or, according to some versions of the story, chess) 
when he received the message. Engrossed in the game, he stuffed the note into his 
coat pocket without reading it. Rall was later killed during the battle, with the 
unopened note still in his pocket.  
If the British had been prepared for the attack, Washington (who would later 
become the United States’ first president) as well as other key leaders could have 
been killed. The victory at Trenton, though relatively small in scale, was seen as a 
turning point in the war because it boosted morale and increased enlistments in the 
revolutionary army.  


The United States eventually won the war and gained independence from British 
control. If not for Colonel Rall’s poker (or chess) game, it’s possible that the United 
States would not exist as an independent nation today. 
 
Extra Vocabulary 
"staggering numbers of people used to die from tuberculosis and pneumonia" 
The word “staggering” means astonishing or surprising – often in a negative 
way. 
"the American Revolutionary War was in full swing" 
 
The expression “in full swing” means in an intense period of activity. 
"the harsh winter weather didn’t help" 
 
The word “harsh” means severe and unpleasant.  
 
Activity 2 Answers 
1. b 
2. b 
Activity 3 Answers 
1. c 
2. c 
3. b 
4. a 
5. c 
6. b 
7. a 
8. b 
9. b 
10. c

lessons.title: Volunteer-Work
lessons.fullText:
Lesson 42: Volunteer Work 
Warm-Up: 
Have you ever done volunteer work? What type of volunteer 
work would you like to do? 
 
 
 
Activity 1 – Pre-Learn Vocabulary 
rambunctious (adj.) = full of energy and disorderly (often used to describe kids) 
Ex) It’s hard to focus on reading a book when you have a rambunctious five-
year-old in the house.  
semblance (n.) = an appearance 
Ex) She tried to present some semblance of regret, but I could tell that she 
wasn’t really sorry for what she did. 
bluff (n./v.) = when you pretend confidently that you are going to do something, in 
order to trick another person into reacting in a certain way (this word comes from 
card games, when people try to deceive their opponents by acting as if they have 
better cards than they really do) 
Ex) The enemy claims they have a nuclear bomb, but we believe they’re bluffing 
in order to force us to give in to their demands. 
disruptive (adj.) = causing disturbance to the normal status 
Ex) There’s construction work being done on the building next door to our 
office, and the noise is really disruptive to our concentration. 
stunned (adj.) = filled with strong and sudden surprise (may be positive or 
negative) 
Ex) We were stunned when the six-year-old was able to multiply large numbers 
in her head. She’s a math genius! 


anticlimactic (adj.) = describes something (usually a final result or what should be 
a high point) that is disappointing when compared with the expectations for it 
Ex) The end of the movie was anticlimactic. The mystery was so intriguing, but 
the solution to it wasn’t very satisfying. 
obsessed (adj.) = if someone is “obsessed with” something, it means that thing 
occupies their thoughts excessively 
Ex) My teenage daughter is obsessed with boys. Sometimes it seems like getting 
a boyfriend is the only thing she talks about!  
 
 
Activity 2 – Listen for the General Idea 
Speaker: Amanda – British  
In this audio, Amanda... (one correct answer) 
a. describes her personal experience volunteering 
b. gives suggestions for involving children in volunteer work 
c. explains how volunteer work benefits communities 
d. offers tips for finding volunteer opportunities 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Activity 3 – Listen for Specific Details 
True or False? 
1. Amanda was teaching martial arts. 
2. The class was of 10-12-year-olds. 
3. The kids behaved better when Amanda was nice. 
4. Amanda had to handle the class alone. 
5. She had to cancel the class several times. 
6. The most effective activities were group tasks. 
7. The game involved two teams. 
8. Teams could lose points for bad behavior. 
9. Each team had finished with thirteen points. 
10. The kids were disappointed with the results. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Activity 4 – Listen for Specific Words 
I once volunteered to give martial arts classes to kids at a _____________________ 
school in a poor neighborhood. I had about twenty students ages six to nine, and I 
know kids that age are _____________________ rambunctious, but these kids were 
just completely out of control. If I looked away for two _____________________, they 
would be climbing onto tables, hitting each other, knocking over 
_____________________, and otherwise doing everything except for the activity I 
had asked them to do.  
It seemed like there was nothing I could do to maintain _____________________ or 
even any semblance of order whatsoever. I tried being nice, and the kids just 
_____________________ me. I tried being firmer and stricter, and that would work 
for a few minutes but then they would start bouncing off the walls again. Even with 
another teacher _____________________ me, we just could not control the class. I 
even had to threaten to cancel it if they didn’t _____________________ – and then I 
had to follow through on that so they could see I wasn’t bluffing. 
Well, after a lot of trial and _____________________, I found that the best activities 
for holding their attention were ones that involved everybody working 
_____________________ as a group. One day we were doing a game that involved 
three teams, and I came up with a points system where the teams could gain points 
for following _____________________ and doing the movements I asked for, or lose 
points if they disobeyed or were disruptive. I asked the other teacher to 
_____________________ score on a piece of paper, and so many points were won 
and lost that by the time the game finished I had no clue which team was in the 
_____________________. 
The other teacher gave me the scorecard, and when I tallied up all the points I saw 
that all three teams had tied with eight points each. I _____________________ I’d 


need a tiebreaker, but I had no time to think of one – all the kids were looking at me 
and waiting for me to _____________________ the results. So I said that team 1 had 
eight points, team 2 had eight points, and team 3 also had eight points.  
Well, the room just exploded in _____________________. The kids all started jumping 
up and down and hugging and congratulating each other. There was a huge 
_____________________ on every face. I was stunned by their reaction. I had been 
expecting them to be kinda disappointed since the result was pretty anticlimactic. I 
mean, I had really played up the whole “_____________________” aspect, and in the 
end there was no clear winner. But the kids showed me that maybe it’s more 
important to _____________________ things all together than to be obsessed with 
winning. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Complete Transcript 
I once volunteered to give martial arts classes to kids at a public school in a poor 
neighborhood. I had about twenty students ages six to nine, and I know kids that age 
are naturally rambunctious, but these kids were just completely out of control. If I 
looked away for two seconds, they would be climbing onto tables, hitting each 
other, knocking over chairs, and otherwise doing everything except for the activity I 
had asked them to do.  
It seemed like there was nothing I could do to maintain discipline or even any 
semblance of order whatsoever. I tried being nice, and the kids just ignored me. I 
tried being firmer and stricter, and that would work for a few minutes but then they 
would start bouncing off the walls again. Even with another teacher helping me, we 
just could not control the class. I even had to threaten to cancel it if they didn’t 
behave – and then I had to follow through on that so they could see I wasn’t 
bluffing. 
Well, after a lot of trial and error, I found that the best activities for holding their 
attention were ones that involved everybody working together as a group. One day 
we were doing a game that involved three teams, and I came up with a points 
system where the teams could gain points for following instructions and doing the 
movements I asked for, or lose points if they disobeyed or were disruptive. I asked 
the other teacher to keep score on a piece of paper, and so many points were won 
and lost that by the time the game finished I had no clue which team was in the lead. 
The other teacher gave me the scorecard, and when I tallied up all the points I saw 
that all three teams had tied with eight points each. I realized I’d need a tiebreaker, 
but I had no time to think of one – all the kids were looking at me and waiting for me 
to announce the results. So I said that team 1 had eight points, team 2 had eight 
points, and team 3 also had eight points.  


Well, the room just exploded in joy. The kids all started jumping up and down and 
hugging and congratulating each other. There was a huge smile on every face. I was 
stunned by their reaction. I had been expecting them to be kinda disappointed since 
the result was pretty anticlimactic. I mean, I had really played up the whole 
“competition” aspect, and in the end there was no clear winner. But the kids 
showed me that maybe it’s more important to achieve things all together than to be 
obsessed with winning. 
 
Extra Vocabulary 
"they would start bouncing off the walls again" 
The expression “bouncing off the walls” is used to describe it when kids are 
running around and acting crazy in an indoor space. 
"I had no clue which team was in the lead." 
 
“I had no clue” means “I had absolutely no idea.” 
"when I tallied up all the points" 
The phrasal verb “tally up” is another way to say “add up” various numbers to 
discover the final total. 
"I realized I’d need a tiebreaker" 
A “tiebreaker” is an extra activity that can break a tie (such as 1-1 or 3-3) and 
determine the winner and loser. 
"I had really played up the whole “competition” aspect" 
 
The phrasal verb “played up” means “emphasized.” 
 
 
 
 
 


Activity 2 Answer: 
a. describes her personal experience volunteering 
 
Activity 3 Answers 
1. True 
2. False 
3. False 
4. False 
5. True 
6. True 
7. False 
8. True 
9. False 
10. False

lessons.fullText:
Lesson 43: Utopia 
 
Warm-Up: 
The word “utopia” refers to a society that is 
perfect politically, socially, economically, 
and culturally. If you could design a 
“perfect” society, what would it be like? 
 
 
 
Activity 1 – Pre-Learn Vocabulary 
flawless (adj.) = perfect, without errors, mistakes, or problems 
 
Ex) Her piano performance was flawless – she didn’t play a single wrong note. 
virtue (n.) = a morally excellent quality 
Ex) Sam never gives up when there’s a problem to be solved. Persistence is one 
of his strongest virtues.  
tyrant (n.) = an oppressive ruler who exercises power in a cruel manner 
Ex) The tyrant ordered his entire family to be killed so that nobody could 
challenge his claim to power. 
hereditary (adj.) = passing from parents to children 
Ex) I have a chronic illness, but luckily it’s not hereditary – so I don’t have to 
worry about passing it on to my future kids.  
destabilize (v.) = make something unstable, disturb it from its state of balance 
 
Ex) If anything destabilizes the nuclear reactor, there’s a risk of explosion. 
able-bodied (adj.) = people in good health, without any disabilities 


Ex) It makes me mad when I see able-bodied people park their cars in the 
handicapped parking spots. 
inevitable (adj.) = cannot be avoided 
 
Ex) Making mistakes is inevitable when you’re learning something new. 
brainwash (v.) = do psychological programming/manipulation so that a person 
adopts a specific set of beliefs 
Ex) The people in that religious cult are brainwashed into believing the end of 
the world is near.  
squash (v.) = suppress, eliminate 
Ex) I wanted to be a doctor, but my parents squashed my ambition by 
constantly telling me I wasn’t smart enough. 
sinister (adj.) = suggesting or threatening evil 
Ex) Jane’s ex-husband has sent her several sinister notes, and she’s afraid he 
might turn violent. 
overthrow (v.) = when the citizens of a society remove the existing 
rulers/authorities from power 
Ex) After ten years of fighting, the population finally managed to overthrow 
the dictator and establish a new government. 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Activity 2 – Listen for the General Idea 
Speaker: Peter – American 
Put two characteristics into the categories of each 
utopia/dystopia described: 
• artificial production of children 
• completely free sexual relations 
• equality and simplicity 
• gold, silver, bronze, and iron classes 
• individuality strongly repressed 
• slavery permitted 
Plato’s utopia 
More’s utopia 
Huxley’s dystopia 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Activity 3 – Listen for Specific Details 
True or False? 
1. The word "utopia" has a double meaning. 
2. The first documented description of utopia comes from the Bible. 
3. In Plato's utopia, the “bronze” class consists of soldiers. 
4. Plato viewed art and poetry as the highest virtue in his utopian society. 
5. In Plato's society, the state would categorize people into their social classes. 
6. In Sir Thomas More’s utopia, goods are communally owned. 
7. Only slaves are required to work in More's ideal society. 
8. The citizens of More's utopia do not participate in wars. 
9. Marriage is very important in More's ideal society. 
10. Dystopias have some of the same features as utopias. 
11. Aldous Huxley's novel shows the dangers of scientific progress. 
12. The common element in almost all dystopian stories is that the hero escapes 
the dysfunctional society in the end. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Activity 4 – Listen for Specific Words 
The term “utopia” is a play on words – derived from Greek, it can mean both “a good 
place” as well as “no place” – perhaps implying that a completely flawless society is 
_____________________ to attain. 
The first documented description of a utopia is from Plato’s Republic, written in 380 
B.C. Plato, a Greek _____________________, described a society in which the people 
were organized into four socioeconomic classes.  
The “golden class” would be the _____________________ and decision-makers, 
possessing great wisdom and receiving training to become “philosopher-kings” who 
would ensure the fair distribution of _____________________. The main

The term “utopia” is a play on words – derived from Greek, it can mean both “a good 
place” as well as “no place” – perhaps implying that a completely flawless society is 
impossible to attain. 
The first documented description of a utopia is from Plato’s Republic, written in 380 
B.C. Plato, a Greek philosopher, described a society in which the people were 
organized into four socioeconomic classes.  
The “golden class” would be the rulers and decision-makers, possessing great 
wisdom and receiving training to become “philosopher-kings” who would ensure 
the fair distribution of resources. The main characteristic of the “silver class” would 
be courage, as they would be soldiers responsible for defending the state as well as 
enforcing laws. The “bronze and iron” classes would be the producers, with the 
primary virtue of moderation, so as to work for the good of the collective rather 
than accumulating individual wealth. 
Plato argued that the union of these three virtues – wisdom, courage, and 
moderation – would result in the ideal society. To prevent the members of the gold 
and silver classes from becoming tyrants, they would not be allowed to own private 
property; instead, they would be entirely dependent on the bronze and iron classes 
for their sustenance. Also, membership in the classes would not be hereditary; each 
child would be evaluated by the state and assigned according to their character and 
skills. 
In Plato’s utopia, artists and poets were prohibited by law, as he believed that the 
introduction of new ideas could destabilize society. Marriage and family would not 
exist; instead, sexual relations would be completely free and children would not 
know who their parents were.

his version, there is no private ownership whatsoever; goods are kept in 


warehouses and people request what they need. Equality and uniformity are central 
themes – clothes and houses are simple, and the use of cosmetics and jewelry is 
discouraged. Meals are eaten in community, and everyone receives the same food. 
In More’s utopia, there are no lawyers because the laws of society are simple enough 
for everyone to understand. Agriculture is the primary profession, and every able-

slaves being criminals or foreigners captured in wars. Although the citizens of 
More’s utopia are pacifists, they recognize that war is sometimes inevitable – but 
they try to capture rather than kill their enemies.

esteem, with punishments for having sex outside of marriage. Divorce is permitted 
only in very special circumstances, and considerable priority is placed on the 
educated selection of a lifelong mate. 
While some writers imagine utopian societies, others speculate about dystopias – 
societies containing fundamental and frightening flaws. Dystopias are often 
invented to highlight current, real-world issues which, if left unchecked, could 
develop into nightmares for humanity. 
Interestingly, the strict laws and social structures found in utopias also figure 
prominently in many dystopias. In Aldous Huxley’s novel Brave New World, children 
are produced artificially through cloning, and the population is genetically 
engineered to produce different social classes. Each person is then brainwashed 
from birth to fulfill their specific role in society, and any hint of individuality is 
squashed.  
Whereas in most utopias the role of science and technology is positive, Huxley 
shows us a sinister side to scientific progress. Modern movies like The Matrix are 
also dystopias, projecting the possible dangers of technology and the power of mass 
psychological manipulation. 
Almost all dystopias share one common feature – a group of rebels or members of a 
secret society who are not under the control of the system, and often work actively 
to overthrow it. This reflects the truth that no matter how heavy-handed the 
oppression, the human spirit is unconquerable.

I think the main problem with my country is that it has become weak both as a 
nation and as a people. First, I would work domestically to improve the lives of the 
citizens. One cannot expect a nation to be strong if the citizens are weak. 
What I mean by this is that I believe the mentality of the American citizen today is 
that they should be able to have everything without working hard for it. Now, this 
does not cover every citizen - blanket statements never do. But I think a majority of 
people are starting to believe that they should get something for nothing.  
This is evident in systems like welfare, food stamps, Medicare and Medicaid - these 
systems are being exploited more and more every day, to the point where they're 
not only bankrupting the country, but they are making slaves out of people who do 
not even realize that they have become addicted to these programs. I would keep 
these programs in place, but I would make them as unattractive as possible to be 
on. Far too many people get into these programs and never get out. 
I have a little bit of experience with this, as my family is on food stamps right now. 
What started out as extra money every month to help us get to a better place has 
become something that we now would be in serious trouble if we did not have. In 
order for us to move beyond food stamps, not only would we have to make what we 
get in food stamps every month, we would have to make even more than that to 
make it worth our while. If I go out and expend effort only to make what I was 
getting for free - most people would not bother. 
Another thing that has happened with food stamps is that they are no longer food 
stamps; they are credit cards, which makes them less embarrassing to use. Now, I do 
not want to embarrass people; I am not saying that I would take those things away - 
but I don't want to incentivize people to accept that this is their lot in life. I want 
these programs to be safety nets and not ways of living. 
Another way that I would help empower the people is to reduce the scope of 
government; I believe in a limited government. This nation was founded upon the 
idea of freedom of people, and the federal government has expanded far beyond its 
powers than it was ever intended to be. Most of the power of the government was 
supposed to be tied up in state and local governments.  


The reason this is, is that the closer the people are to the government, the more 
accountable they can hold their government in both the laws that they pass and the 
way that they spend their money. The farther away you are from the money that is 
being spent, the less likely that you are to do anything about it. It doesn't seem real 
to you. 
Another thing that I would do is to put term limits on every elected official. There 
have been people in the government for 40 and 50 years of their life. They have 
grown stagnant and complacent; they are more focused on gaining power than they 
are in making the lives of average Americans better.  
By placing term limits on these people, they will not be focused on their long-term 
gain of power, but instead focused on what they can do for their terms that they 
have been elected for, which will be limited to one or two - just like the president of 
the United States. He can only be elected for a total of two terms. 
I believe these are some of the major points that I would address as president. I 
would have a hard sell, because there would be a lot of short-term pain, and people 
are always operating in the here and now more than in the future - and that's why I 
believe my country has run into these problems. So I don't know that I would be a 
popular president in the present.  
But if I were elected and was able to implement these programs and these changes, 
I believe that future generations would look to me and applaud me and thank me 
for having the courage to do what so many government officials do not have the 
courage to do. So thanks for listening to me, and if I ever run for president, I hope I 
have your vote!

Someone's "lot in life" means their general circumstances and condition 
 
in life, which was destined for them to have.

accept it. The expression "in the here and now" means in the present 
moment; it's often used to describe when people are focusing only on current 
things and not thinking about the future.

Complete Transcript 
The world of medicine continues to make innovative leaps forward in identifying, 
treating, and even preventing certain diseases and conditions. Here are three 
developments that show great promise. 
 
Every year, about 1,000 children in the U.S. are born with only half of a functioning 
heart – a condition known as hypoplastic left heart syndrome. It is the result of a 
genetic anomaly that causes the left ventricle of the heart, which is the main 
pumping system, to be underdeveloped and unable to function at all.  
 
Without surgery, it is fatal – and even with surgery to redirect the blood flow into 
the right ventricle, over 30% of children born with this condition do not survive into 
adulthood. The problem is that the right side of the heart normally handles only the 
low-pressure pumping into the lungs, and it cannot sustain both the high- and low-
pressure systems for many years.  
 
However, researchers at Boston Children’s Hospital have devised a new method that 
takes advantage of the body’s natural healing processes. In a series of four 
surgeries, they meticulously route the blood flow into the left ventricle rather than 
away from it. This actually helps the left side of the heart grow and develop, and 
twelve of the patients in the experimental study ended up with two fully-functional 
ventricles. It does require longer hospitalization, but the long-term benefits 
definitely outweigh this drawback. 
 
Another new technique has the potential to revolutionize the treatment of cancer, 
which kills eight million people per year worldwide. While we still do not have a 
viable cure for cancer, there is a new type of genetic testing that can make 


treatment more specific and personalized. It tests a tumor sample for 280 genetic 
mutations that may affect the tumor’s growth.  
 
The results can identify medications that may work, even though they are not 
typically used for a particular type of cancer. For example, a woman with pancreatic 
cancer was tested with this new method, and her tumor was found to respond to a 
medication that is used primarily in breast cancer patients. These surprising 
connections lead to treatments that can target each patient’s tumor more 
effectively. 
 
A third trend in medicine aims to put health care literally in the palm of your hand – 
using a smartphone. There is one device that connects your smartphone to 
electrodes, records your heart rhythm and stores the data for a doctor to analyze. 
Although not as powerful as an electrocardiogram (EKG) machine, the smartphone 
gadget is still sufficient for routine testing or general heart rate monitoring.  
 
Another app helps patients track moles for signs of skin cancer, and one company is 
developing an iPhone-based instrument that will allow parents to check the inside 
of their children’s ears for infections and send photos to a pediatrician. Perhaps the 
biggest impact of this technology is its potential to reduce health care costs and
